Tanuki: Pon's Summer will steal your heart, too

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I don't remember much about my coverage from Steam Next Fest this past June, but I remember my time playing the demo for Tanuki: Pon's Summer very vividly. I mean, how could I forget? I rail-grinded around an adorable Japanese town as a potbellied Tanuki on a BMX bike doing tricks in the air while delivering packages for residents. The little demo that could is now a full-fledged game with "Very Positive" Steam reviews, and although it pains me to say it probably won't take home any Game of the Year awards in December, it deserves its time in the spotlight even with an incredibly unfortunate release right smack-dab between Zelda: Ocarina of Time's remake and GTA 6. Naturally, its director agrees.

Talking to GamesIndustry.biz, Denkiworks co-founder and game director Liam Edwards acknowledges the disadvantages of releasing a niche indie game in-between two of the biggest games of the year, one of which is considered to be the largest entertainment product ever made in terms of scope and budget. "What I don't think we could have accounted for was Nintendo shadow-dropping the release of Ocarina of Time [on November 5]," says Edwards. "There's probably a fair bit more of an overlap with Switch 2 Zelda players for Tanuki than there would be for GTA 6."

Still, the team at Denkiworks is taking it all in stride, basking calmly in Zelda and GTA's shadow, and hoping Tanuki will get caught in our collective headlights at some point. He argues that Tanuki: Pon's Summer could be the "lovely little underdog" waiting for you when you're doing playing the two November behemoths.

"I don't think you can account for what others do even in such a crazy period," he says. "You know your game's strengths best, and you have to continue to promote it as such. We've worked with the publishing team [Critical Reflex] to find places that Pon would shine and have seen a lot of success with that.

"Hopefully, in the long term, word-of-mouth and the fact that it's been well-received means a long tail; when players are done with Zelda and GTA 6, they'll be looking for what's next and might think, 'Oh, yeah! There was that BMXing Tanuki game!'"

Tanuki: Pon's Summer is out now on PlayStation, Xbox, Nintendo Switch 1 and 2, and PC.

#3612. Is it time to retire Dragon Quest as a series? Chrono Trigger composer Yasunori Mitsuda thinks it might be

Chrono Trigger composer Yasunori Mitsuda thinks it may be time for Square Enix to retire Dragon Quest, while reflecting on the direction of the popular RPG series after Akira Toriyama's death. The mangaka, whose art and distinct style were foundational to Chrono Trigger and Chrono Cross - and are still used in Dragon Quest to this day - died in 2024 at the age of 68.

Today, speaking via a blog post on his personal website (hat tip, Power Up Gaming), Mitsuda - a colleague of Toriyama's back in the SNES/Chrono Trigger days - suggested that maybe it's time to retire the franchise in favour of something new. This was all triggered by the announcement of Dragon Quest RPG: The Island of the Demon Tree and the Guided Island, an iOS and Android game that uses art that is very reminiscent of Toriyama's.

"The Toriyama-style illustrations for [Dragon Quest RPG] have become a hot topic, but I feel that this direction is not good for the artist, Toriyama Akira fans, and even for the late Toriyama Akira himself," said Mitsuda. "As a personal opinion, since it's impossible to create anything truly new no matter how hard you try, I feel that the Dragon Quest series should be brought to an end for now, and [Dragon Quest creator, Yuji Horii] should create a new RPG. (There have been many remakes already.)"

Horii himself seems undeterred: with the new mobile game's announcement last week, he noted that the goal of his new project is to "capture that unmistakable Dragon Quest feeling" that comes with "exploring towns, meeting new allies, gearing up and steadily growing stronger". As Mitsuda calls for the series to retire, and for something new to take its place, Horii is keen to bring "the same classic adventure" to your smartphone.

"What's important is that the game provides dreams, hope, and experiences that can only be had through games to the younger generation of children who will play it in the future," concluded Mitsuda. "But every time I see topics like this, I realise just how wonderful Dragon Quest is and how it has captivated so many people."

It's unlikely Square Enix is going to want to drop the series, of course: the Dragon Quest 3 HD-2D Remake exceeded Square Enix's (in)famously lofty expectations, and as the company aggressively pursues its multiplatform strategy, it's hard to imagine a world in which it's going to want to move away from a series that routinely pulls in millions of sales.

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week after details about multiple extramarital affairs came to light, will not be allowed to un-resign, says the company.

"On November 12th, our board of directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO, and board member," said Nvidia chairman Harvey C. Jones during a regularly scheduled investors call today. "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

Huang was open to the idea of returning: After AI enthusiasts and tech CEOs including Tim Sweeney and Elon Musk rallied around the former CEO, he said that he would return to Nvidia if the board came calling.

"I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," Huang said in a statement to press. "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."

At the same time, reports circulated that the Nvidia board was not interested in having him back, which Jones has now stated in no unclear terms.

The Nvidia chairman went on to recap the actions Nvidia has taken since Huang's resignation, which include putting CFO Colette Kress in charge as interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement and establishing a "national security and export control oversight committee."

The affair Huang admitted to, before reports of others came out, was with a suspected Chinese spy. China has denied the accusation of espionage.

#3610. A Look Inside the Scorpion Ball, Princess Grace Kelly’s Scorpio-Themed 40th Birthday Party

Grace Kelly always had a deep passion for astrology. Born on November 12, 1929, she was a Scorpio, and very proud of it. To celebrate her 40th birthday on November 15, 1969, the Princess of Monaco organized a party themed by her astrological sign, resulting in the extravagant Scorpio Ball, held at the Hôtel de l’Hermitage in Monte Carlo. For the occasion, she only invited celebrities who were also Scorpios. Among the 60 or so guests were Swedish actress Hjördis Paulina Genberg, American actor Rock Hudson, and Italian actress Virna Lisi.

Actor Richard Burton was also in attendance, accompanied by his wife Elizabeth Taylor, even though she was born under the sign of Pisces. An exception was made for the actress, who was granted special permission thanks to her husband’s astrological sign—Scorpio, born on November 10. For the occasion, Taylor chose to dazzle, wearing a Cartier diamond necklace with an estimated value of $1 million around her neck—a gift from Burton two weeks earlier. She also wore a spectacular evening cape by Tiziani, made of black velvet and adorned with two rhinestone scorpions on the front and a third on the hood.

Guests were required to adhere to a dress code devised by Kelly, inspired by the colors associated with the sign of Scorpio. Red, black, and white were therefore strongly recommended. The princess, for her part, opted for an off-the-shoulder black velvet dress by Balenciaga from the fall-winter 1967 couture collection. Two ruby brooches set with diamonds—a wedding gift from Prince Rainier III—completed her ensemble.

The decor also reflected the evening’s theme. Red candles, portraits of famous Scorpios, and a lavish cake adorned with golden scorpions set the tone. No detail had been left to chance: The waiters, wearing powdered 18th-century wigs, dressed in velvet suits embroidered with sparkling stars and held silver candelabras adorned with red candles.

Princess Grace was seen on numerous occasions alongside Carroll Righter, an astrologer and Hollywood columnist nicknamed “the astrologer to the stars.” According to People magazine, the princess’s birth chart also revealed a Scorpio ascendant, while her Midheaven was in Leo. In astrology, the Midheaven is associated with career, public image, and reputation. Some attributed her commanding presence and magnetism in the spotlight to this configuration.

Kelly embodied the mysterious aura that her admirers associated with her astrological sign. Unfortunately, that light was extinguished on September 14, 1982, when the Princess of Monaco lost her life in a tragic car accident on the hills above the principality.

#3608. Call of Duty might have swapped guns and tanks for knights and swords if an Infinity Ward experiment had panned out

"If it's a war story, sure, it can be COD."

As much as Call of Duty is criticised for delivering the same thing every year, reports occasionally surface of attempts to take the series in bold new directions, even if none of these experiments have so far seen the light of day. And it turns out a medieval Call of Duty was also explored at one time.

This latest revelation comes from Infinity Ward veteran Taylor Kurosaki, who led development on the studio's Infinite Warfare and 2019 Modern Warfare game. "Call of Duty is a massive tree with a lot of branches, right?" Kurosaki told PC Gamer. "It can be World War 2. The team at IW had prototyped a medieval Call of Duty. Where you were a knight and had a sword and all kinds of crazy shit. But if it's a war story, sure, it can be Call of Duty."

This isn't the first time we've heard of an unusual Call of Duty prototype. When Activision brought Sledgehammer Games into the fold as another lead studio for the lucrative shooter series, the team briefly worked on a third-person horror off-shoot set in Vietnam, which was referred to as Fog of War.

Activision's legal battle with Infinity Ward founders Vince Zampella and Jason West, however, caused the project to be cancelled, as Sledgehammer was roped into helping the studio finish Modern Warfare 3.

As for Kurosaki, he currently leads That's No Moon alongside creative partner Jacob Minkoff and other Infinity Ward and Naughty Dog veterans. The studio is currently working on Crossfire, a narrative-driven third-person shooter set in the universe of Smilegate's free-to-play series of the same name.

Understandably, it’s a question whether that renaming will still happen given…everything. There’s my ode to the death of the Cybertruck. And there’s all the details from the star-studded MoMA Film Benefit honoring Steven Spielberg. Tom Cruise shocked the crowd with surprise remarks, and Bruce Springsteen roasted the director. It was a whole night.

MENTIONED IN THIS ISSUE: Donald Trump, Jason Calacanis, Brendan Dugan, Siniša Mačković, David Zwirner, Lorenzo Amos, Kate Capshaw, Zohran Mamdani, Jessica Craig-Martin, Dean & DeLuca, Indochine, Stanley Whitney, Marina Adams, Will Whitney, The Beverly Hills Hotel, Elon Musk, Lana Del Rey, Grimes, Travis Scott, Pharrell Williams, 21 Savage, Tyler, the Creator, Bad Bunny, Julia Wachtel, Todd von Ammon, Frieda Toranzo Jaeger.

The major arts institution named for Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori, appears to be—shocker!—very much in jeopardy.

Just months ago, Huang was getting a phone call from President Trump while onstage at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles. “I’m here with the besties, Mr. President,” a laughing Huang said, putting his phone up to the mic. “Tell him I say hi!” said All-In cohost Jason Calacanis.

But Huang’s recent weeks have not been marked by good times with the besties. First, the Democrats took over Congress, throttling all the goodwill he built with the administration. Then he admitted to having an extramarital affair with a woman suspected by the US to be a Chinese spy—and then news of another affair, this time allegedly with a subordinate, came via a shocking New York Times bombshell. Amid rumors that yet another affair would soon break, he stepped down as CEO and, according to Forbes, has watched nearly $20 billion of his estimated net worth vaporize since Monday.

What’s unknown is the current state of his relationship with his wife, Lori Huang—and their ambitious plans for an arts organization that was set to bear their name. Earlier this year, the Huangs pledged $75 million to Vanderbilt University in order to help transform the soon-to-be-closed legendary San Francisco art school California College of the Arts into part of Vanderbilt’s SF campus. Vanderbilt announced that it planned to name a portion of its SF campus the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang College of Art, Architecture and Design.

Which is now a bit awkward, given the multiple alleged affairs, and the whole Chinese-spy thing. Plus, Huang is no longer affiliated with Nvidia, which teamed up with CCA in 2025 to form the CCA-Nvidia Incubator for Creative Intelligence. Will Jensen and Lori Huang still put their names together on arts organizations after all that’s happened? And if there is no Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang College of Art, Architecture and Design, what will happen to Vanderbilt’s SF campus when it opens next year?

The CCA was started in 1907, and Huang and his wife were expected to support its transition to a new chapter. It would be a shame if this is how it ends. Reps at Vanderbilt didn’t get back to me.

It’s a new era in Tribeca. Tonight, Karma, a burgeoning mega-gallery with spaces in New York’s Chelsea and LA’s Hollywood, opens its new gallery at 38 White Street. Founder Brendan Dugan and director Siniša Mačković took me on a tour earlier this week, and it’s easily one of the most generous spaces anywhere in the neighborhood. Plus, an outpost of Karma Bookstore—a much needed bookstore for a neighborhood shockingly lacking in one—is coming in right across the street.

This will be the latest big-tent blue chipper to take a space in the Triangle Below Canal, as they used to call this neighborhood. Something to consider: In the last few years, mega-galleries such as David Zwirner and Hauser & Wirth have shut their uptown townhouses and opened downtown.

Also opening tonight is a White Street outpost of Gratin gallery, which has a roster of incredibly exciting young stars, including Lorenzo Amos (whom we wrote about a year ago). I’m hearing about other younger dealers grabbing spaces in the neighborhood. The art market isn’t exactly on fire, but dealers are betting on one thing: the enduring power and capital of New York City.

Speaking of New York, guess who’s lived here full-time for almost a year? Steven Spielberg, that’s who. On New Year’s Day 2026, the GOAT American director—who is married to the artist Kate Capshaw—moved his official residence from California to New York, and has made the apartment in the San Remo his home base. You will not be surprised to hear that, post-move, Spielberg is doing extremely cool stuff in town. He’s walking around with a script and a Tracy Kidder book while slugging down an iced McCafé. He’s getting lunch at Benvenuto Cafe. He’s having Mayor Zohran Mamdani over to the crib.

The only thing left was for one of the city’s great museums to throw a big party for the Hollywood-royalty-gone-Gotham. Last night, Spielberg got just that: He was honored at the MoMA Film Benefit, sponsored by Chanel. I was there. Read the full report—with fun pictures!—here.

Also on VF this week: an exclusive excerpt from an uproarious new memoir by artist Jessica Craig-Martin, I Regret I am Able to Attend. Craig-Martin is a real treasure of the art world, a great photographer—and, as it turns out, a hell of a writer. The whole book is a compulsively readable blast. The chapter where Craig-Martin recalls working as an extremely inexperienced, occasionally larcenous teller at Dean & DeLuca is one of the funniest, most satisfying New York vignettes I’ve read this year. And of course, all the scuttlebutt from the ’80s art scene is fabulous. Read the excerpt, in which our narrator spills all the tea—and, um, stuff stronger than tea—about working as a waitress when Indochine opened.

Happy 80th birthday to the great painter Stanley Whitney. His wife, the artist Marina Adams, and son, dealer Will Whitney, threw Stanley a party to celebrate his octogenarian status on Nine Orchard’s roof, overlooking Dimes Square. Writers, artists, dealers, old heads, everyone was there. A fabulous Wednesday night.

#3606. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 is the US' best-selling physical game so far this year

The very popular and critically-acclaimed The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has set another record. After selling 5.2m copies in four days and becoming the Switch 2's fastest-selling game, Ocarina of Time has now been revealed to also be a major seller at retail.

The remake has sold more than 1m physical copies in the US alone in its launch week (ending 7th November). That's according to Circana analyst Mat Piscatella, who revealed on Bluesky that the record also makes it the first title to surpass 1m physical sales since 2023's Tears of the Kingdom. That is, no other game - from any publisher - has managed to sell over 1m copies in the US within its first week in three years.

While Nintendo games tend to perform better at retail than those from Sony, Xbox or third-party publishers, physical sales in general have been declining in the US. In July, Piscatella revealed that just seven PlayStation games have sold more than 100,000 physical copies up to that point in 2026, and that was after all the backlash to Sony's decision to end physical disc manufacturing by January 2028.

Ocarina of Time's lead of this particular segment likely won't continue, however. That's because, as Piscatella pointed out in a follow-up post, Circana's tracking considers disc-less, code-in-box versions to be physical editions. This means Grand Theft Auto 6 will likely overtake the remake in short order, just as it's expected to break records elsewhere.

In Eurogamer's glowing review of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, Christian Donlan argued that Nintendo has done just enough to modernise a timeless classic while maintaining what made the original so special for many players.

Qud's co-creators discuss dogs with guns, handless tattooing, and the tragedy of a sinning tree.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In a GDC interview with Freehold Games in 2025, I asked the developers of magnificently mutated, indulgently arcane science-fantasy roguelike Caves of Qud the same thing anyone would in my situation: What's the ideal number of limbs for a being to aspire to? Their answer was none, because "a perfect sphere is the ideal form" and "we started in perfection and only moved farther from God."

As you can imagine, I was eager to speak with co-creators Brian Bucklew and Jason Grinblat earlier this month about Diaspora, the roguelike's upcoming first expansion. Diaspora aims to add an "influx of riotous life" to Qud, expanding its body plan-agnostic mutation system with playable animal and plant characters. With Qud's mutagenic possibility space about to erupt even further, I posed its developers another pressing question: Is it a greater moral tragedy for a sin to be committed by a man who mutated into a tree, or by a tree who mutated into a man?

"We have text on this in-game," Grinblat said, citing Aphorisms About Birds—an in-game book which notes that our fairy tales pay plenty of attention to the man who's turned into a bird, but little to the cruelty fate's inflicted on the bird who's turned into a man. "I think that's probably even more true if you're a tree. There's one tree mayor in the game. He's pretty happy. He's been around for a while. If he were a guy just walking around out there, getting acid gas shot at him, I think he'd be pretty upset."

"It hits too close to home, right? We're having trouble in our world dealing with things transforming into the facsimile of man," Bucklew said. "It's hard for me to think about turning into the facsimile of man without becoming sad about the way the world is and how real that question's going to be in our lives for the next 20 years."

Conversely, Grinblat noted, "becoming a tree sounds really nice." To that, Bucklew agreed, wondering whether "there's some way we can get into that business," possibly through marketing "some random peptide."

With an air of existential horror comfortably established, we moved into a more mechanical discussion of Diaspora's new plant and animal playstyles. In Caves of Qud, it's already possible for a player character to end up with all sorts of bodies: A mutant character could end up sprouting a bouquet of new limbs and body parts, each capable of equipping items and using abilities. And a number of the game's existing mutations allow a character to acquire some very animalian or plantlike characteristics, whether it's antlers, ape fur, or photosynthetic skin.

With Diaspora's plant and animal gene-stocks, however, the developers are aiming to lean even harder into exploring what more specialized body types provide—and what they don't.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

"They have different body plans. That's one that jumps out immediately," Grinblat said. "I'm a crab: I have six legs, I might have a claw. I'm a bear: I'm a quadruped that doesn't have hands in a traditional sense. That's already a space to play with."

That's elaborated on further with species traits, a new feature exclusive to Diaspora character types. Species traits are a kind of stock-specific mutation bonus, representing the inherent features of an animal's—or plant's—anatomy. While a human character can mutate wings, a mutant bird's inherent wing mutation will advance faster and allow access to new, bird-specific flight advancements. Same with tails: Mutant animal characters that possess a tail as a species trait will be able to mutate the appendage to be prehensile more quickly than mutant characters that don't.

"We want every animal to have something weird and unique about them that you can't just get if you were a human and you advance that mutation a bunch," Grinblat said.

Species traits will introduce a breadth of new opportunities for Qud's already-rich buildcrafting, but creating a new plant or animal character will mean opting out of some things that are standard to the human experience. For example: If I make a mutant dog, can I hold a gun without mutating new hands or opposable thumbs?

"This is a big thing. No," Grinblat said. "Right now, no."

There are, of course, ways for my mutant dog to achieve its dreams of weapon-wielding. I might seek out the helping hands artifact already present in-game, which provides the wearer with two extra arms and hands—or I could pick up that aforementioned prehensile tail mutation and grant my tail the gift of gunslinging. But while Grinblat acknowledged that "hands are very powerful," he said implementing those kinds of natural animal limitations are an intentional design decision, made in the hopes that players will explore new ways of surviving Qud's countless dangers.

"You might end up with a dog with a gun, but you might be doing a lot of dog stuff—running with a pack of dogs who each do their own thing," Grinblat said. "What an actual dog looks like in Qud is up for grabs, but we want to encourage different playstyles that animals can lean into without just feeling like, 'oh, I'm always going to get hands and use guns.'"

Unfortunately for Freehold, introducing a yet wider gradient of body types into the absurd complexity of Qud's systems and simulations has produced exciting new problems to solve—and philosophical riddles to ponder.

"We've spent so much time figuring out the ontology of tails," Bucklew said. "Are tails arms? Can they wear bracelets? How different is a prehensile tail from a regular tail? Is a tail different from a head in terms of what it can wear? A necklace? A bracelet? A lot of hours in meetings about tail ontology."

Freehold's "last three months," the Qud creators said, have been dominated by "people having strong opinions about limbs." Many of the emergent issues are related to Qud's core questline, which is requiring the devs to reevaluate all sorts of interactions that were designed under the assumption that the player would be roughly human-shaped.

"The limbs have taken the bulk of it, but there are other issues," Grinblat said. "Like, oh, I can't tattoo myself because I'm a crab, so I can't tattoo the Mark of Death on me. Or, oh, I can't eat because I'm a plant. I can't eat the Eater's Flesh that lets me advance past that part of the quest. There's all sorts of problems."

Crabs, in particular, seem to be a source of constant headache as Qud is reconfigured to accommodate animal playstyles.

"How does a crab get high? Like, it's an integral part of a Caves of Qud quest, and a crab is not very good at it," Bucklew said. "Do we need a tattooing booth? If you don't have hands, how are you going to tattoo yourself? We're going to need a tattoo grenade or something. But you can't throw stuff either. Oh man, I have no answer."

"God," Grinblat said. "It's so much to do."

By the end of our conversation, the developers remembered that crabs can probably hold a tattoo gun in their claws. Deciding how plants will tattoo themselves, they said, was a problem for another day.

Caves of Qud: Diaspora launches in early access on Steam on December 9.

#3604. Sci-fi RPG Exodus continues evoking Mass Effect by revealing female lead and nicknaming her FemJun

Sci-fi role-playing game Exodus continues to play into the Mass Effect comparisons by revealing the female version of its main character Jun, and with studio Archetype referring to her in marketing material as FemJun.

If that moniker sounds familiar it's because it is: the female Commander Shepard character in the Mass Effect series was nicknamed FemShep. FemShep became an iconic part of BioWare's iconic series, eventually proving that female leads could front games just as successfully as male leads could, and be every bit as popular.

Is the nickname FemJun too blatant? Possibly. But there's well publicised BioWare pedigree at Archetype Entertainment, in the studio's co-founders and in the people leading the project. Key Mass Effect writer Drew Karpyshyn is in charge of writing Exodus, for example, and the similarities to Mass Effect are something the Exodus team has not been shy about in the past. In the wake of Mass Effect 5 being cancelled and BioWare being closed, they become even more alluring.

There are, however, big and important differences between Exodus and Mass Effect, key among them, time dilation. In Exodus, there are special Exodus missions whereby you leave your home planet and fly far away, and in doing so experience time differently to the people back home. Many years will pass for them while only days will pass for you, which provides the game with a way to show you long-term consequences of your actions when you return.

Archetype hasn't shown the female version of Jun before, despite having released many videos of Exodus, perhaps to build anticipation for her reveal. It's a press beat that's also provided Archetype - a studio owned by Dungeons & Dragons company Wizards of the Coast - with an occasion to reveal the two actors playing Jun in the game.

Female Jun is portrayed by Carina Conti, who played the lead in the recent Mafia game, The Old Country - Isabella Torrisi. She's appeared in HBO's Winning Time and Hulu/Freeform's Good Trouble as well. Male Jun, meanwhile, is portrayed by Stephen Oyoung, who played Mister Negative in Insomniac's Marvel's Spider-Man 1 and 2 games, and Red Hood in Gotham Knights. He also appeared in Mission: Impossible - The Final Reckoning, The Wrecking Crew, and Twisters. The game also famously stars Matthew McConaughey.

Archetype announced a Dark Horse hardback art book to go on sale alongside the game next year as well. This arrives a week after the game; Exodus arrives 7th April 2027 on PC, PS5 and Xbox Series S/X, and the art book on 13th April.

Matt played Exodus at Gamescom relatively recently and came away impressed, referring to it as "the best kind of surprise". "I wasn't expecting quite such a bombastic 45 minutes when I first picked up a controller and settled into Exodus, admittedly, but the more I played, the more it made sense," he wrote. "I might not be much of a Mass Effect fan (damn you M35 Mako once more), but Exodus is now firmly on my radar ahead of its arrival next year."

Rick Devens has simple advice for those who want to be on reality television, and for anyone who wants to be on the best reality shows, I'd listen up. Apparently the key to getting in the position to win Big Brother, or make wild moves on Survivor, is to be bold... even if you look foolish.

While we've seen people win Big Brother and Survivor by playing the middle, the most memorable winners and players are the ones who make the big moves. Other reality stars may suggest being chill, but not Devens. He told The Observer the key to his moves is this:

I think that's some universal advice most reality stars would give, which is why they were put on TV to begin with. Casting directors don't seek out people who will strive to worry about every move that's on camera, what could go wrong, or make rash decisions.

Rick Devens just won Big Brother, so he's a great person to ask this question. Not many people get the chance to play on both BB and Survivor, so those should continue to listen when it comes to why it's important to be fearless. As he continued:

You’re going to handicap yourself. You’re going to keep yourself from doing amazing things and having the most fun. Just go for it. Be fearless.

All this to say, not every person on reality television is Rick Devens. He's speaking with the bias of someone who was put on Survivor initially and welcomed back because of how he played. It's that same fearlessness that got him on Big Brother, hoping that "Chaos Devens" would be activated.

There's been some debate of whether Devens played as fast and loose on BB as he did on Survivor. Coming in the game with built-in allies in Dee Valladares and Angela Murray, as well as being voted to receive powers, certainly allowed him some freedom to make moves that other Houseguests weren't afforded. I would imagine that if any of those other Houseguests had been given those big of powers, they would've also jumped on the opportunity.

Rick Devens and Big Brother's producers, for that matter, would argue he and the icons had the biggest targets on their backs going into the game. The advantages allowed them to "even the odds" and prevent being targeted from the jump and being sent out of the game immediately. Neither had pointed out that former winner Rachel Reilly played in the previous season with only one week of safety as an advantage, but I digress.

In any case, Rick and the Icons playing Big Brother again resulted in big ratings for the series and a two-season renewal. Bringing in the viewers will also work a lot toward getting someone back on reality television, so I'm just waiting to see if we'll see him again if Season 30 of BB does end up being an all-star season. In the meantime, I'll enjoy all his previous reality TV appearances on Paramount+.

He graduated from the University of Southern Indiana with a degree in Journalism and a minor in Radio and Television. #3602. Martin McDonagh Calls Sam Rockwell “One of the Best Actors of His Generation, If Not the Best”

Director Martin McDonagh has become as well-known for making memorable films as he is for writing the complex male friendships within them.

"I like mining down into the sensitivity that I think a lot of male relationships do have, but aren't as – especially in American films – explored sensitively," he said about the subject during a panel conversation at the inaugural Vanity Fair Screening Room at LACMA on Friday. "It's not just a buddy film, and it's not a romance, and it's not just about cool CIA guys," McDonagh continued. “It's sort of the opposite in other ways. And that I think is interesting to explore because I think my male relationships are that way. They can be sensitive and sad and happy and all the things that a female relationship can be. So I think that's why I keep coming back to it.”

The conversation, which featured McDonagh and the film’s stars John Malkovich and Mariana di Girolamo, was moderated by VF's Senior Hollywood Correspondent Rebecca Ford following an exclusive screening of their new film, Wild Horse Nine. The acclaimed dark comedy follows two CIA agents (Malkovich and Sam Rockwell) who are not only behind the plan to overthrow the Chilean government in 1973, but have also had a hand in several other significant historical moments in the US and abroad.

Maria di Girolamo, John Malkovich and Martin McDonagh, in conversation with Rebecca Ford at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on Friday, November 13, 2026.

Malkovich and Rockwell's characters engage in pithy, often hilarious banter throughout the film, and their onscreen chemistry is a highlight.

John Malkovich at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

"I love Sam," said Malkovich. “I knew him a bit socially before this, but I'd worked with him once before, which was a great pleasure on a film called A Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy. He's like a kind of expert trainer at SeaWorld who can get the whales and the sharks and the dolphins to show things in exchange for a fish. And Sam is a great student of acting. He is a great student of film and of theater, and he's great fun, very hardworking, and just an ideal colleague. I couldn't imagine a better colleague than Sam and I've had some excellent colleagues.”

"He's one of the best actors of his generation, if not the best," adds McDonagh of Rockwell. "He's always surprising, always dangerous, always sensitive, always smart, always coming up with new stuff. And I think there's a danger to him that's lovely to write for. We always hope the characters will always be surprising, and with Sam's voice in the head, that really helps."

Mariana di Girolamo at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

For rising star Mariana di Girolamo, a Chilean actress making her English language movie debut with Wild Horse Nine, she was excited and only slightly intimidated to be a part of the cast.

"It was quite a challenge to perform for the first time in English," she said. "I prepared myself with a coach and we rehearsed with John, Sam and Parker [Posey] and Ailin [Salas] in a public theater in New York where I heard the script for the first time. That was amazing for me, for us." di Girolamo, who is very familiar with the fraught period of Chilean history depicted in the film, said she appreciated how McDonagh put it all in context. "It was my first time approaching that period of time in this way with this very beautiful dark humor. I was laughing about these things and feeling empathy with these CIA agents that committed a lot of horrific, horrific things. I've never read something like that, and the arc of my character is so beautiful, unique, I really wanted to be part of this."

Martin McDonagh at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

The invitation-only events are welcoming an audience from the worlds of film, fashion, culture, politics, media, and tech, much like the magazine itself. VF editor Daniel Kile introduced the first screening, welcoming the audience to the Steve Tisch Theater at LACMA, which is not yet open to the public.

#3601. PlayStation defeats £2 billion UK lawsuit that alleged Sony forced consumers into "excessive and unfair prices"

12.2 million gamers can be wrong, apparently.

Sony has defeated a major £2 billion UK class action lawsuit concerning the price of games on the PlayStation Store (thanks, TheGameBusiness). The judgment came after a 30-day Competition Appeal Tribunal that took place in London, where PlayStation users claimed Sony had removed "all actual and potential competition" in relation to selling digital games on the console.

The case, brought by Alex Neill, who said he represented roughly 12.2 million gamers, accused Sony of applying "excessive and unfair" pricing on games that appeared on the storefront accessible by PS3, PS4 and PS5 consoles - the PlayStation Store. In a judgment published by the London’s Competition Appeal Tribunal today (17th November), the case was rejected. The judgement noted that market definitions used to define Sony's conduct were "unsafe", and that consumers "would be likely to make informed choices when purchasing consoles" and games on the hardware, too.

"Potential PlayStation console purchasers had both access to sufficient information and an incentive to consider that information in order to make informed purchasing decisions at the console level, especially in the case of high-value users who spend significant amounts in the digital gaming aftermarket," read the judgment.

The lawsuit made the argument that, upon purchasing a PS5 or other PlayStation console, you were then trapped within its ecosystem, and forced into paying the prices determined by Sony. The Tribunal disagreed, however, and ruled that Sony competed within a wider 'systems market' alongside Xbox, Nintendo and PC, for example. Furthermore, the Tribunal found no evidence that the existence of other digital storefronts would have actually brought any PlayStation Store pricing down.

Interestingly, the Tribunal used the argument that consumers can also opt and buy physical games instead of using the PlayStation Store - something that is changing as of the start of 2028. That did not seem to have any bearing on today's decision, though. It's also worth noting that this case did not seek to interrogate the ownership status of digital games - something that's been at the heart of the movement rallying against Sony's decision to kill off physical media. Earlier this year, spokespeople from Sony's legal team argued "reasonable consumers" already know they don't actually own their digital games.

The London Tribunal has a fairly long history. Back in 2022, it began as a case that attempted to sue Sony to the tune of £5bn for "ripping people off" on PlayStation Store. Sony argued the case brought against it in this trial was "flawed from start to finish". This isn't the only situation where we're seeing consumers pursue legal action against the platform holder. Last year, PlayStation was sued in the Netherlands over the so-called "Sony tax" that highlighted artificially inflated prices on the Store, and sought to represent more than 20,000 participants that felt short-changed by the company.

Even the best reality TV shows can be accused of being scripted, and while not every claim is substantiated, there are a lot of allegations. Personally, like many others, I might be taken aback on the off chance that such a claim turns out to be true. Just recently, I found two stories from people who allegedly got a first-hand look at the inner workings of America's Got Talent and Bar Rescue, and they're fascinating to read.

AGT regularly draws claims online, with people alleging that it's scripted or faking parts of its programming. This latest claim from Reddit comes from someone who allegedly worked on the set and took issue with how one contestant's story was edited in the episode. Take a read:

I worked on America's Got Talent's 7th season and I never watched the show before working on it. I spent 4 days working, interviewing talented people with a camera crew and producer. I will not forget, we interviewed this one older woman who was a drummer. She was vibrant and friendly and we had a great talk, and then I watched when the episode aired and they recut the interview to make her seem flighty and mentally... off. Then she goes out on stage in front of the country for Sharon Osborne to mock her. It was bad, it was heartbreaking, that this woman's crime was 'older than 40 and good at drums' and the people making that show took liberty to destroy her on a national platform. They asked me to work on season 8 and I turned them down without a conversation.

It's not uncommon for reality TV show subjects to complain about receiving unflattering or dishonest edits. Over the years, stars have alleged that producers can get the response they want out of them and then edit the footage to make it appear they said something entirely different from what they meant. If AGT actually engaged in this, it wouldn't be different from claims against many other shows on the 2026 TV schedule. Regardless, this should be a gentle reminder for viewers not to believe everything they see.

The thread also revealed someone who was pretty upset with Bar Rescue after the show allegedly "ruined" one of his favorite locales. The renovation show is wildly popular and entertaining, but that doesn't always mean it's tackling bars that are in trouble. On that note, per the aforementioned user, his go-to bar didn't even need to be rescued:

This bar was packed ALL THE TIME. You drive by at 3 PM on a Tuesday, packed. 2 PM on a Sunday, packed. On more than one occasion, we had gone to the bar on a Friday or Saturday to find no place to sit because it was so full. They even bought the space next to them and knocked out a wall to make more room...Then we heard that Bar Rescue was coming. We wondered why they would need to 'rescue' this bar that was always full of people. But we got excited to see our bar on TV.

From there, the writer claimed the bar's owners removed all the furniture and revamped the menu with new cocktails. His wife apparently stood in line to attend the reopening and was instructed before entering that she could only order the signature cocktail.

When the Bar Rescue episode aired, it pushed the narrative that the cocktails were super popular and that "no one wants beer." As mentioned, attendees were allegedly told they could only purchase cocktails, which made it seem like the show's producers decided that would be the story before filming ever began. In the end, the "rescue" ended up ruining the bar, at least in this person's opinion:

People stopped going. Last time I went, it was a Friday night, and there were like 6 other people in the place. The bar ended up moving locations, and now I don't have a neighborhood place anymore. Fuck Bar Rescue.

The whole account really makes me rethink the times I've seen Jon Taffer give advice on how to fix a bar. Of course, this is all alleged, and it's not like there are receipts or concrete proof of these claims. It isn't necessarily hard to believe, but given the lack of hard evidence or even any identifiable information, I'd take it with a grain of salt.

While America's Got Talent and Bar Rescue aren't the only reality television shows accused of scripting their unscripted moments, they are two established legacy shows. I'm sure they won't be the last shows to be accused of being deceptive to the audience watching at home, but I'm not sure it'll actually keep anyone from watching.

The 2026 TV schedule is winding down, but there is still lots of good TV to watch. Even if it is reality television, there's no shortage of entertainment as we close out the year.

Mick Joest is a Content Producer for CinemaBlend with his hand in an eclectic mix of television goodness. Star Trek is his main jam, but he also regularly reports on happenings in the world of Star Trek, WWE, Doctor Who, 90 Day Fiancé, Quantum Leap, and Big Brother. He graduated from the University of Southern Indiana with a degree in Journalism and a minor in Radio and Television. He's great at hosting panels and appearing on podcasts if given the chance as well.

#3597. The Game Awards just confirmed who plays GTA 6's Lucia

Manni L. Perez has been confirmed as the actress behind Grand Theft Auto 6's Lucia Caminos, just days before the game launches.

As spotted by IGN, the confirmation came during The Game Awards' nominations livestream today, where Perez was nominated for Best Performance for her role as co-lead Lucia.

Perez had been widely rumoured to play Lucia for months, and fans have regularly filled her social media livestreams with questions about GTA 6, which she has been oh-so-carefully sidestepping.

Lucia is one half of GTA 6's lead pair alongside Jason Duval, making it the first Grand Theft Auto game with a playable couple.

Jason's actor wasn't among the nominees, so who plays him is still a mystery.

Funnily enough, Lucia isn't her first Lucia - she also played Lucia Santiago in a 2023 episode of CBS's East New York.

GTA 6 arrives 19th November on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. It is now available to pre-load for anyone who pre-ordered the digital version, and those with the code-in-box physical version.

It's long been revealed that GTA 6 will have a regional release, meaning that some lucky, soon-to-be players will be able to access the game much earlier than others. Rockstar's regional release schedule sees the game launching at midnight on 19th November regardless of what region you're in, and if you wish to join those playing almost a day early, there's the good ol' Xbox New Zealand trick for eager players to try.

#3596. Creator Dhar Mann Unveils 5 Original Scripted Vertical Series

Dhar Mann Studios, founded by creator Dhar Mann, is unveiling the first five original scripted vertical dramas from its partnership with Fox Entertainment and Holywater Tech.

“I’m very involved in the overall creative direction, including what stories we’re telling, how we want people to feel, and what they take away from watching,” Mann, 42, exclusively told Us of the process. “We also have an incredible team led by Erin McFarlane, Dhar Mann Studios’ Head of Film and TV, who’s leading the day-to-day work of bringing these verticals to life.”

The first five series, which span romance, action, suspense and music-driven drama, are developed specifically for vertical viewing. For Mann, the romance genre is “exciting” because it “opens up so many stories about trust, heartbreak, forgiveness, and second chances.” Mann noted that “those are themes we’ve always cared about,” and this is “another way to explore them.”

“I think the appeal of vertical dramas is pretty simple: you can get invested in a story quickly, right on your phone,” he said. “You might have a few minutes to watch, but you still want to feel something. The episodes are short, but the emotions can be big. I think that’s going to influence how Hollywood tells stories. People’s viewing habits keep evolving, and there’s a real opportunity to meet them where they are. That’s what we’re excited to do with Fox Entertainment and Holywater.”

Mann gained an online following more than one decade ago, sharing videos while at the lowest point in his life. While reflecting on hitting rock bottom before reaching success, Mann shared that those hardships made him a better storyteller.

“I think people might be surprised by how much that chapter still shapes the stories I want to tell today,” he said. “When you’re going through a really difficult time, you don’t know how your story is going to turn out. You can feel alone and misunderstood. I know that feeling, and it’s something I can connect with when we’re writing a character who’s struggling.”

He continued, “That period also taught me to take responsibility for my own choices and circumstances. That’s why, in our stories, I care about seeing what someone actually does to change. You want to believe they’ve earned that second chance.”

Mann noted that his experience gave him “more empathy,” adding that “you never really know everything someone is carrying.”

“I want our stories to remind people that their hardest chapter doesn’t have to be their last chapter,” he said. “That’s a message that means something to me personally.”

While balancing his online persona, Mann is also navigating parenthood as a father of three daughters. Being a dad — and husband to wife Laura Avila — has influenced the stories that Mann chooses to tell on his platform.

“Having daughters has made me so much more emotional. It’s opened up a part of me that absolutely influences how I connect with stories,” he said. “As they get older, I think about the messages they’re going to receive about who they should be, what makes them valuable and how they should expect to be treated. I want them to know their voice matters, that they deserve respect and that kindness is a strength.”

He continued, “That carries into the characters we create, especially our female leads. I care about them having a voice, making their own choices and discovering their own worth. And being a father keeps me thinking about my own example, too. The lessons I put into our stories are lessons I have to keep practicing in my own life.”

While reflecting on the storytelling process, Mann told Us that he listens to his fans “a lot” about what type of content they want to see.

“One of the biggest advantages of what we do is having that direct relationship with our audience. They tell us what they love, what they want more of, and when something doesn’t connect. We take that seriously,” he said, adding that vertical dramas are a perfect example. “Our community had been asking us to explore this, and we learned that many of them were already watching these shows regularly.”

He continued, “What’s exciting is realizing how open they are to seeing us try different kinds of stories. They connect with the emotion, the characters and the lessons, and they want to see what we can do with that in a new format. Our audience has helped us build this company. It makes sense to listen to where they want us to go next.”

Mann, whose brand has always been associated with uplifting stories and positive life lessons, shared that he is balancing his signature message while also giving the audience entertainment.

“I’ve always believed you can entertain people and leave them with something meaningful,” he said. “A story can have a love triangle, a betrayal or a shocking twist and still say something important about how we treat each other. For example, a romance can also be about learning your worth or understanding that someone wanting you and someone treating you well are two different things. There’s a lot of room for meaningful storytelling there.”

Mann shared that characters who “make mistakes, face consequences and have to earn their growth” is what “makes a redemption story satisfying,” adding, “You’ve seen what it took for that person to change.”

“With The Brothers Who Love Me, there’s the romance and rivalry, but Abby is also dealing with loss and figuring out who she is. That emotional journey matters to us,” he explained of the first vertical drama. “We want you wondering what happens next while also caring about what happens to these people. That’s always been at the heart of our storytelling.”

Mann’s partnership is just the latest accomplishment in his impressive portfolio, having amassed more than 170 million followers across social media platforms. But Mann noted that “celebrity” is “still a funny word” to associate with himself.

“I spend so much of my time thinking about the next story, working with our team and being a dad that ‘celebrity’ isn’t really how I think about my everyday life,” Mann said. “I’m grateful that so many people connect with what we create. When you hear a number like 170 million, it’s hard to even picture that many people. But every one of those people has their own life, their own struggles and their own reason for watching.”

He continued, “That’s the part that means the most to me, the possibility that something we created helped someone feel understood or gave them a little hope. It also makes me appreciate the responsibility that comes with having a platform.”

At the end of the day, Mann is still working toward his mission every day of not just telling stories — but changing lives.

“There will always be someone who needs encouragement, someone who feels alone or someone who needs a reminder that things can get better,” he said. “What matters to me is what someone does after watching. Maybe they treat a classmate differently. Maybe they apologize to someone. Maybe they find the courage to try again. Those choices can seem small, but they can change a relationship or the direction of someone’s life. I want the impact of a story to last longer than the time someone spends watching it.”

He continued, “And I want us to build a company where that work can continue for a long time, where talented people have opportunities to tell meaningful stories and inspire others to do the same. That would make me incredibly proud.”

#3595. Firaxis reportedly cuts a third of its staff as studio head departs and new XCOM struggles

Civilization and XCOM developer Firaxis Games has laid off around 60 people.

The cuts, which took place today, account for about a third of the studio’s staff, Bloomberg reports, citing people familiar with the matter. Studio head Heather Hazen is also leaving.

Its sources say Firaxis' unannounced XCOM game has faced development struggles and missed "a significant milestone over the summer". The project will continue, but "may face a shakeup as a result of the cuts".

A spokesperson for 2K, the Take-Two label that runs Firaxis, confirmed Hazen's departure to Bloomberg, and said the studio is "restructuring and recentering around the studio's core strength - designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years".

"As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis," the spokesperson continued. "These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis."

The layoffs come two days before the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6, which is developed and published by Rockstar, a separate label at Take-Two.

In September, around 18 months after Civ 7's widely criticised launch - and as the legendary 4X series celebrates its 35th anniversary - Firaxis unveiled a host of new updates coming to the game as it continued to improve it. These included an atomic age update, dragging Civ 7 into the present and beyond, as well as its first paid expansion, Earthrise, both arriving next year.

Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick admitted earlier this year that the studio "got it wrong with Civ 7".

"The game is a really good game. And it's certainly a profitable enterprise for us. But this is one where I think what we tried to do was a bridge too far, from the consumer's perspective," he told Game File in May.

It’s not the first round of cuts at the studio - 2K confirmed an unspecified number of layoffs at Firaxis in September 2025, and around 30 jobs went in 2023.

Consoles cost more than ever, and even if you can afford to buy one you don't have as much left over to buy games for it as you used to. That's made 2026 an underwhelming year for console gaming sales, but according to the latest forecast from videogame market analysts Newzoo, the imminent launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 will turn that around.

"As we explored in the Global Games Market Report 2026," said Newzoo's director of market intelligence, Emmanuel Rosier, "without GTA VI the console market would likely be down year-over-year in 2026. Instead, the game's launch is expected to generate billions of dollars in revenue and give console spending a significant boost."

Rosier is the analyst who, back in August, was skeptical about the idea of BioWare surviving long enough to make another Mass Effect game. I wish he'd been wrong about that, but it turned out he was right on the money with that prediction.

"Western console has been losing ground," he went on to say. "Its share of global games revenue fell from 21.5% in 2015 to 17.1% in 2025, and its revenue has been broadly flat since 2021. Console adoption shows the same pattern. In Western markets, the console player base has been flat since 2022. Most people who want to play on console already do."

Newzoo's prediction is that GTA 6 "will lift console full-game spending by 17.5% this year". But that's just the start of the story. "So while GTA VI is undoubtedly one of the most important releases of the decade," Rosier says, "its initial impact will be concentrated in Western console. That’s still a big market, which we forecast will be worth $36.3 billion in 2026, but it's only part of the industry. The longer-term global story will depend on what happens next, particularly on PC and online."

Though tradition has plenty of people expecting a delay of roughly a year and a half between GTA 6's console and PC releases, general console malaise and the value of GTA Online—likely to be bigger on PC, and perhaps launch alongside the PC port—is a reason to think maybe the wait won't be so long. A recent GamesBeat report claims it'll be out in early 2027.

"PC is far bigger than console in several major markets, including China," Rosier says, "and a PC release could expose the game to a much broader international audience.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

"The online mode is another key unknown. Depending on how it's positioned and monetized, it could significantly expand the game's audience. If Rockstar adopts a model that lowers barriers to entry, the long-term opportunity outside the traditional Western console audience could be much larger than it appears today."

GTA Online was a huge part of GTA 5's long-tail success. While Newzoo's data says at least 37% of players who preordered GTA 6 have spent money on GTA Online, only 15% did so in the last 12 months. It's in need of a refresh, and though Rockstar haven't confirmed anything, Twitch's CEO also says GTA 6's multiplayer component will be out in 2027.

Jody's first computer was a Commodore 64, so he remembers having to use a code wheel to play Pool of Radiance. A former music journalist who interviewed everyone from Giorgio Moroder to Trent Reznor, Jody also co-hosted Australia's first radio show about videogames, Zed Games. He's written for Rock Paper Shotgun, The Big Issue, GamesRadar, Zam, Glixel, Five Out of Ten Magazine, and Playboy.com, whose cheques with the bunny logo made for fun conversations at the bank. Jody's first article for PC Gamer was about the audio of Alien Isolation, published in 2015. Jody edited PC Gamer Indie from 2017 to 2018, and he eventually lived up to his promise to play every Warhammer videogame.

#3593. Andrew Scott On What Makes Elsinore “So Moving”

Although the emotional core of Elsinore is centered around beloved actor Ian Charleston dealing with terminal illness, its star Andrew Scott says the film has as much heart as it does humor.

“The most singular thing about our film I think is the humor in it,” he said during a panel conversation at the inaugural Vanity Fair Screening Room at LACMA on Friday. “The tragedy in some ways is a little bit like Hamlet itself, but you can't make a film about Ian Charleston without having gags in it. He was incredibly funny. Every person [who knew him] said he was just wickedly funny, and flirtatious, and he was always looking towards the light, and he had a certain degree of courage. So that is something I think that we all share as a sense of humor.”

Andrew Scott, Billie Piper, Stephen Beresford and Rebecca Ford at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

Elsinore tells the story of Scottish actor Ian Charleson (Scott) who attempts to perform Hamlet at the National Theatre while secretly living with AIDS. Scott has received early acclaim for his powerful portrayal of Charleson. Before the film began Vanity Fair’s West Coast Editor John Ross warned the audience that "first you're going to laugh, then you're going to cry," while watching Scott’s performance.

“I think … why the film is so moving is because [Charleson’s] not wallowing at any point. He was insanely courageous,” continued Scott. “So that to me was the thing that we were the most

insistent on in some ways. And that's really all down to finding actors who in this extraordinary ensemble have a really terrific sense of humor. And we kind of knew that we could, with the screenplay, get the best actors in the country. And I feel we did.”

The panel conversation featured Scott, costar Billie Piper, and writer Stephen Beresford, moderated by VF's Senior Hollywood Correspondent Rebecca Ford, following an exclusive screening of the film.

Billie Piper at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026

For Piper, who plays Charleston's close friend Patsy, she relied heavily on Beresford's script for her prep, as well as information she gleaned from those who actually knew Patsy, and Charleston.

“I've spoken to a few members of the family, their friends, and then I sort of cherry-picked things from people I'd known in the beginning of my career, the louder figures in our industry,” she said. “And then I did my own interpretation and just had a good time. It's a very moving story, but I had a lot of fun playing that part. She's a really joyful character to play, I enjoyed the comedy. And I understand that a lot of her jokes are coming from a place of despair.”

Beresford, who has known Scott for 25 years, said he didn't initially think of his longtime friend for the role, but should have.

“The story of Ian, and Ian's Hamlet [performance] is legendary in the British theater,” he said. “So many people said it was the greatest Hamlet they'd ever seen, and that it had this incredible quality. So I knew about the story, and then it was brought to me actually as an idea by a producer who said, ‘What about writing about Ian Charleston, and what about Andrew playing Ian Charleston?’ And then I just thought, ‘Well, why didn't I have that idea myself five years ago?’ So yeah, that's really how it happened, and I started to research it, the details of the story were so incredible, and so moving.”

Stephen Beresford at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026.

Scott, who famously played Hamlet onstage 150 times beginning in 2017, prior to filming Elsinore, closed out the panel conversation by reciting his favorite line from the classic tragedy.

“When Hamlet says the line about the war that was going on—and this was written 400 years ago—it just seems so relevant to what he might have been experiencing at the time, which is: ‘I see the imminent death of 20,000 men who for a fantasy, a trick of fame, go to their graves like beds.’ The idea that that was written 400 years ago, and that he was watching 50 percent of his friends die for no reason and be neglected by governments, and derided by the public. And it was just happening, and happening time and time again.”

Scott continued: “The reason that I love it so much is that when I was doing Hamlet myself, of course I wasn't thinking about the AIDS crisis, but the enduring nature of art, something that was written 400 years ago by Shakespeare, could actually be of use to somebody in 1989 and then be reproduced again in 2026 and be of use. And that idea of art being useful down the lines is so moving to me.”

Vanity Fair's Global Editorial Director Mark Guiducci, Elsinore stars Andrew Scott and Billie Piper and writer Stephen Beresford at Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 13, 2026.

The inaugural edition of Vanity Fair’s Screening Room pairs this year’s most compelling films with a slate of programming that includes post-screening panels and conversations with actors and filmmakers. The invitation-only events are welcoming an audience from the worlds of film, fashion, culture, politics, media, and tech, much like the magazine itself.

Following the program in Los Angeles, Vanity Fair’s Screening Room will arrive in New York, where screenings and events will take place at Cherry Lane Theatre from December 4–6.

#3592. The Game Awards 2026 nominees announced, and GTA 6 leads with eight nods before it's even out

The Game Awards 2026 nominees have been revealed, and Grand Theft Auto 6 leads the pack with eight nominations, two days before it even launches.

Rockstar's crime epic is up for Game of the Year, Best Game Direction, Best Narrative, Best Art Direction, Best Score and Music, Best Audio Design, and Best Action/Adventure Game. Its eighth nomination is Manni L. Perez's Best Performance nod for her role as Lucia, which is how we found out who plays her in the first place.

THE GAME AWARDS: 2026 Nominee Reveal! (Game of the Year) THE GAME AWARDS: 2026 Nominee Reveal!Watch on YouTube

For Game of the Year, GTA 6 is up against 007 First Light, Control Resonant, Phantom Blade Zero, Resident Evil Requiem, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Nintendo is the most-nominated publisher, with 12 nominations across its games, followed by Capcom with 11, and Annapurna Interactive and PlayStation with nine each.

The nominees were picked by a jury of more than 160 media and creator outlets, who may get advance or pre-release access to games - which explains how GTA 6 made the cut before launch. The winners will be revealed on Thursday, 10th December, at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles. Fans can vote on The Game Awards' website until 6pm PT on 9th December.

This year's show will stream for free on more than 40 platforms, including YouTube, Twitch, Prime Video, and Steam. Last year's show drew an estimated 171 million livestreams, up 11 percent on 2024's 154 million.

I absolutely loved Channing Tatum's Gambit in Deadpool & Wolverine. His ridiculous Cajun accent, the way Ryan Reynolds' Deadpool couldn't understand half of what he was saying, and the fact that Tatum finally got to play the character after years of trying made his appearance one of my favorite parts of the movie. But with Gambit returning for Avengers: Doomsday on the 2026 movie schedule, I've been wondering whether Marvel would give him more to do than make everybody laugh. Thankfully, Kevin Feige has some reassuring news.

Speaking with Empire about the upcoming Marvel movie and the return of the original Fox-era X-Men, the Marvel Studios president discussed what audiences can expect from Tatum's Remy LeBeau. And it sounds like the character will have considerably more going on this time around. According to Feige:

He's a standout. It's fun to see Gambit be as charismatic as he was in Deadpool & Wolverine, and yet in Doomsday it's not all for laughs. He's a fully-rounded character.

That's exactly what I was hoping to hear. Don't get me wrong, I laughed every time Gambit opened his mouth in Deadpool & Wolverine. Watching the Merc with the Mouth struggle to decipher his thick accent was hilarious, especially when he asked whether the Minions were his dialect coach. But I also want to see Tatum get a chance to actually play Gambit as a full-fledged character. After all, the mutant hero has quite a bit more going for him than an accent and a deck of exploding playing cards.

In the comics, Remy LeBeau is a former thief with a complicated past, and his relationship with Rogue remains one of the X-Men's most recognizable romances. There's plenty for Marvel to work with. Considering how long Tatum fought to play him, I'd hate to see the character reduced to merely comic relief.

For years, the actor tried to get a standalone Gambit movie made at 20th Century Fox. The project went through numerous delays and creative changes before Disney acquired the studio, and the film was ultimately canceled. Then Ryan Reynolds helped bring Tatum's version of the mutant to life in 2024, finally giving him the opportunity he'd been chasing for the better part of a decade.

Tatum has already said his approach to Gambit would change for Doomsday. He previously explained that directors Anthony and Joe Russo wanted him to dial back the exaggerated Cajun accent, allowing the character to have more serious moments without losing what made his introduction so entertaining.

With that in mind, Feige's latest comments become particularly encouraging. It's one thing to promise a slightly more understandable Gambit, but hearing that Marvel considers him a standout character suggests they're giving the 21 Jump Street star room to explore another side of Remy.

The Gambit-Related Mistake Channing Tatum Nearly Made: ‘It Would’ve Just Been A Catastrophe’

Of course, there's still plenty we don't know about his role in the epic comic book movie. Doomsday is bringing back several familiar X-Men, including James Marsden's Cyclops, Ian McKellen's Magneto and Patrick Stewart's Professor X. Empire also revealed a new look at Gambit alongside Cyclops outside the X-Mansion, which is pretty cool considering Tatum never got to appear alongside the original team during Fox's run. With Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom threatening the multiverse, I imagine there will be plenty of opportunities for Gambit to put those playing cards to work.

I'm excited to see what Tatum does with a character he clearly loves, especially now that he gets another opportunity to play him. Keep the charm, let him crack a few jokes, and maybe give the guy a few standout character moments that audiences won't soon forget. That's not asking too much, is it?

Avengers: Doomsday arrives in theaters Dec. 18. But until then, fans can revisit Gambit's appearance in Deadpool & Wolverine, streaming with a Disney+ subscription.

Ryan graduated from Missouri State University with a BA in English/Creative Writing. An expert in all things horror, Ryan enjoys covering a wide variety of topics. He's also a lifelong comic book fan and an avid watcher of Game of Thrones and House of the Dragon.

#3590. 'Boston Blue' Recasts Another 'Blue Bloods' Role After Surprise Cast Changes

Blue Bloods‘ spinoff, Boston Blue, is recasting another role from the original show.

Amaury Nolasco has been cast as Arturo Muñoz in an upcoming episode that will reintroduce the former cartel leader — who is also the biological father of Baez’s (Marisa Ramirez) adopted daughter, Elena. He was previously portrayed by Juan Francisco Villa in two episodes of Blue Bloods before the Boston Blue shakeup.

According to the official synopsis, Nolasco, 55, will appear in the December 11 episode when Baez’s daughter, Elena, “is kidnapped the morning of Sarah’s wedding,” and the Reagans and Silvers “launch a desperate search to bring her home.”

“As Danny and Lena pursue a lead involving Arturo Muñoz, Elena’s biological father and former head of the Mano Sangriento cartel, the investigation takes an unexpected turn,” the description continued.

This isn’t the first time Boston Blue has recast a role that originated on Blue Bloods. Danny’s (Donnie Wahlberg) journey in New York was featured on CBS’ Blue Bloods, which ran from 2010 to 2024. The spinoff, which premiered in October 2025, kicked off with Danny visiting Boston after Sean (Mika Amonsen) ended up in a coma. This version of Sean looked a little different because the role was previously played by Andrew Terraciano.

“It was a difficult decision — certainly for me — and it’s one of the decisions that made me uncertain about doing the show. It’s like, ‘How do we do this with a different [actor]?'” Wahlberg, 57, admitted to Us in February. “I have to say, Mika has the same level of grace and class that Andrew showed. Mika has great respect for Andrew. He stepped into the role very mindfully and carefully and he took his time. He was very thoughtful about how he went about playing this character.”

Terraciano, 23, also broke his silence on the onscreen swap.

“It’s beautiful because you’ll always remember every single line and every day that you had the opportunity to be that character. It doesn’t mean for even a second that somebody else can’t go and do something beautiful with it,” he shared with Us in December 2025. “I got the joy of playing Sean, and I got to send him off into the world. Now somebody else gets that joy. We’re both getting to show what we do and then send Sean off into the world.”

Terraciano specially mentioned Amonsen’s performance, adding, “I appreciate it because not only has there been such an outcry of love from the community, but there’s also a very clear love coming to the show.”

He explained: “It’s hundreds if not thousands of people who depend on their livelihood for a show to be made. It really is amazing that part of that character remains. Somebody can look back and say, ‘I want to pay homage to that. I want to respect that and I want to work on making something beautiful.'”

For Amonsen, 24, the transition has since gotten easier.

“That initial pressure from fans and making sure that I represented Sean in a way that Andrew would appreciate, fans would appreciate and have them understand that I wasn’t just coming into this creating whatever I wanted [was hard],” Amonsen exclusively told Us in March. “It’s been reciprocated well and I’m happy about that. But I think that that was the biggest challenge. At this point, I’ve slipped into comfortability.”

Boston Blue airs on CBS Fridays at 10 p.m. ET.
