#3498. Kelly Bishop Hints at Tension Between ‘Stars Hollow’ Group on ‘Gilmore Girls’

The unauthorized Gilmore Girls documentary, Drink Coffee, Talk Fast, is here to celebrate more than 25 years of the show’s iconic legacy.

Produced by Ink On Paper Studios and directed by Meghna Balakumar and Kevin Konrad Hanna, the doc features interviews with original cast and crew members, including Kelly Bishop, Scott Patterson, Jared Padalecki, Keiko Agena, Chad Michael Murray and more.

Keep scrolling to see the biggest revelations made in the film:

Diner owner Luke Danes, played by Scott Patterson, was originally intended to be a woman named Daisy. However, the character was ultimately rewritten when The WB requested “more testosterone” in the show to balance out the female characters. Of course, that decision brought fans the beloved romance between Luke and Lorelai Gilmore (Lauren Graham), so we can’t be too upset that Daisy never came to be.

Before Jared Padalecki took on the role of Rory Gilmore’s (Alexis Bledel) first boyfriend, Dean Forrester, two other actors had the role.

“We had to recast the role of Dean,” casting director Jami Rudofsky recalled in the doc.

Casting director Mara Casey added, “There was a Canadian Dean and then there was this other Dean. I think they fired two dudes.”

Padalecki, who was 17 years old when he auditioned for Gilmore Girls, was ready to return home to Texas if he didn’t land the part. Thankfully, Casey, Rudofsky and series creator Amy Sherman-Palladino were all instantly sold on him playing Dean.

Likewise, Lorelai’s best friend, Sookie St. James, was initially played by Alex Borstein in the unaired pilot episode before Melissa McCarthy took on the role. Borstein was unable to play the character due to a scheduling conflict, although she went on to appear in the show as Drella, the harp player, and Miss Celine.

Several actresses auditioned for the role of Lorelai, but one crucial line in the script solidified Graham as the lead.

“In that first scene in Luke’s Diner, there was a reference to Jack Kerouac,” director Lesli Linka Glatter said in the doc, recalling how Graham was the only actress to pronounce the famous novelist’s last name correctly.

“Amy’s writing had so many references to theater and literature and contemporary music,” Glatter recalled. “So we said, ‘You know what? We cannot have someone that doesn’t know who Jack Kerouac is.’”

During the early days of filming Gilmore Girls, The WB frequently called Sherman-Palladino with complaints about the script because the show didn’t fit the network’s target audience. She finally got the calls to stop when she issued an ultimatum: fire her or quit complaining. It worked.

Many of the cast members in the doc recalled having to be “word perfect” when reciting their lines on set. Even replacing “a” with “the” wasn’t allowed. They also had to talk very fast, which is where coffee came in handy.

“We used to have delicious coffee drinks on set,” Rose Abdoo, who played Gypsy, recalled. “We all talked even faster, and I thought, ‘OK, they’re not just trying to treat us. We’re really all jazzed up now.’ … It wasn’t one of those shows where people could improvise… no, every word is there for a reason.”

Murray, who played Chilton student Tristin Dugray, remembered being told by Sherman-Palladino, “Talk faster. I don’t want to cut any pages out of this show.”

Season 3 of Gilmore Girls featured an episode where Jess Mariano (Milo Ventimiglia) traveled to California to get to know his father. The episode doubled as a backdoor pilot for a spinoff called Windward Circle. Though Ventimiglia was on board with the spinoff, the WB ultimately canceled the project after the California episode received poor feedback. It was also reportedly too expensive to film in Venice Beach.

In the doc, Sherilyn Fenn, who played Sasha in the episode and was later recast as Anna Nardini, claimed that The WB thought Ventimiglia couldn’t lead a spinoff.

“The studio was so silly. They said, ‘Oh, Milo’s not strong enough to carry a show,’” she said. (Ventimiglia went on to star as Jack Pearson in the NBC drama This Is Us.)

Gilmore Girls had many cameos from actors who would go on to become famous, including Seth MacFarlane, Jane Lynch, Jon Hamm, Rami Malek and more. Ryan Gosling was almost on that list, too, but he bombed his audition, Rudofsky revealed.

Bledel’s first major role was playing Rory in Gilmore Girls when she was 18 years old. Though she expressed gratitude for the opportunities the show brought her, cast and crew members recalled in the doc that she sometimes struggled with the grueling filming schedule.

“She was just like 18 years old, and ‘I’m here for 60, 70 hours a week. What am I doing with my life?’ And it’s pretty, it’s gruelling,” Mark Strasburg, first assistant camera, said. “It’s something you really had to want to do. There were definitely moments she knew she didn’t want to be there.”

The doc also featured footage of an older interview with Patterson in which he admitted, “Alexis was really overwhelmed by being away from her family, maybe having some second thoughts about what she had gotten herself into. ‘Is this really a way to spend my youth?’ She was terribly homesick. And what was nice to see was the bond that formed off the set between Lauren and Alexis, because Lauren really helped her out.”

While the doc’s participants had mostly fond memories of their time on Gilmore Girls, Kelly Bishop, who played Emily Gilmore, alluded to some behind-the-scenes drama between cast members.

“I loved working with that little nucleus of a family. The Hartford group got along great,” she recalled, referring to herself, the late Ed Herrmann (who played Richard Gilmore), Bledel and Graham. “I guess there was a little bit of problems here and there in Stars Hollow, and I’m not gonna tell you what they were because it’s none of my business, and it was hearsay and I don’t do that.”

While Bishop did not name-drop anyone, others suggested that Graham and Patterson didn’t get along off camera. George Anthony Bell, the show’s dialogue coach, noted that he didn’t think the pair “hung out after the show,” while Strasburg added, “Off screen, I’m not sure if they’re besties, but they don’t really seem to really like each other. But on screen they’re amazing.”

Graham and Patterson previously shut down rumors of a feud. In 2007, Graham told TV Guide that their friendship was a “working relationship like most of them are. But he was so great in that part. I really loved my scenes with him and the chemistry we had. Our banter was among the most fun stuff to do.”

Patterson told 7News in 2023, “I love her, she loves me, we get along very, very well.”

#3497. Lil’ Kim Takes The Spotlight—With A Symphony

When you hear the name Lil’ Kim, a variety of images come to mind. She’s forever known as the force of nature from Brooklyn who turned the music industry on its head when she entered the scene, and her bodacious lyrics and unique fashion sense have kept her as a source of inspiration on your favorite designer’s mood board ever since. On November 18 and 19, to celebrate the music that cemented her icon status, Lil’ Kim will perform in front of a symphony orchestra at the Kings Theatre in Brooklyn, not far from her humble beginnings.

Today she’s less interested in being in the spotlight and more focused on raising her 12-year-old daughter, Royal Reign. In between practices for her performances, Lil’ Kim spoke with Vanity Fair to reflect on her career, how she spends her days, and her standout looks.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vanity Fair: What do you remember about putting your debut album, Hard Core, together?

Lil’ Kim: I remember Biggie and Un [Lance Rivera], who was the label owner that we had. I watched Un build a record label called Undeas, which [stood] for “Un ideas,” and then he finally sold it to Atlantic Records. At the time, we didn’t know the process, but we became Undeas-Atlantic. I remember Biggie having the idea of how he wanted my album to be red, and he explained it to me and Un. I was able to write according to how his idea was to present me, because when they met me, I was who I was—in high heels, jeans, motorcycle jackets, and furs at 13.

Portrait of members of R&B group 112 and rappers Notorious BIG and Lil’ Kim circa 1996

That’s incredible. It sounds like your fashion-icon status started very early. Was there anyone that you looked to back then? What inspired you to dress that way?

My mom was a big inspiration to me when it came to fashion, and so I looked to her for a lot of things. I used to wear her mink coat. She used to wear big sunglasses with her fur coats, with the diamonds and jewelry. She was always taking vacations and I would see her pack her stuff, and she would always have the cutest outfits. They were all matchy-matchy. It’s funny because she would have her outfit to go play tennis in and her outfit would match her tennis racket. So when I bought my big house, I bought a Chanel tennis outfit and I bought the racket to match it, because of my mom.

I love that. Do you keep up with tennis or specifically the ladies in tennis?

No, I haven’t in a while, but, of course, you know, Serena and Venus were like my heroes.

Well, maybe we need to see you on the court one day.

I know. I’m pretty sure I’m rusty, but I like to get out there, though. I used to beat my cousin’s butt back then.

How did the symphony performances come about?

My agents called me and they’re like, “Kim, what do you think?” And I was like, “That’s a freaking awesome idea.” I love performing with bands. And so I imagine that it could be very similar, if not very close. And I thought this could be something really different for me. Sometimes I even listen to classical music. I don’t have to know who the artist is, but I just put on a station and let it flow.

Do you have a favorite song from Hard Core?

I love “Queen Bitch”; it’s my favorite song. It’s still my favorite to perform. And “Crush on You.”

Salma Hayek, Donatella Versace, Pamela Anderson, and Lil’ Kim at Versace’s spring/summer 2001 fashion show

When it comes to fashion, you’re obviously on everyone’s mood board, from stylists to designers, so how important was fashion for you as part of the Lil’ Kim persona?

I just was being myself, honestly. When I first met Biggie, I was coming from my after-school job at Bloomingdale’s. I was probably 13 or 14 at the time, and they would let the teenagers work there.

But I had on a motorcycle jacket and high heels. And one of my best friends told Biggie, “You know, my girl can rap,” because we knew he was rapping around the way. And he was like, “I heard you can rap.” And I just laughed. He was like, “Yeah, see, I knew you didn’t know how to rap.” He was very condescending. He knew how to get you to do what you wanted to do, because I was really shy.

And then I started rapping, and he was blown away because I had on high heels. No one had ever seen someone just bust a rap in high heels. When Biggie, Un, and Jacob York started really talking to me, they didn’t want to change me because that was just what they were so blown away about. That was just who I was.

Do you think people ever misunderstood the way you presented yourself?

To be honest, I never really felt misunderstood by my hardcore fans—the kids my age and the younger kids, they totally got it. I think that’s why I had such a cult following and there was such pandemonium about me when I came out. They understood me. I think it was the older people and the politicians, those are the people who I think misunderstood me.

What did you think of the midterm elections and all of the women who broke barriers in the Senate and gubernatorial offices?

I’m going to be honest with you, I stay away from politics.

Are you keeping up with all of the changes within fashion today? When I listen to your music, you’ve mentioned so many designers and houses, and since then the creative directors have changed. Are you following all of the changes within fashion and seeing how you’re still a part of the conversation?

That’s what I’m trying to say. As a fashion icon, if you really her, and I’m considering myself really her, that’s never gonna change. That’s never going to change. I might put on a fur coat that my stylist or myself will get asked about, because I style myself a lot. And I was styling myself then.

Lil’ Kim and daughter, Royal Reign, on June 16, 2016, in New York City

Extremely rewarding. My daughter’s with me all the time. This world is so cruel and so evil; it’s so different. She’s my safe haven. I feel the extra need to keep her safe.

What does a regular day look like for you?

Lately, I’ve just been really getting into myself. I get up and go have a little spa day. I might take my daughter to go do whatever she wants.

Singer Mary J. Blige with Diana Ross and Lil’ Kim at the 1999 MTV Video Music Awards on September 9, 1999

How do you feel that we’re still talking about your MTV VMAs look in 1999?

I think it’s iconic and I love it. I love when they bring that up, because it was a fun day and it was so good to see people’s faces when they saw my outfit.

Are there any other looks that don’t get as much love as you wish that they did?

I don’t know, because most of the looks that I love, they get the love. There’s a look when I was on the cover of Nylon magazine and I had the teddy bear dress on; that’s one of my favorite looks. The Louis Vuitton look is one of my favorite looks; I love that look. A lot of the Chanel looks and the Versace and the Chanel in the hair.

Johnny Depp returning to theaters in Ebenezer on the 2026 movie schedule, renewed interest has grown in whether he'll ever play Captain Jack Sparrow again. Producer Jerry Bruckheimer has already confirmed that discussions have taken place about bringing Depp back for Pirates of the Caribbean 6, although nothing has been officially announced. Now another familiar face from the original movies has weighed in, and I have to admit, this is one reunion I'd love to see happen.

Mackenzie Crook, who played the perpetually confused Ragetti in the first three Pirates movies, recently discussed the possibility of returning to the franchise during an appearance on The Daily Beast's Obsessed podcast. The actor, who starred alongside Lee Arenberg's Pintel as one of the series' most entertaining comedic duos, hasn't appeared in a Pirates movie since 2007's At World's End. Although nearly 20 years later, he sounds more than willing to dig out that wooden eye. Crook explained:

Yes, I think I would for the hell of it. It would be so interesting – obviously it would depend on the script – to even just have a cameo to see what happened to those characters, Pintel and Ragetti, what happened to them after we last saw them. Again, I was really fond of those characters and working with Lee Arenberg, who plays Pintel. Yeah, we had a blast doing that stuff. It was great.

I would absolutely love this. Pintel and Ragetti were two of my favorite supporting characters from the original trilogy, and their ridiculous behavior provided some great comic relief between all the sword fights and increasingly more extravagant set pieces.

For anybody who needs a refresher, the pair started as members of Barbossa's cursed crew in The Curse of the Black Pearl. Ragetti was the skinny, somewhat dimwitted pirate with a wooden eye. Pintel was his considerably louder and equally incompetent partner.

Somehow, they survived three movies filled with undead pirates, sea monsters and increasingly complicated betrayals. That's honestly impressive considering how frequently they seemed to have no idea what was going on. While I certainly want to see Johnny Depp return as Jack Sparrow, I think bringing back characters like these could be just as important to making another Pirates movie feel connected to the originals.

Crook also had some interesting memories of working on the films. During the interview, he recalled the sometimes exhausting experience of shooting aboard actual ships at sea. He also discussed the rather uncomfortable process of bringing Ragetti's wooden eye to life, which required wearing two contact lenses, including one designed to create the appearance of wood grain.

Apparently, playing a pirate wasn't quite as glamorous as it looked. The actor also reflected on the amount of practical filmmaking involved in the original trilogy. Although the movies relied heavily on visual effects, Crook remembered productions where crews actually rigged ships with explosives rather than recreating everything digitally. He described those experiences as some of the last examples of old-fashioned blockbuster filmmaking.

I think that's part of what makes those first three movies so much fun to revisit with a Disney+ subscription. Even when the stories got complicated, something fantastically chaotic about watching these characters run around enormous pirate ships, usually making whatever situation they were in considerably worse. Of course, whether any of them actually return is another matter.

Bruckheimer previously confirmed that he's been speaking with Depp about a sixth movie, although the project remains in development. Depp recently suggested he'd be interested in helping give the franchise a proper sendoff, particularly if it meant working with Bruckheimer again.

Meanwhile, other original cast members have expressed interest in returning. Orlando Bloom has discussed the possibility of another Pirates movie, though there's still no indication that Will Turner will be part of whatever Disney ultimately decides to make.

That's really where we stand. There's no confirmed cast or release date for Pirates of the Caribbean 6, and Crook's comments are just an expression of interest, not evidence he's been approached.

I do like his idea of a cameo that lets audiences catch up with Pintel and Ragetti. It's been almost two decades since we last saw the two idiots, and I can't help wondering what they've been doing with themselves.

Ryan graduated from Missouri State University with a BA in English/Creative Writing. An expert in all things horror, Ryan enjoys covering a wide variety of topics. He's also a lifelong comic book fan and an avid watcher of Game of Thrones and House of the Dragon.

#3495. Jennifer Connelly's Forgotten '90s Disney Superhero Movie Deserved Its Own Franchise

After Tim Burton's "Batman" film became an inescapably huge success in the summer of 1989 and set off to expand into its weirdly experimental sequel in 1992, there was a mad rush by other studios to hop a trend and get their own piece of that lucrative superhero pie — sort of. Studio executives of the early '90s seem to have been drawn more to Burton's retro aesthetics than the actual idea of a superhero, so rather than expanding into bringing other iconic DC characters like Wonder Woman to the big screen, or heading across the street to give the Marvel universe a shot at cinematic glory, we got a rush of big-screen revivals of other throwback comic strip heroes. The results were, well, let's just put it nicely and say they were pretty mixed in terms of quality.

While they undoubtedly have their fans out there, pulp hero movies like 1990's "Dick Tracy," 1994's "The Shadow," and 1996's "The Phantom" simply were not able to reach the same levels of success. It may have been that audiences just liked Batman way more than they liked characters who had never been as popular as the Caped Crusader, or that these movies just weren't very good. Maybe people were just simply not prepared to slam evil. Whatever it was, none of those movies managed to launch their heroes into a franchise.

There is, however, one member of that crowd that absolutely deserved better: 1991's "The Rocketeer," in which Jennifer Connelly, Billy Campbell, and a rocket-powered jetpack faced off against Nazis in Los Angeles circa 1938.

One big difference that set "The Rocketeer" apart from the surrounding crop of pulp hero flicks was that its source material was actually pretty contemporary. Cliff Secord and his supporting cast were created in 1982 by the legendary comics creator Dave Stevens, and had been an indie favorite since its introduction. All things considered, Stevens produced a relatively small number of comics about the Rocketeer — his entire run with the character fits into a single 120-page hardcover — but his lavish, gorgeous art and incredible storytelling make it a timeless classic even today. Sadly, Stevens passed away in 2008 after a long battle with leukemia, which had long affected his output.

Looking back, it's easy to see why Disney jumped on "The Rocketeer." Since it was a throwback to the adventure serials and comic strip heroes of the '30s and '40s, Stevens' work already had the modern spin on the kind of pulpy action that movies like "Dick Tracy" and "The Shadow" struggled with, and incorporated a lot of the same elements. In fact, the "Rocketeer" comics even included thinly veiled versions of pulp heroes like The Shadow and Doc Savage in supporting roles, with just enough of their serial numbers filed off to avoid a copyright lawsuit. (Needless to say, those characters didn't make it into the film version.)

There were real-life influences, too; in the film, the jetpack was created by Howard Hughes, and Timothy Dalton's villainous Neville Sinclair was based on actor (and real-life villain) Errol Flynn. Connelly's character, appropriately renamed Jenny, was based on Cliff's comics girlfriend Betty, who was in turn inspired by pin-up icon Bettie Page, of whom Stevens was a dedicated and unabashed fan.

As for the film, while it lacks the lushness of Stevens' comics art, it told the classic story of "boy loves girl, boy finds rocket pack, boy has to rescue girl from an evil Nazi actor played by one of the lesser James Bonds" in a fun, engaging way that made it a cult classic. It also has a connection to the modern Marvel Cinematic Universe. Two decades after "The Rocketeer," its director, Joe Johnston, would direct another, more successful retro-inspired superhero movie, 2011's "Captain America: The First Avenger."

According to an interview with Stevens, the original plan for "The Rocketeer" had been to make a trilogy that would've skewed slightly more adult:

"So, we had a lot of interesting meetings with executives who passed on it but gave us some good criticisms. The last studio on the list was Disney. They took one look at it, and said 'toys!' So ... that's where we eventually made the deal. We originally signed on as a trilogy at Touchstone, the division of Disney doing more adult-themed films. [...] As soon as we all signed on, [Disney executive Jeffrey] Katzenberg pulled a switch and said, 'Nope, it's going to be a Disney release, because Disney needs a live-action hit.' So immediately, Betty and anything else "adult" went right out with the bathwater."

We'll never know if a more adult-oriented version of "The Rocketeer" that kept elements like Betty's glamour modeling day job intact would've been successful enough to get us that trilogy, but the movie we got is well worth revisiting, even though it was crushed by "Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves" and "Terminator 2" at the box office.

#3494. The Mighty Nein Season 2 Officially Has Fans Worried About One Major Plot Change

Prime Video teases a pirate-soaked second season, but will some major developments be left behind?

The Mighty Nein season 2 is officially set to return to our TV screens in March 2027. And while Critical Role fans may be a little put out by Amazon's new episode schedule, the season’s content has Critters excited for what’s to come from our band of lovable misfits.

However, there does seem to be a significant catch: Season 2 may be widening the gap between the show and the original Dungeons & Dragons campaign even further than season 1 did. While the first season already moved away from the source campaign in several ways, the second season could be taking those departures even further.

[Ed. note: This article contains spoilers for the tabletop campaign of The Mighty Nein.]

Prime Video’s announcement for season 2 of The Mighty Nein gave Critters a glimpse of what to expect. You can read the summary below.

“In Season Two, The Mighty Nein set off on a pirate adventure across the high seas as they face their complicated pasts and hurtle toward a treacherous future. While Fjord’s burgeoning powers tempt him down a dark path, the Beacon reveals its own enticing possibilities, and the group must choose between newfound magic and their friendship.”

On the surface, it looks like business as usual for the Mighty Nein (there are only seven of them, but we digress). However, some eagle-eyed Critters who have watched the original 141 episodes of the tabletop campaign have started to speculate what this new plot summary could mean for The Mighty Nein season 2’s story.

Last time, Critters left off with the Mighty Nein encountering the aasimar barbarian Yasha in the Zadash sewers after stealing the Luxon Beacon. Briefly free from the mind-control of Obann, a cambion, Yasha pleaded with the group to help her.

Though season 1 has already introduced several differences — for example, Yasha wasn’t introduced alongside Mollymauk as part of the Fletching and Moondrop Traveling Carnival of Curiosities troupe — the new season’s summary, combined with season 1’s ending, has fans speculating that the Iron Shepherds arc may be skipped entirely in favor of jumping straight to the Mighty Nein’s pirate arc.

The Iron Shepherds arc is a formative experience for the group, as it comes shortly after the Mighty Nein are given a task by the Gentleman (a crime boss in the city of Zadash) to head to Shadycreek Run and retrieve an ally of his. However, on the way there, the group is ambushed in the middle of the night, resulting in the capture of Fjord, Jester, and Yasha by a group of slavers known as The Iron Shepherds. When the rest of the group tries to deal with the slavers, they find themselves overwhelmed, with Mollymauk dying in the process.

The plot summary of Season 2, however, suggests nothing of the sort; its main focus is the pirate arc that comes afterward. Now, this could be Critical Role and Prime Video choosing to obscure the Iron Shepherds arc entirely to surprise new fans with what’s to come. That said, given how many changes Critical Role has already made to the campaign — and for what it’s worth, we think they are for the better — there’s also a chance the Iron Shepherds' encounter will be woven into the pirate arc. After all, the Mighty Nein make plenty of enemies during that arc, too, including Captain Avantika, who plays a major role in Fjord’s storyline. Could she be the one who ends up slaughtering Mollymauk?

It’s hard to predict what changes are coming to The Mighty Nein season 2, but given how much the first season changed from the original campaign, Critters should brace for even more in March 2027.

The Mighty Nein airs exclusively on Prime Video. Season 1 is available to watch now, with season 2 set to debut on March 24, 2027.

#3493. Teresa Giudice Claims 'Well-Known TV Actress' Was 'So Rude' to Her in New Book

Teresa Giudice might be the self-proclaimed queen of New Jersey, but that hasn’t protected her from being slighted by A-list celebrities from time to time.

Teresa, 54, recalled in her new memoir, The Queen of New Jersey, that unlike meeting the “gracious” Taylor Swift at Coachella Music Festival, “Not every celebrity interaction goes quiet as well.”

She recounted an alleged incident in the book involving an unnamed TV actress that transpired shortly after she rose to fame in 2009 on The Real Housewives of New Jersey.

“[I] was once instructed by my PR team to pose with a well-known TV actress for a photo,” Teresa wrote, noting that the women were both in Los Angeles for an appearance with TV host Mario Lopez. “After we took the photo, I overheard her telling her PR people, ‘Why are you making me take a picture with that woman?’”

The Bravolebrity remembered, “The tone of her voice was so surprising,” writing, “Look, I get if she didn’t know who I was, but to me, that’s just so rude.”

Teresa didn’t identify the actress, but revealed that years later she was back in L.A. having dinner with her husband, Luis “Louie” Ruelas, when a fan came in and asked her for a picture.

“It’s part of this life, and one I happen to enjoy. We took a photo together and chatted for a minute, and then she left us to be seated at her own table,” she shared. “Ten minutes later, who walks in? The actress who had definitely not wanted to take a picture with me all that time ago backstage at Mario Lopez’s show.”

Teresa recalled, “We made brief eye contact — there was definitely no need to say hi — as she was shown to her table.”

The cherry on top for Teresa was when she realized that the actress’ dinner date was the fan who asked her for a photo moments earlier.

“I hope she enjoyed feigning interest as her friend showed her the pictures we’d taken just moments before,” Teresa jokingly wrote.

The reality star added, “I’ll always have respect for a celebrity who doesn’t forget where they came from or who made them. There are a lot of people in this business who can’t stand to stop and pose for a photo or sign something for a fan. Like, really? You think you’re such a big deal that you can’t spare a moment for the very audience whose attention made you who you are?”

The actress in question has not been identified, but there are publicly available photos that show Teresa filming a segment with Lopez, 53, in May 2011 for Extra, which fans speculate could be when the alleged slight took place. No other famous individuals are visible in the pictures.

In addition to juicy tales of celebrity run-ins, Teresa’s new book promises to tell-all — including the highs and lows of her RHONJ break, her first husband Joe Giudice’s deportation and her road to a second love. (Teresa will be back for season 15 of RHONJ, premiering in January, following the show’s hiatus.)

“Only a true queen can rise and fall and rise again, sweetheart. Take notes,” the book tease reads.

The memoir will reflect on Teresa’s “two tumultuous decades in the public eye,” as well as her “biggest triumphs, heartbreaks, feuds, and controversies of her life with newfound perspective,” according to the brief synopsis.

“Raw, funny, emotional, and unapologetic, The Queen of New Jersey is the story of a woman who has been cast as everything from villain to victim — but refuses to let anyone else write her legacy,” the publisher adds. “After all, if the crown fits, wear it.”

The Queen of New Jersey is now available for purchase.

#3492. Netflix Adds The 2026 Horror Movie That Made Over 500x Its Budget At The Box Office

"Obsession" passed a box office milestone only five other horror films ever have when it crossed the $500 million mark. That would be an achievement regardless of its budget, but this movie only cost $600,000 to $750,000 to make. That means that when "Obsession" brought in $524.4 million by the end of its unprecedented box office run, it had made more than 500 times its budget.

For a while, that made "Obsession" the most profitable movie ever at the box office, until it was technically dethroned by the low-budget Chinese movie "Niu Lai." Still, it remains one of the most stunning horror success stories of recent years, which is especially impressive considering we've seen multiple low-budget horror movies become hits of late. But if you somehow managed to miss out on all of this, or just want to revisit one of the best horror movies of 2026, Netflix has you covered.

"Obsession" has a relatively simple premise, yet its execution and the lead performances elevate it beyond your typical low-budget horror fare. The film stars Michael Johnston as Baron "Bear" Bailey, a luckless music store worker who has a major crush on his friend/co-worker Nikki Freeman (Inde Navarrette). After buying a One Wish Willow toy, he wishes that Nikki loved him more than anyone in the world and gets everything he asked for and more. The only problem is, Nikki becomes absolutely obsessed with him, to the extent she's willing to hurt anyone who gets in her way.

It's well worth doing so. "Obsession" is a confident crowd-pleaser with a killer lead performance from Navarette. In fact the actor's portrayal of Nikki proved to be her breakout turn, landing Navarrette a role as Rogue in the Marvel Cinematic Universe's upcoming "X-Men" movie reboot. No doubt, more high-profile roles await. As such, even if you're not too intrigued by the prospect of a twisted girlfriend causing violent chaos, you should at least check out "Obsession" to see one of the best performances of 2026 and the beginning of a star's ascendence. The film is streaming on Netflix as of November 17, 2026.

We’re only a few days away from the Traitors: New Blood finale, and I’m willing to admit the obvious. This has not been the best season of The Traitors. In fact, you could easily say this has been a below-average season. Fans on social media and those I have talked to in real life seem to all be in agreement on that. There’s a growing consensus that the show needs to change. I think producers are going to listen, though I’m terrified they’re going to misunderstand the why.

The biggest, loudest and most obvious change we’ve gotten this season has been the casting of non-celebrities. The US version of The Traitors has historically relied on reality television personalities to provide the drama and bring their fanbases. This season, NBC decided to move the property from Peacock to network television and cast it like a more traditional competition show with randoms. It would be easy to just look at that decision and blame all the problems on the newbies, but that’s actually not the right takeaway.

The biggest problem by a very large margin with Traitors: New Blood is the episode runtimes. The show simply does not work in an hour-long time slot on NBC. In theory, the episodes on Peacock are the same length, as they’re typically between an hour and an hour and ten minutes. Because they’re on streaming, however, that runtime is the actual length of each episode. On network television, an hour-long time slot is actually forty-two minutes or so of real content, which isn’t even close to the amount of time the players need to complete one cycle of the game.

That means every single episode, the editors are making an impossible choice. They can either not include one or more major elements of the show (the breakfast, the mission, the roundtable and the turret), they can completely remove all of the strategy scenes that happen between those major elements, or they can drop most of the confessionals where the players talk directly to the camera and tell us their motivations and theories. There is simply no way to get through all of that in forty-two minutes. So, that has left every episode feeling either incomplete because it didn’t make it through a full cycle of the game, or feeling like a highlight video that simply recaps the basics of what happened.

That format and structure are the problem. The runtime is the problem. It’s not the cast. Even with less confessionals and less screentime, we’ve gotten good content from these players. I’m not saying the Traitors: New Blood cast is better than the cast on Big Brother 14 or Survivor: Heroes vs Villains, but there are some breakout personalities here and plenty of likeable, solid characters who have popped and would have looked even better with more of a chance to talk to the camera.

Victor is an all-time great Traitors character and should be a reality television mainstay moving forward. He’s electric. I’m personally obsessed with Jay and have had probably ten conversations with people trying to figure out his vibe and what’s going on in his head. It’s not just those two standouts either. There are a half dozen or so other players who play hard and are capable of delivering strong confessionals. Joe, Katie, Tomica, Michael and Shane have all had great moments, and when given a chance, secondary characters like Wyatt, Clyde, Abby, Abbey, Kriste, Ben, Morgan and others have delivered too. They’re just not always getting the screentime because, once again, every episode feels like it’s set on 1.5X speed.

Survivor and The Amazing Race have lengthened their episodes in recent years to help develop the characters and let the episodes breathe more. That’s the obvious solution here for The Traitors. It either needs to move to 90 minutes, or it needs to move back to Peacock. What it absolutely does not need to do is give up on casting newbies. The UK and other countries have had fantastic seasons using randoms, and in an ideal world, it would be a delight to watch Peacock/ NBC switch back and forth between a season with reality stars and a season with plumbers, farmers and firefighters.

I love The Traitors. It’s one of my favorite shows on television, and despite the obvious format issues, I still enjoyed the content we got this season. I’d like to see producers listen to the fan frustration and make a change, but those alterations should be exclusively focused on the format and not on casting.

#3490. Stacey Abrams in Conversation With Ta-Nehisi Coates

When I first met Stacey Abrams in 2015, she passed on to me the message that she was then passing on to anyone who’d listen: Someday soon, Georgia would be blue. This struck me as unlikely. But three years later Abrams ran for governor, and shocked the country by coming within two points of winning. Then two years later, when Joe Biden sealed his presidential election in 2020 with a win in Georgia, and Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff won Senate seats, Abrams looked prophetic. Now, Democrats have gone beyond Georgia, penetrating into the deepest reaches of the South—Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas. To understand how the GOP’s Solid South grew brittle, I could think of no better person to talk to than Abrams.

The following conversation has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Ta-Nehisi Coates: My recollection of our first meeting goes back to 2015, when I was promoting Between the World and Me. You interviewed me for the book. We had a wonderful discussion. My family was actually in the audience, because, like all Black folks, I have family in Atlanta. They were so excited. I was talking to Stacey Abrams—Minority Leader Stacey Abrams. And one of the things you said backstage was, “We’re going to make Georgia blue.” And I don’t know that I scoffed at you. I like to think I wasn’t quite that rude.

Stacey Abrams: Your eyebrow arched a bit.

I confess to the eyebrow arching. And so the eyebrow arched and you made the case. Can you tell me what you saw?

I’d gone through redistricting, and one of the component pieces of redistricting, of course, is that it’s predicated on the census. The US census is a tool that is incredibly powerful and deeply inexact. It was the first time Republicans had power to draw the lines since Reconstruction. And I took a posture in my caucus, and it was this: “If you vote for their maps, I will come after your seats.” And I was not only unequivocal in saying it, I wrote it down because I didn’t want anyone to misquote me.

In order to take that posture, I had to read the maps myself. And what I saw was that Republicans were placing bets that, by drawing the lines a certain way, they were going to give themselves 124 of 180 seats. So 67% of the seats, even though they’d only won the election by 57%.

But I looked at those same maps and I’m like, In this place, in this part of Paulding County, there is a new subdivision that is predominantly Black. And in this part of Gwinnett County, there is a burgeoning Korean population that is now going into its second generation, which means a lot of those will be eligible voters. And down in South Georgia, you have third-generation migrant farm workers who are Latino, but who have decided to plant their roots here and raise their families here. When you looked at those numbers, the maps had a very different story to tell about Republican dominance: They could win for a decade. They could not win for a generation.

We tell ourselves stories about the information we get, and people repeat stories without ever reading it themselves. There are a lot of people who can quote Tom Sawyer who’ve never read the book. And so in our politics, that happens a lot, that the story that becomes popular doesn’t ever get traced back to its origin or to the original text.

What I saw in Georgia is true in Louisiana, in Mississippi, in Tennessee, in Alabama, in South Carolina. We just saw it happen in North Carolina.

So when you saw this wave of redistricting happening around the country this year, did you see a similar opportunity?

Oh, absolutely. I was in Tennessee the day that they passed the maps and what stuck out for me was Raumesh Akbari, who’s the Senate minority leader, she asked to see the bill, and the Republican chair of the committee said, “Well, we don’t have a bill yet, but we know what it’s going to say.” They planned to vote on it even though they did not have the text of the bill.

The Republicans were moving so fast because they thought they understood what they were pulling together. Justin Pearson didn’t pick up the seat he wanted, but they were at risk of losing a seat they thought was going to be theirs because they misread the topography, but they didn’t do a deeper dive into exactly what was laying in the crevices. And that’s where opportunity for us is born.

There are not enough Black people to win any single seat outright on their own in most legislative districts, and no statewide elections, especially post–Louisiana v. Callais, but there are coalitions that can be built. And what I saw from the very beginning was the possibility of coalition.

What I see for the South, what I think the South proved on Tuesday, is the possibility of coalition, but coalition does not happen without conflict. It does not happen without conversation, and it does not happen when we have convinced ourselves of the permanence of our second-class citizenship and our subjugation. What we saw on Tuesday was a moment where people realized that the power to improve their own lives had become so desperately thin that they had to use it or lose it. We cannot rely on that for the next two years.

What I hear you saying is that the last two years created an emergency. But that can’t be depended on. It can’t be “The Most Important Election of Our Lifetime” every two years. Desperation is not enough.

It can’t be. Desperation gets you one moment. There’s a whole body of medical research on people that have heart attacks and they get saved. And what it shows is that they are exercise fiends for about six weeks and then they fall back into their patterns because it’s a normalcy bias.

If we constantly feel on the edge of danger, we cannot function. And so we reorient our understanding of normal to survive. And therefore our responsibility in this moment is to look at the opportunity that was revealed on Tuesday, but not read into it that that opportunity either requires desperation or it requires this milquetoast approach, because our default is not just normalcy, but the most banal form of normalcy we can imagine.

I know you have some concerns about some of the narratives emerging out of the midterms. Would you talk a bit about that?

I saw something on Axios that I think was well-intentioned and it essentially said that the threats to our democracy were overblown, that our courts held, that our Congress held, that our presidency wasn’t overreaching, and that for normal people, things were fine. How have we reached the place where we think it is normal that the capital city in the United States of America is under military occupation? How is it okay that the courts held when it permits the incarceration of children in Dilley, Texas, and the kidnapping of people of color because of race and the language that they speak? There is something aggressively privileged about this idea that democracy is not in jeopardy because those who are the most protected don’t feel harm.

But Tuesday was a repudiation of this idea that things are normal. You saw turnout at extraordinary levels from a cross section of communities, almost all of whom have been directly impacted by the harms of this administration. Not just the economic harms that hit everyone, but harms that were amplified and refined for their cruelty.

At the same time, there’s a worry that I have that, because we won control of Congress for the patriots—and that’s how I frame it, I no longer think it’s just Democrat versus Republican, it’s patriots versus authoritarians—even though the patriots may have gained more purchase in Congress, we still have a Supreme Court that gutted the last vestiges of protection for the Voting Rights Act. We still have a Supreme Court that stripped women of their bodily autonomy. We still have a Supreme Court that has said that protections that are afforded by DEI are somehow suspect. And when those are true, then the successes of Tuesday don’t signal that we’ve won. They signal that we have to work even harder because the harms have not dissipated, they just haven’t penetrated.

You said something a few months back that’s stuck with me—that our elections are ripe for entertainment. As a sports fan, I think it’s not a coincidence that so many sports figures are now commenting on politics because the way they appear on TV is actually quite similar to the way sports appears. You have these long campaigns, which is like your season. Then you have primaries, which are like your playoffs, and then you have this big Super Bowl that happens on Tuesday. And so, it’s an entertainment and ratings bonanza. And I think, as I recall, you were cautioning against that as a view of politics. Can you speak a little bit more about that?

Yeah. When you think about politics, if you think about elections as an event, and to extend your analogy, if the elections are the finals, if the elections are game seven, if it’s the Super Bowl, when that happens, then the day after, you go home, the game is over. But the challenge I have is that it’s not just that we treat it as a sporting event, it’s that we treat politics as though we are spectators at a sporting event. And when we look at the other party, it’s like we are spectators watching a very disciplined, seasoned team that practices in the off-season, that travels together, that plays overseas. They’re constantly engaged and we are on and off. We think of politics, again, as entertainment as opposed to the job.

How did we end up with this entertainment narrative?

Theodore White did this series where he examined elections 1960, 1964, 1968, 1972. And when you read it, as someone who is reading it in the 21st century, the arc of how we have viewed politics changed dramatically, specifically in 1960 with the advent of television, because the election contest between John Kennedy and Richard Nixon hinged in no small part on that televised debate. And I think for you and me and for anyone who wasn’t old enough to see it, I did not realize that it was one of the most watched programs in American history. We take for granted how many people are going to watch the debates these days, but with that first debate, it was one of the most watched programs in the world because it had never happened before. And the moment it became a television spectacle, it became entertainment because you were watching, you picked winners and losers, you picked your villain and you picked your champion.

It’s human nature, we put things into these narrative arcs. As someone who writes comic books, you understand this. As someone who writes thrillers, I think about this. You create a villain, you have a protagonist, an antagonist, you have to have a storyline, you have to have complications, and when television became the medium, it added a layer and a texture to what had long been the mechanics of politics. Then you add into it the drama of Black and brown people getting to participate. And then you layer on top of that “blue state versus red state,” and the sharp division, and the attribution to entire regions of a value system and a personality based on a single day.

What would it mean to remain engaged beyond elections? When I think about the conservative movement, I think about the degree to which the religious right is engaged. I think about Trump rallies. I think people were baffled by this at first—the clothes, the trucks, the boats. But what I would say is those are markers of community. They aren’t my politics. But they seem part of something larger than a particular bill or policy.

There’s a lot of talk in organizing about going for belief first, or belonging first. On the left, we are often accused of belief, that you have to be in line with all of our ideas, our values, our ideologies, but also the tactical, practical ways of exercising them, and that because we say you have to believe first, we filter out people who haven’t had time to understand or adapt or even decide what they believe. The right uses belonging. They say, “Come and be a part of us, and we’ll tell you what we are.” So you get the jersey, you get the cap, you get the red, you get to use the language, even if you haven’t decided that you actually believe all they believe, which is why you have people who are suddenly surprised that this is what happened.

We have to shift. Not to say that we don’t have beliefs, but we have to give people time to grow into those beliefs. I come at this from my time as minority leader. I had a caucus of 60 members in a chamber of 180, and my members included suburban white mothers and rural Black pastors and everything in between. We were the most racially diverse caucus. We were geographically diverse. And I had no power. I was the minority leader. My job was to help harmonize their approach. I could not lead with belief, because people were entitled to their beliefs, but my job was to bring them into belonging first because they were members of the caucus. And then my second job was to make sure that anyone who needed them to believe something had the platform to offer the tutelage.

That’s the place where I think we are failing. We don’t do the tutelage. We say, “There has been a conversation, this is now our truth. And if you don’t adopt that truth, you are somehow opposed to it,” as opposed to, “You haven’t adopted the truth because you don’t know what it means and you don’t understand it and you haven’t experienced it. Let me give you time and space to come in,” or, “You have legitimate disagreement, and maybe on this, we will not be in alignment, but your disagreement should not lead to hostility against my community.”

The Democratic Socialists of America have attracted a lot of attention recently, but one thing they seem to do is this “belonging” piece. I can’t say I understood this before, but I was talking to someone for a story, and then mentioned the social environment. So here in New York, when people go out to canvas, afterwards, they all go out for beers. The beers are not really the point, but making people feel like they belong to something is.

Yeah. I mean, what they are doing is what works in most effective social movements. During the Vietnam War, one of the most effective protest waves happened at coffee shops. You brought people together around the table, they got to vent about what they were upset about, they went out and protested and then they came back together. People like being liked.

In terms of belief, how does one do that and not make those who are in that coalition who are particularly vulnerable feel abandoned? Obviously, I mean, this is not the only case, but I’m thinking about the tremendous amount of negative attention brought on the trans community. What do you do when the “belonging” comes in conflict with actually protecting the members of your coalition?

My first position is, if you have a faith that tells you it is okay to cause harm because you feel uncomfortable, I need to understand where your faith lies. Our first responsibility is the protection of difference. And it is to say you don’t have to embrace, but you cannot lift up pitchforks. You cannot demonize, you cannot revile, you cannot scapegoat because all of those are hostile actions of cruelty that not only cause harm to the victim, they diminish your ability to learn. So the worry I have is that too often we sacrifice that education piece because it’s uncomfortable and because it requires defending those you may not be in complete alignment with, and it’s an easier thing to just jump on the bandwagon.

In my caucus, when I was a minority leader, another issue I had was abortion, and I had two members who were pastors. I was not going to be able to change their ideological position and I wasn’t going to try. But I had these members walk off the floor, instead of voting, on abortion bills. And there were some who got mad and they’re like, “Oh, we should know their position.” I said, “A yes vote on this bill causes harm, and no vote is a help. Not voting is the same as a no vote. So why do you need them to make a declaration when their declaration of refusing to do harm is progress?” So there’s a complexity that we often elide because we failed to measure what harm looks like, and the path from good to harm is a lot shorter than we want to believe.

Did you work with Angie Nixon during her race?

I feel like she excited a certain element of the base in a way that we haven’t really seen before.

I contributed and then I went down to Florida, actually did an event at Florida A&M University and did one at Cafe Resistance. I got to know her mama. I knew of her as a state representative. And when I decided to support her campaign, it was because she has always put the work of serving people first. She has built networks, but more importantly, she solves problems.

When Florida started banning books, she started a bookstore for banned books. That kind of tactical response with strategic intention is often lacking and it has been part of how I try to operate. We’ve got people who are good at being diagnosticians and we’ve got folks who can offer prescriptions and we’ve got people who can actually administer the medicine. And we need more people who are willing to do all three. You need people who are specialists; I’m not saying you don’t, but what she has demonstrated is the capacity to do the three.

Have you heard some of the negative commentary after the election about her campaign? I’m thinking about James Carville, for instance—this notion that somehow she was a poor fit for Florida or was a bad candidate. It’s not great. Have you seen any of this?

Well, I have thoughts on the fact that we keep thinking the solution to the problem is the thing that failed before. And I believe in experimentation. If you look at my history, I have never been top of mind as the solution to problems. And some of it is timing, some of it is capacity, and some of it is helping change the public imagination, but we’re never going to get what we need if we only use what we’ve always had.

I just find it interesting that she is attracting negative commentary, from certain quarters, in a way that David Jolly is not, even though they both lost and the margin wasn’t that much between the two of them. She came very, very close to winning, in a state Democrats really didn’t expect to compete in two years ago. And look, I just have to say, you are somebody who in 2018 came really, really close too. You’re both Black women. I just wonder what you make of the critique.

The critique is easy because Angie Nixon is different. She’s different than what they are used to, and she is different than 250 years of expectation has led us to presume is right. I am excited about Juliana Stratton and Angela Alsobrooks and Lisa Blunt Rochester being in the US Senate. That is an extraordinary thing. Adding Angie Nixon would’ve been an amazing, amazing addition. But for pundits whose sense of success is grounded in past history, she strains the imagination.

David Jolly ran a smart race. Angie Nixon ran a smart race, and we know that because they came close to winning, but you are never entitled to victory. You are entitled to effort. And this notion that there is some magical formula for what wins in the South got completely obliterated yesterday when Scott Colom won a seat that we haven’t held since 1874. We know that what can win is a combination of a smart candidate, an invested campaign, and an electorate who sees and hears themselves in the story told.

Angie didn’t get that opportunity because she had a late primary and no resources. And to judge her using a metric that was never designed for her is deeply problematic. And it’s not just about her being a Black woman, it’s about how do we win an evolving electorate if all we know is to do what we’ve always done? And so my argument for the Democratic Party is that our notions of electability have to evolve with the democracy that we deserve and that we design, and it cannot be anchored to these sometimes antiquated notions that the only thing we can do is not lose as opposed to let’s try really hard to win by meeting the moment. And I think Angie Nixon did an incredible job of meeting the moment.

And what about you—do you still have ambitions for public office?

Do you worry that some of the work you do as a kind of public political strategist (like in this interview, frankly) will conflict at all? When I think about people seeking office, they often try to say as little as possible.

Politics is a tool. It is not an identity for me. It’s a tool. And that’s different. And there are people for whom this is what they do and we need those people. This is not a disparaging comment about others, but for me, it is a tool. It is one of the ways to do the work I believe needs to be done. I think that poverty is immoral. I think it is solvable. I think it is economically inefficient. And for most of my life, the work for me has been about how do you solve this economic poverty? When I got deep in the work, I realized that we also had a moral poverty that we had to contend with, and we have this poverty of imagination. And the problem is you cannot convince people to believe that their problems can be solved if you won’t talk about them.

And in the South, silence is protective. It has been a way to nibble around the edges, but the only people who could be loud about it were the people who could afford volume. And politicians rarely can afford volume. I want things to be better and I’m not willing to forgo any tool that will make that happen. But I’m also not willing to protect my future opportunities by rejecting my current responsibilities.

#3489. 5 Reasons Why Robert Pattinson Could Be The Best James Bond Yet

Robert Pattinson has officially been cast as James Bond, beating out several promising contenders to take the coveted role. Denis Villeneuve will oversee the upcoming 26th Bond installment, and he couldn't have chosen a more dynamic and interesting leading man.

Thus far, Bond fans have reacted to Pattinson's casting with both excitement and wariness — which is to be expected. After all, the British actor is one of the biggest stars in Hollywood and is therefore unlike any actor to be cast in the role throughout the franchise's more than 60-year history. But clearly Villeneuve and new Bond custodians Amazon MGM have been impressed by the actor, and frankly it's not hard to see why.

The "Primetime" star has been delivering consistently compelling performances for years now, and if nothing else it will be fascinating to see what he does to make England's greatest spy his own. Sure, on the surface he seems like a safe choice — A-lister white guy with a string of hits to his name. But part of what makes Pattinson so exciting as an actor is his unpredictability. Beyond that, there are myriad reasons why he could not only make a great 007, but might just give us the best Bond yet. Here are five of them.

Robert Pattinson is a big star with the kind of look you'd associate with James Bond. But he's made no secret of the fact he's also a bit of a weirdo underneath it all, and in that sense he shares something in common with Bond.

007 is a similarly deceptive character. Like Pattinson, he's a refined, handsome white guy with an urbane manner. But in the first Bond book, "Casino Royale," author Ian Fleming described him as a "blunt instrument." That element has been integral to the character since his inception. That is to say, Bond is much more than a posh boy with a licence to kill. He's damaged, troubled, maybe a little rough around the edges. Sure, his cinematic history has proved the character lends himself to interpretation, but the best Bond performances have integrated that dark side to some extent.

Pattinson could give us the best version of that to date. Remember that short film he made for GQ about his mounting anxiety over leaving his hotel room to get a hotdog? Something's up with this guy in the best way possible, and every role he's taken since then has been testament to that fact. From his lecherous, questionably-accented preacher in "The Devil all the Time" to his delightfully unhinged nineteenth-Century lighthouse keeper in "The Lighthouse," Pattinson has clearly been having a ball playing crazy (and that's not to mention some of his most Pattinsoniest performances in films such as "Good Time" and "The King"). He'll have to keep it under control for Bond, but 007 needs an edge to be interesting, and Pattinson has a wild unpredictability could be the best thing to ever happen to the character.

Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond breaks a 60-year tradition of unknown actors being given the role. For Bond purists, such a thing is basically sacrilegious. For everyone else, it might just be the most exciting thing to happen to Bond since 1962's "Dr. No" kicked off cinema's most enduring franchise.

Look, there's a chance Pattinson could be distracting as 007. Bond is a male fantasy come to life, and part of the series' success could well be attributed to the fact it's easier for audiences to project themselves onto relative unknowns. On the other hand, it only takes one Bond movie for an actor to become a major star, so there'll always be diminishing returns in that respect. What's more, I think it's fair to say we need big changes after the multiple duds that characterized Daniel Craig's last few years as Bond. The franchise was in danger of becoming less relevant than it once was, and casting a star of Pattinson's standing, in a movie directed by the similarly esteemed Denis Villeneuve is a way to remind people of the saga's blue chip status.

What's more, we're not talking about any A-lister here. Pattinson has proved time and again he has the ability to completely disappear into a role. So, what we're actually getting is an actor with the gravitas and appeal of a megastar who is simultaneously able to become a cinematic cipher onto which we can all project our fantasies of becoming the most lethal instrument the Secret Intelligence Service has at its disposal. As the first millennial Bond, and the first major star to take on the role, Pattinson could prove to be a master stroke of casting on Villeneuve's part.

There was a major turning point in Robert Pattinson's career whereby he seemed to throw caution to the wind and embrace the most challenging, unusual, and downright insane roles he could. In 2017, the year "Good Time" debuted, GQ exclaimed that "the new Rob Pattinson is defined by his willingness to go berserk or go home." Ever since then he has delivered back to back unforgettable performances that have seen the middle class London boy disappear into some of the most unique characters to appear on-screen in the last decade.

Part of it was an attempt to escape the shadow of the "Twilight" saga, with which he'd made his name. But his portrayals of these more off-kilter characters that came in the wake of his decision to recalibrate felt so natural and honest that it was like he was finally able to be himself, paradoxically by playing people so completely unlike himself.

What's even more impressive is that he hasn't slowed down since deciding to "go berserk." 2026 saw him deliver yet another electric performance in the dark, unsettling media satire thriller "Primetime," in which he completely disappeared behind the mask of "To Catch a Predator" host Chris Hanson. Pattinson just can't seem to deliver a bad performance. Wild, sure. Unpredictable? Absolutely. But he's never been anything less than magnetic and seems incapable of being boring. That should be hugely exciting for James Bond fans.

"Tenet" was full of confusing moments but Robert Pattinson's ability to portray a debonair spy with a quietly simmering intensity was not in question. The actor played Neil in Christopher Nolan's thriller. A mysterious operative who helps John David Washington's Protagonist throughout the film, Neil possesses all the charisma of James Bond and even seems to have a bit of a dark side.

All you need to see to be convinced Pattinson has what it takes to play Bond is the scene in which Neil scopes out the freeport where he plans to steal a priceless art piece. As he's shown around the facility, Pattinson's agent simultaneously exudes a polite charm and a kind of palpable ruthlessness, smiling at his tour guide before staring intently at possible escape routes and security measures. You can feel the cogs turning as he looks around, with Pattinson managing to convey a real sense of Neil's thought processes. When he's told about the freeport's security system, which sucks the air out of a room within 10 seconds, he simply says "Blimey," an ironic understatement accompanied by a wry smile more than worthy of 007.

Surely nobody ever doubted Pattinson could play an urbane sleuth who looks remarkably sharp in a suit. But his "Tenet" performance hints at something more interesting. The brief moments when Pattinson's agent drops the charming facade and focuses his attention on various parts of the building's design convey a cold, calculating intensity that bodes well for a Bond with a truly dark side. Nolan's confounding thriller is an exciting proof of concept for Pattinson's Bond and his ability to exude both charisma and a striking cold-bloodedness unlike any 007 yet seen on-screen.

If you were told Robert Pattinson went to Eton and Oxford you probably wouldn't have a hard time believing it. He didn't, but it feels like he'd be very much at home in the public school boy milieu. That's interesting because while previous James Bond actors have managed to affect that kind of high-born aura, Pattinson is the first to just sort of have it from the get go.

He's an upper-middle class white Londoner with a Received Pronunciation accent and an urbane, sophisticated manner. Sure, he's also the guy who can't stop nervously laughing in interviews and who seems to run on pure anxiety most of the time. But there's no denying he has the sort of heritage you'd associate with Bond.

Roger Moore — the only other London-born actor to play Bond — had something similar, but undercut it with his famously tongue-in-cheek portrayal. Sean Connery was, of course, Scottish, Timothy Dalton was born in Wales, Pierce Brosnan is Irish, and Daniel Craig is from Chester in North England. Each of them brought something unique to the role, but of all the James Bond actors Pattinson seems like the first who won't have to work too hard at exuding the kind of aura we've come to expect from a character Idles frontman Joe Talbot described as a "murderous toff."

#3488. New Jersey Teacher Arrested for Allegedly Possessing, Distributing Child Porn

A charter high school teacher in New Jersey was arrested for allegedly possessing and distributing child pornography, authorities confirmed.

Middlesex County Prosecutor Linda Estremera and Woodbridge Police Department Director Joseph Nisky announced in a Friday, November 13, joint press release that Joseph Severini was taken into custody that same day following a child pornography investigation that was conducted by the Middlesex County Prosecutor’s Office.

Police said that the teacher was arrested at his home in Woodbridge, New Jersey, and was taken into custody without incident following the execution of a search warrant.

Severini, 32, was working as an English teacher at North Star Academy’s Lincoln Park High School in Downtown Newark at the time of his arrest.

The investigation into Severini’s alleged crimes began when the Middlesex County Prosecutor’s Office’s Internet Crimes Against Children Unit received a cyber tip from the state police. Detective Stenly Vertus then oversaw the investigation. Authorities have not revealed how long the investigation lasted before they were able to take Severini into custody.

Police searched Severini’s residence, where they found enough evidence to arrest him. He was then charged with second-degree distribution of child sexual abuse material and third-degree possession of child sexual abuse material, according to authorities.

Following his arrest, North Star Academy Spokesperson Maria Alcon-Heraux said that police notified the charter school on Friday and informed them that a Lincoln Park High School teacher had been arrested on child pornography charges, according to Tap Into Newark.

Alcon-Heraux said that Severini’s role at the school was immediately terminated in light of the news and stated they are cooperating with law enforcement.

The families of Lincoln Park students were then notified via ParentSquare, the district’s communications platform, about Severini’s arrest and termination. Also in the message, Alcon-Heraux told the parents that all staff must pass a background check before they are hired.

“Our students’ safety is our number one priority at North Star Academy,” she said to the district’s community. “As this is an ongoing police and legal matter, we are fully cooperating with the local police department and the district attorney’s office in their investigation.”

Authorities asked that anyone with information regarding Severini’s crimes call Detective Vertus of the Middlesex County Prosecutor’s Office at 732-745-8391.

It’s not currently clear if Severini has entered a plea or retained legal counsel following his arrest. The investigation into the case remains ongoing.

#3487. 8 Biggest Snubs in the 2026 Game Awards Nominations

The Game Awards has announced its official list of nominees for this year’s prizes. Among the nominees are plenty of obvious contenders, such as Grand Theft Auto 6, Resident Evil Requiem, and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. There was stiff competition across several categories, meaning that some worthy games — and Polygon favorites — didn’t make the shortlist for certain prizes. These are the biggest TGA nomination snubs of 2026.

As one eagle-eyed Resetera user pointed out, Sony just broke a streak that dates all the way back to 2015. This marks the first time in 11 years that a first-party PlayStation release hasn't received a Game of the Year nomination. During that 11-year streak, Sony took home three GOTY trophies: God of War (2018), The Last of Us Part 2 (2020), and Astro Bot (2024). This year's big first-party game from PlayStation was Marvel's Wolverine, which is currently sitting at a 75 on Metacritic and incited a whole lot of debate about difficulty and UI design. The game was nominated in two categories: Best Performance for Liam McIntyre and Innovation in Accessibility.

This outcome won't come as a surprise to Polygon's Oli Welsh, who predicted Marvel's Wolverine missing out on a GOTY nomination and snapping Sony's impressive streak all the way back in September.

There were a ton of fantastic video game performances this year, and somebody’s favorite was bound to get left out. Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave fan favorite Jimmie Yamaguchi gave an outstanding performance as the oddball scholar Fabio, and by every measure, it deserved a nomination. In less capable hands, Fabio’s starry-eyed devotion to Fortune’s Weave co-protagonist Dietrich could have been played for laughs, but Yamaguchi makes the budding romance between these men believable and heartfelt.

Manni L. Perez was nominated for GTA 6, presumably for portraying Lucia Caminos. (Funnily enough, developer Rockstar Games has not yet officially confirmed Perez is actually playing Lucia, despite longstanding online rumors.) Apparently, the actor who played co-lead Jason Duval didn’t make enough of an impact with players to score a nomination.

Blizzard’s World of Warcraft has had a massive year, with the launch of its reimagined Classic experience, World of Warcraft: Forever. The team also released major updates for the modern version of the beloved MMORPG, like March’s Midnight expansion. Those changes weren’t enough to move the needle with voters, and WoW was also left out of the Best Community Support category.

The popular farming sim, which entered early access in 2024 before its full release this year, may have more than 26,000 “overwhelmingly positive” reviews on Steam, but that wasn’t enough for it to snag a nomination in any category. Best Debut Indie might have been Fields of Mistria’s best shot at a prize, but it wouldn’t have been out of place in Best Sim/Strategy or the broader Best Indie category, either.

Despite a wobbly third act, Fortune’s Weave is one of our favorite games of 2026, one of the best games available for the Nintendo Switch 2, and one of the best-reviewed games of the year. Surprisingly, developer Intelligent Systems’ epic strategy RPG only managed to pick up one nomination, for Best Role-Playing Game. It stands a decent chance of taking this one home: other nominees include Final Fantasy Resonance, Monster Hunter Stories 3, The Blood of Dawnwalker, and Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter.

Pearl Abyss’s open-world adventure game was an early-year frontrunner for a GOTY nom, even after middling reviews and a rocky launch. While it wasn’t a critical darling, it did have a pretty massive online following that made the prospect of several nominations seem likely. Surprisingly, Crimson Desert will compete in just one category: Best Community Support.

Bungie’s extraction shooter managed to snag a nomination for Best Multiplayer Game, which it frankly stands little chance of winning against a field that includes two indie chart-toppers and a well-regarded Call of Duty. However, the stylish game was overlooked in the Best Art Direction category, perhaps partly due to the shadow cast by a 2025 plagiarism scandal where Bungie admitted to using an artist’s designs without proper credit. (Bungie later credited her as a Visual Design Consultant.) Marathon’s retro-future meets Y2K cyberpunk aesthetic truly stands out in a sea of Unreal Engine 5 homogeneity, and it’s a shame to see it overlooked here.

Both the Best Indie and Best Debut Indie categories have some stiff competition this year. However, no independent game managed to get a nomination for Game of the Year in 2026. While there weren’t a ton of indie contenders for the top category this year, Polygon’s Oli Welsh had the co-op adventure Big Walk pegged as a dark horse, though developer House House’s recent AI controversy likely didn’t help matters.

The lack of an indie GOTY nominee represents a pretty massive shift from the 2025 crop, which included a record-setting three games developed by independent studios: Hades 2, Hollow Knight: Silksong, and Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. Sandfall Interactive’s much-loved RPG managed to take home the top prize and a total of nine Game Awards, the most wins by a single game. 2024 also saw one indie crack the category, Balatro, though the top honors went to Astro Bot.

The Game Awards 2026 will stream live on Disney+, YouTube, and Twitch, on Thursday, Dec. 10, starting at 7:30 p.m. EST / 4:30 p.m. PST.
