#3470. 20 Years Ago Today: The Best James Bond Movie Ever Made Was Released In Theaters

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

There are very few franchises in cinema history that can compete with James Bond in terms of sheer viability across multiple decades. From "Dr. No," which kicked off cinema's most enduring franchise, to Daniel Craig's swan song "No Time to Die," 007 has endured. But 20 years ago, Bond reached his full potential as an icon of the silver screen.

20 years ago today, director Martin Campbell's "Casino Royale" first hit theaters. At the time, Craig was an up-and-coming star who wasn't a popular choice to take over as author Ian Fleming's beloved British creation. He was taking over for Pierce Brosnan, who had an uneven four film run that ended with arguably the worst James Bond movie of all time, "Die Another Day." To put it lightly, the pressure was on, but Campbell and Craig delivered in a huge way. "Casino Royale" is an undeniable masterwork of blockbuster filmmaking.

In stark contrast to "Die Another Day," which came out just four years earlier, "Casino Royale" was gritty, grounded, and opened up Bond to a new generation, while also serving as a welcome surprise to those who'd loved 007 for years. Opinions vary as they always do, but two decades removed, this pitch perfect piece of franchise filmmaking stands head and shoulders above everything that's come before or since. At the very least, it sits firmly in the top three with some room for debate.

What wasn't up for debate? Bond, James Bond was back, baby. Be it someone's first "Bond" movie or their 20th, this worked like gangbusters. It's the kind of movie that can make someone a fan of a franchise for life.

Just to show my hand, I've been watching "James Bond" for over 30 years and "Skyfall" was the movie that made me a lifelong fan. That said, I can admit that "Casino Royale" is very arguably the "better" movie, even if I personally enjoy "Skyfall" more. Every single time I watch it, I marvel at how perfect it is.

It certainly doesn't hurt that Martin Campbell has a real eye for 007. "GoldenEye" was the most important box office hit in "James Bond" history, as it had to relaunch the franchise following a six-year gap. Campbell is the man who knew how to bring Bond into the '90s with a fresh take. Similarly, when it was time to bring Bond into the 21st century, Campbell was called upon to work his magic. What's fascinating, though, is that "GoldenEye" and "Casino Royale" couldn't be more different.

"GoldenEye" was something of a grab bag, mixing some of the best elements of the Sean Connery and Roger Moore eras into one. "Casino Royale," on the other hand, was a full-blown origin story, adapting Ian Fleming's very first "Bond" novel. It was also very modern, totally willing to embrace the future and move away from the past. But that doesn't mean it forgot what Bond can and should be.

Campbell managed to get the most out of Craig's performance, turning him into both a handsome, charming devil of a man, as well as a ruthless killer. It's fun. It's glamorous. It's hair-raising. It's sexy. It's not so serious that it loses the fun along the way. It's truly the platonic ideal of what a "James Bond" movie should be, and the culmination of more than four decades of filmmaking up to that point.

"Casino Royale" has something for every fan. There are people who grew up with movies like "Goldfinger" who will always love that as the quintessential "Bond" movie, but those classics don't resonate with some modern viewers. There are those who relish the camp and deeply British sensibilities of something like "The Spy Who Loved Me," but that may not work for a younger viewer who is trying to understand who this 007 fellow is.

This movie encapsulates the Bond-ness of it all in a way that everyone can enjoy. It certainly doesn't hurt that Mads Mikkelsen's Le Chiffre is one of the greatest James Bond villains ever. Or that the big climax at the center of the film is at a poker table, rather than some giant action sequence. Don't get me wrong, we get plenty of action, but the poker game is a subversion of expectations and embraces a big part of Bond's history.

Then there's Vesper Lynd. Vesper Lynd in "Casino Royale" was the most difficult Bond girl to cast, but Eva Green ate the role up and gave an emotional core to the movie. A meaningful love interest is something that so many of the Bond films are missing, as he tends to think of women as "disposable pleasures," to quote Lynd. The relationship here raises the stakes, and the chemistry between Green and Craig is off the charts.

2012's "Skyfall" became the biggest Bond movie ever, but there's no way that would have happened if "Casino Royale" didn't tee up the ball so beautifully. This is the movie that this franchise is going to have to measure up to from now until the end of time. This set a new high-water mark for one of cinema's most long-lasting icons.

You can grab "Casino Royale" on Blu-ray from Amazon.

Spoiler alert! This story discusses the Live Shows' Y2K Week on The Voice Season 30, which aired November 16. Episodes are available to stream the day after they air with a Peacock subscription.

The Voice Live Shows are in full swing on the 2026 TV schedule, and have been narrowing down Season 30’s incredible talent to the Top 10. In the latest episode of NBC’s long-running singing competition, they continued to pay tribute to the hits of the late ‘90s and early 2000s with Part 2 of Y2K Week with Team Riley and Team Kelly. From the Goo Goo Dolls hit “Iris” to The Chicks’ tune “Cowboy Take Me Away” to Keane’s indie rock track “Somewhere Only We Know,” there was a blend of musical genres that traveled all over the map and gave a glimpse into how challenging it will be to continue to cut singers, moving ever closer to the winning coach and star. I need to talk about the country music.

While veteran coach Kelly Clarkson knows firsthand what it takes to win, having taken the title four times in nine seasons, including during her first season as a coach, The Voice newbie Riley Green should not be deterred, as Season 30 is proving to be anyone’s game. Take it from this rock music fan, who’s quickly being won over by one of Team Riley’s country singers. Sure, Kelly has 14-year-old and 16-year-old powerhouse singers on her team – Brianna Cameron, who sang “Reflection” by Christina Aguilera, and Koumba Diallo, who sang the Alicia Key’s hit “Fallin’” – but it’s the teenager on Team Riley that is making the best case for crooning his way to the finals.

Country singer Joe Henley (not to be confused with Joe Hendry) is only 19 and had never played a gig before auditioning for The Voice, which only makes his journey on the show more impressive. After grabbing the attention of Kelly Clarkson and Riley Green during the Blind Auditions, making it through the Battle Rounds, and hands-down reclaiming his spot on Team Riley for Cut Week, he took on Lee Ann Womack’s “I Hope You Dance.”

It's one of those country tracks that has crossed over into the mainstream, with deeply emotional lyrics that I’ve personally connected with and that always pull on my heartstrings when I hear it. It was an unexpected choice to hear the #1 hit covered by a male, but Joe crushed it, reinforcing the possibility that he really could win it all in Season 30.

For a rock girlie to be saying that is a big deal! Just saying!

Sure, Team Adam and Team Kelly have the numbers advantage, with three singers still left on each of their teams while the other coaches only have two. I can’t believe I’m still on the country train, but I actually think that Team has a very good chance of winning in his first season, whether that’s with Joe Henley or the duo Ferryn & Brinkley. He’s proven to have an excellent ear for talent and has given great advice and guidance to his team as their performances have only gotten stronger.

While we already know the competition series will be shaking things up with Season 31’s The Voice: Celebrity, we won’t learn who will take it all in Season 30, and if that could be country singer Joe Henley, until December. So, be sure to keep tuning in to NBC on Mondays at 8 p.m. ET until then.

#3468. Target Officially Reveals Big Pokémon TCG Deals On Black Friday

Target expected to offer a wide range of Pokémon 30th Anniversary products in November

November is here, and retailers are finally revealing how they'll handle the year's biggest shopping event: Black Friday. Target has offered Black Friday deals on the Pokémon trading card game in previous years, and 2026 looks to be no different.

The retailer's BF deals initially leaked in late October, but the retailer has since begun putting out fliers advertising the incoming Pokémon promos. Target also just broke the news that some stores will have their stock delayed for after Black Friday. Here's what you need to know.

The news is sourced from Target's own weekly ad sneak peek, which you can peruse here. Target locations are expected to receive shipments of the following products starting on Nov. 15:

According to leaked images, these products will be stocked on new shelf displays that advertise Pokémon's Electronic Dance Music event, which still has a couple of dates left on the calendar.

Initial reports from those leaks indicated that the 30th Anniversary TCG products won't be put up for sale until Nov. 27, or Black Friday proper. However, the weekly ad as well as signage at individual Target stores suggest these TCG products will go on sale on Nov. 28, the day after Black Friday. Limits for these products will vary by store, if they're enforced at all. Targets that do observe purchasing limits typically only allow one product type per customer for 30th Anniversary products. Other products, like Delta Reign, come with more lenient limits of two per person.

It's worth mentioning that none of these products are technically cheaper than their normal price tags. That's in contrast to last year, when Target offered two Pokémon TCG exclusive bundles for a decent price. Though Target charges a markup for its Pokémon TCG products, its prices are cheaper than some competitors and not more prone to price fluctuations than retailers like GameStop.

It's still an (apparent) guaranteed drop date for a highly in-demand product that Target locations are struggling to keep on shelves. By that fact alone, the rumored Pokémon product display will motivate people to visit the store — and perhaps, while they're there, entice them to check out other Black Friday offerings. And if you want to maximize your TCG purchases for the shopping holiday, make sure to check out Walmart's Pokémon promotion here.

#3467. There's a New Way to Automatically Back Up Your Android Photos for Free

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you're an Android user looking for a way to save your photos and videos without maxing out your cloud storage space, your device may soon be able to back up automatically to your PC. As spotted by Android Authority, Google included automatic backups from Android to Windows via Quick Share in its release notes for Google Play services v26.43.

Quick Share is a wireless file-sharing feature for Android that allows users to send photos, videos, and documents to nearby devices, including Windows computers and iPhones with AirDrop. The new automatic backup feature, which is likely to roll out gradually, uses Quick Share's functionality to transfer copies of photos and videos on your phone to your PC when nearby.

Since these backups happen locally, you don't need to rely solely on cloud storage in your Google account, nor do you need to remember to initiate transfers of photos and videos between devices. Plus, this is all free and doesn't require a separate cloud service subscription. While you can back up your media to Google Photos, as of earlier this year, more data from your Android backups count toward your Google Account storage cap unless you exclude specific types. Alternatively, you can also cobble together a decent amount of cloud storage from other providers at no extra cost, but automatic backups between Android and Windows minimize the likelihood that you'll forget to save data, and your PC provides plenty of space for free.

Once the feature is available on your device, you'll be able to initiate backups in the Quick Share for Windows app. Your Android and Windows devices must be in close proximity and signed into the same Google Account. You can toggle Automatic backups on and change the settings for what gets backed up and to where. The transfers will then occur wirelessly in the background.

As Android Authority reports, early hints at this feature suggested that Samsung phones and PCs would be excluded from automatic backups, but the release notes don't specify any further details.

#3466. Robert Pattinson Escaped The Batman 3 Contract Ahead Of James Bond Casting (Report)

The search is over, Robert Pattinson is officially our newest James Bond, and director Denis Villeneuve can now look forward to filling all the various supporting roles surrounding the title character for the upcoming "Bond 26" ... but there's plenty of uncertainty to go around. We'll likely be dissecting this casting choice in all of its infinite implications for weeks and months and even years to come. For now, though, more details continue to be revealed as we attempt to wrap our minds around what Pattinson's newest role will mean for his other high-profile franchise.

That's the Batman-sized question of the day. There has been no official word on the status of Matt Reeves' "The Batman" movies going forward. As fans know, the director stepped away from filming "Part II" due to personal reasons and welcomed Steven Soderbergh to carry the production across the finish line. On top of that, the recent turnover at DC Studios further has thrown the future of the DC Universe and all of its various offshoots into flux. Rest assured, nothing short of an act of the movie gods will prevent "The Batman Part II" from eventually releasing — but what comes after that?

A new report is finally beginning to provide answers. According to The Wrap, all the fevered debate over whether the same film star should be playing both Batman and Bond might be for naught. Journalist Drew Taylor suggests that the recent turmoil with "The Batman Part II" has given Pattinson an out from his deal, which originally included a third trilogy-capping movie. Instead, the outlet cites an anonymous source who indicates that the "protracted production" of the long-delayed sequel "has allowed Pattinson to slip out from under his contract."

In short, this could be what freed up Pattinson to pursue Bond.

The many complicating factors going into Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond are starting to come into focus. We only just found out that the "Primetime" star and "The Odyssey" scene-stealer wasn't initially the first choice for Bond – Josh O'Connor was, until he reportedly dropped out. Now, it seems that Pattinson's days in the cape and cowl are numbered, which we speculated about soon after the Bond news first broke. We certainly hate being the bearers of bad news, as most fans would've loved to see Matt Reeves and Pattinson complete a full-fledged trilogy of "The Batman" films. Unfortunately, this may be the closest we get to confirmation that this simply isn't to be.

While nobody from Skydance or Pattinson's camp have commented on the situation, The Wrap does suggest a way for Pattinson to balance his roles as both Batman and Bond, should the need arise. (As we know, things in Hollywood can always change on a dime and, theoretically, nothing is preventing Pattinson, Reeves, and Skydance from coming together to hammer out terms for a third film together.) While both tend to require lengthy productions, it's possible neither franchise may even overlap much, allowing Pattinson to work out his schedule so that he can spend time at MI6 and Gotham City.

This added responsibility as Bond will only make Pattinson even busier than he already is, but he knew what he was signing up for with this role. On the face of it, we're erring on the side of "The Batman Part II" marking the end of his tenure with DC. If so, a series of movies with Pattinson as the world's most famous super-spy isn't anything to sneeze at, either.

#3465. Who Killed Fashion Founders Bryan Walker and Michelle Min?

Panoramic Hill looms above the UC Berkeley campus, a tree-covered neighborhood cut by steep paths and outdoor staircases. Century-old homes by brand-name architects like Bernard Maybeck and Walter Steilberg dot the incline, which straddles the border of Berkeley and Oakland. Each residence is worth millions; increase the amount for the occasional bit of newer construction. Unlike the busy urban streets below, the area is incredibly quiet. That’s one of the reasons everyone heard the shots.

“I have that stored in my memory, as I will for the rest of my life,” Daniella Salzman tells me, looking out her window at the former home of Michelle Min and her husband, Bryan Walker. The couple, creators of the Bryn Walker clothing brand, were found just outside their residence around 10:45 a.m. on October 2, 2026, shortly after neighbors called 911 to report the sound of gunfire. Initial confusion about jurisdiction sent police from both Berkeley’s and Oakland’s departments to the scene.

By the time paramedics arrived, Walker and Min were dead from what OPD assistant chief Casey Johnson characterized as “apparent gunshots” in a press conference later that day. A firearm, he said, was located at the scene. He declined to offer further details on the case, saying that the department’s homicide division would handle the investigation.

Nearly seven weeks later, we still know next to nothing about how Walker and Min died. While OPD turned down my request to speak with Johnson, it sent me a press release with the same details he laid out on October 2. Follow-up questions were met with: “There are no updates being released other than the information below.”

Bryn Walker store on Vine Street in Berkeley, California.

“I don’t know what has publicly been shared or what privately has been learned about what took place,” Salzman says carefully. Police have been silent since the brief press conference the day the bodies were discovered. But Michelle Min’s brother, Paul Min, hasn’t been quiet.

Within two days after his 63-year-old sister was found dead, Paul spoke with outlets including the LA Times and the California Post, accusing his brother-in-law of killing his wife, then himself, following a series of disastrous financial decisions that led to significant losses and a collapse in his mental state. The interviews, given so soon after the crime, suggest Paul was still in a state of shock over his loss. Walker, who was 61 when he died, was “the most honest, responsible, hardworking guy you have ever known,” Paul told the LA Times. “I loved him like a brother.” Michelle “was utterly devoted to Bryan to the very end,” Paul told the Post, “and he shot her.”

After those interviews, which were published that first weekend in October, Paul fell silent too; I made multiple efforts to arrange an interview but was ultimately unsuccessful. But according to the Post’s interview, Walker “had quietly taken out loans against their properties, and had gambled on risky options and leveraged positions,” with estimated losses of “well over $100 million.” The debt, per the LA Times story, allegedly prompted Walker to suggest that he and the Min siblings “end things”—a proposal that alarmed the Mins, but only because of its implications for Walker’s mental health. Paul didn’t see Walker as a danger: “He said the idea that Walker would or could harm them was absurd to the two of them,” reported the Times.

The Mins came to the US from Korea in 1977, settling first near Kansas City. Michelle met Walker there in the 1980s, and after the Mins’ parents chose to move to California, the siblings, and Walker, followed. In 1992 the couple opened a clothing store in Berkeley that sold goods from other makers. As time went on, they began to manufacture more and more of their own goods.

Eventually, Bryn Walker evolved into a clothing brand known for loose linen looks with an Asian-meets-Swedish flair. “Flowy, a touch eclectic, made for perhaps older women who want to mesh elegant/sophisticated with a bit of boho uniqueness,” a longtime Berkeley resident told me over email. “Women who want to look expensive but with a bit of verve.” When I described the company to one San Francisco resident as “elevated Chico’s,” I got a stern look. “You better not let any of the Bryn Walker moms at Lowell hear you say that,” she said, referencing the city’s hotly competitive public high school. “These are not humorous people.”

Bryn Walker store on Fourth Street in Berkeley, California.

According to the Post piece, Walker “had stepped aside and allowed his designer wife to control their mutual business and his eponymous fashion label,” but it’s not clear when that management change occurred. As the brand grew, it struck a chord with fashion businesses across the country—from luxury boutiques to the family-run department store chain Dillard’s. Bryn Walker also opened its own brick-and-mortar storefronts beyond Berkeley.

Many of those stores are now gone. One Bryn Walker location in Santa Monica closed prior to mid-March of 2021, while a 22-year-old outpost in Palo Alto shuttered in 2020. On the East Coast, a shop in Edgartown, on Martha’s Vineyard, went dark in 2024. A call to its shop in Vineyard Haven was met with a recorded message saying the business would be closed until further notice. That leaves just two company-owned shops, both in Berkeley, where Bryn Walker began.

One of those stores is on Berkeley’s buzzy Fourth Street, a glossy shopping destination lined with outposts of national brands like Apple, Lululemon, and Herman Miller. With items generally priced between $130–$300, it fits right into the overall ethos of that street—and Berkeley—where almost everything is spendy but not flashy; theoretically accessible, though not to those on a budget. During my recent visit to the shop, the sole staffer remained pleasant even after I identified myself as a journalist—but her tone grew firm. “It’s all still too raw,” she said of the tragedy.

I asked if, as he’d said he would in his Post interview, Paul Min had taken over management of the company following its founders’ deaths. “I don’t know about that,” she replied, before declining to speak further. I was told by another local business owner that Bryn Walker employees are actively seeking other employment; it’s unclear what will happen to the label now that its creators are gone. I tried to reach Bryn Walker management by phone and email for this story, but did not receive a response.

Emilie Raguso was one of the first journalists to report on the deaths, for her independent outlet, The Berkeley Scanner. As she began investigating, she “saw that the number of open shops was different based on where you looked,” she says. “I was getting this early inkling of what others later reported as far as the business being in trouble.”

“The writing was on the wall,” she continues, “but there was nothing explicit. It did seem like, Oh, this is not a thriving business.”

Paul’s comments to the media didn’t address the health of the business. Instead, he was focused on Walker and Michelle’s personal finances, which he alleged were laid to waste by Walker’s mismanagement. “Your spouse lied to you and lost over $100 million and you might be out on the streets,” Paul told the Post. “You might go from being one of the wealthiest people in the country to being homeless because your husband lied to you and wagered everything on crazy bets.”

According to Paul, things grew so grim for Walker that the Mins spoke about institutionalizing him. But it’s also unclear how they would have acted on that without Walker’s cooperation. California enacted its CARE Court program in 2023, more easily allowing court-ordered treatment plans for those who might pose a threat to themselves or others. But in practice, courts have been reluctant to take that drastic step, frequently rejecting petitions from those closest to the person in crisis.

Bryn Walker-Pacific Cotton store on Main Street in Vineyard Haven, Massachusetts.

Speaking with the LA Times, Paul said that in Walker and Michelle’s home, he “found a note that lists a couple of [mental health] facilities. I speculate he saw that note or somehow figured out she was going to institutionalize him, but I have no idea.”

Paul’s claim that Walker killed Michelle over snowballing financial fears isn’t out of the realm of possibility, even in a place as wealthy as the Bay Area. One year before Walker and Michelle died, almost to the day, entrepreneur Paula Truong fatally shot her husband, Thomas, and their daughters, Mackenzie and Alexandra, before hanging herself in the garage of their $2.2 million San Francisco home. Reporting found that the family had experienced a string of financial challenges, including several failed business ventures, a home foreclosure, and a number of unpaid debts.

But that was in San Francisco—a sometimes gritty city that people escape with moves to places like Panoramic Hill. “When you get up into the hills, it does feel like a world apart,” Raguso says. “It feels insulated from a lot of the more common disturbances and things that we deal with down on the flatlands.”

Salzman has lived on that hill for more than 20 years, and she’s still struggling with the notion that her neighbor might have killed his wife. “Bryan was very engaged with neighbors who were needing support that were near him,” she says, characterizing him and Michelle as “committed to the community.” But she also believes that the fear of losing wealth can drive people to desperate acts. “We see wealth as being both our greatest need and our greatest opportunity here,” she says, “and we are told that we will be happy when we consume. This is the message that we’re given everywhere we look”—especially in a region with more billionaires than anywhere else in the world.

Raguso isn’t sure why Oakland police are taking so long to announce the results of their investigation. “At some point, there would be a ruling,” she says, citing possible delays with the medical examiner’s office as a reason things haven’t been resolved. According to Salzman, the vacuum of information has inspired her to look at all her neighbors with a little more care. “Part of what I awoke to was how little I know about really what’s going on with people that I’m geographically so close to,” she says.

“I just would have loved for there to have been a way to be a part of showing up for them, even around the little things. The more people that are aware of what is happening, the more people are potentially able to heal.”

#3464. Windows Laptops Just Closed a Major Gap With the MacBook Neo

To say the MacBook Neo disrupted the laptop market would be an understatement. When the Neo dropped, former Apple CEO Tim Cook said Apple had its best-ever launch week for first-time Mac customers, and the company is reportedly planning on doubling the MacBook's sales for 2027. It's not hard to see why the MacBook Neo is such a hit: Apple is offering the essential Mac experience at a fantastic price point. You no longer need to spend $1,000 or more for a MacBook, so long as you're okay making some sacrifices to get there—which, it seems, many customers are.

While the MacBook Neo has been a boon for Apple and Apple fans alike, I can only imagine the stress it brought to PC manufacturers—especially those with budget or midrange machines. Windows PCs have long won the price war against Apple. While MacBooks have their passionate customers, buyers looking for the best value have had to weigh expensive Apple laptops against many far cheaper options from companies like Dell, HP, ASUS, and Lenovo. But with the Neo, suddenly a MacBook was competing in this space, and well.

Part of the issue for PC manufacturers was Apple's control over its own ecosystem. Unlike most PC makers, which only produce the hardware for each machine, Apple makes both the hardware and the software for its MacBook lineup. As such, the company has the advantage of optimizing that hardware. It can design macOS to run more efficiently on weaker hardware, in a way that companies like Dell or ASUS can't. You might be comparing the MacBook Neo against a Windows laptop with similar specs, or even better specs, but because Microsoft makes Windows, not the laptop manufacturer, it's possible the Neo ends up with the better overall experience. While that might still be the case, Microsoft may have just closed that gap in a meaningful way.

This week, Microsoft announced key upgrades to memory-management efficiency, particularly for machines with 8GB of RAM. This is the amount of memory the MacBook Neo has, as well as many budget and midrange Windows laptops. That's not much memory for 2026, regardless of platform, but Apple seems to have squeezed a lot out of it for the Neo. Now, Microsoft may have just done the same for PCs, as Windows is reportedly 20% more responsive, with 40% faster multitasking.

In its blog post, Microsoft highlighted improvements that users with 8 GB of RAM can expect from Windows going forward. First, Microsoft says it focused on better utilizing the RAM your machine already has. The company compares its memory management to a desk: Anything on the "desk" is stored in RAM; anything in your "drawer" is stored in your drive. As you use your PC, Windows used to move more of your apps and tabs to your drawer to free up more RAM for other things, meaning you'd need to reload those items whenever you returned to them. Going forward, the company says that Windows can keep up to 2GB more of your active data in RAM instead of moving it to slower storage elsewhere. That means apps and tabs should refresh less frequently when you leave and return to them.

Microsoft also says that small actions should be faster across the board. When you open the Start menu, search across your PC, right-click, open Settings, launch the Snipping Tool, and open File Explorer, those actions may be up to 20% faster than they were in January. Microsoft Edge may open up to 33% faster, while Teams can enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which means it can launch up to 20% faster too. Microsoft put together an interesting stress test to compare multitasking performance between today and January. It opened 20 tabs in Edge, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, then Outlook and File Explorer, all without closing any windows. That experience was 40% faster following this latest update.

Microsoft says it also improved the memory efficiency in its apps: The company claims it reduced committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB, and saved up to 360 MB in RAM across Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook. That extends to third-party apps as well: Microsoft says that WhatsApp has double-digit memory improvement now. Widgets also only load when you open the app, which saves 200 MB of RAM when the app is closed, while Edge tabs go inactive after 15 minutes instead of two hours.

Microsoft isn't making these upgrades in a vacuum. Hardware costs, particularly for RAM, have skyrocketed in the age of AI. Microsoft knows that people are likely going to hold onto existing hardware for longer than they usually do, or that they'll opt for less-expensive configurations, including, perhaps, machines with 8 GB of RAM.

PCMag's Chris Hoffman was adamant before this latest Windows update that buyers should steer clear of PCs with 8 GB of RAM. Now, he's pulling back a bit. In his testing, Hoffman noticed improvements when multitasking on an 8 GB PC when compared to similar tests from months ago. He could run multiple Chrome tabs, a Microsoft Word window, and Spotify without bogging down the computer much. Hoffman isn't a lightweight user, so he still wouldn't personally choose an 8 GB machine, but he admits, "If I were an average PC buyer looking for a reasonable desktop experience and could save hundreds of dollars by opting for 8GB of RAM, I might be happy with the performance."

To that point, I think this new Windows update makes 8 GB PCs competitive, especially against the MacBook Neo. We'll still need direct comparisons to know how well this new Windows experience holds up across the board, but these updates are promising. Users with 8 GB machines just got a free, valuable update overnight; new customers can opt for a more affordable PC without feeling like performance will take a nosedive just because they opened one too many Edge tabs.

As Hoffman says, 8 GB of RAM is not ideal for any user looking for serious multitasking or professional workflows, regardless of whether they choose a Mac or PC. But for the average computer customer looking for a solid machine without breaking the bank, I no longer see the Neo as necessarily the default choice. After all, Apple has slowly raised its price, too, from $599 to $699. If you're platform-agnostic, or even prefer Windows to macOS, these updates from Microsoft are quite promising. If you're in the market, check out PCMag's excellent list of budget laptop recommendations.

What does the future hold for DC Studios?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

To say that DC Studios is in the midst of a big change would be a major understatement. It was announced a little over a week ago that in the aftermath of the Warner Bros./Paramount merger, James Gunn and Peter Safran would step down as co-CEOs of the studio. As a result, film producer (and Marvel Studios alum) Jeremy Latcham will lead the brand moving forward. There may, however, now be reason to believe that DC may be leaving WB and by extension, parent company Skydance. This is all due to some recent rumors.

A common claim that’s been reported in the aftermath of the Gunn/Safran news is that Skydance has acquired a lot of Warner Bros.-amassed debt following the merger. It’s been said that a number of DC Studios’ projects were particularly pricey for the company. In a wide-ranging piece, Page Six mentioned sources who alleged that Supergirl, which flopped at the box office earlier this year, lost WB $135 million. With that, X user @entylawyer alleges that Skydance wants to unload the superhero brand for monetary purposes:

The comic studio heads were fired. They didn't quit. Their boss wants to sell off the entire comic book universe to help get rid of some of that $100B debt.

Of course, all of this should be taken with a massive grain of salt, as Skydance’s David Ellison has not indicated that the company plans to sell DC Studios. If that were to actually happen, though, it would result in the availability of a major asset. If Ellison and co. were to sell it, it could theoretically draw some significant interest on the open market.

I’m honestly just not sure who would seek to acquire DC Studios if Skydance were to theoretically choose to sell it. There’s also the matter of which entertainment company would actually have the money to do it. One of the first brands that comes to mind is obviously The Walt Disney Company, which acquired Marvel Entertainment back in 2009 for $4 billion. However, another brand that should be considered as a hypothetical buyer is Netflix,the company that was set to acquire WB before Paramount made a higher bid.

All of that is just speculation but, of course, James Gunn’s DC exit is real, with him and Peter Safran officially stepping down on December 1. News of Gunn’s departure has generated disappointment from those who were all in on his DC plans, and some have expressed concerns about the future of his DCU continuity. As for the actual decision to part ways with Safran and Gunn, a source for Page Six alleged that their bosses had been in talks with Latcham for weeks ahead of the announcement despite publicly saying otherwise:

It was a little bit strange to have it be so publicly stated that [Gunn and Safran] were safe, and during that time, the [Latcham] process had already been kicked off. They were saying one thing, and then they were actively doing another thing.

Naturally, there are a lot of unknown variables here, and it’s currently unclear as to it or when Skydance might confirm or deny the rumor that DC Studios will be sold. In the meantime, there are still film projects from the brand that are in different stages of development as James Gunn’s Man of Tomorrow is set to hit theaters on July 9 amid the 2027 movie schedule. Matt Reeves’ The Batman: Part II is also filming right now and will hit theaters on February 18, 2028.

#3462. Constantine Sequel With Keanu Reeves Gets Update After James Gunn's DC Universe Exit

The entertainment world is still reeling from the recent shake-up at DC Studios. James Gunn and Peter Safran have departed their posts as heads of the studio, meaning the DC Universe is in for some big changes. In fact, Gunn's DCU is reportedly being dismantled as DC Studios prepares for another reset. Whether that's good or bad remains to be seen and will be a matter of personal opinion. However, it could be good for the long-awaited sequel "Constantine 2."

In an interview with Collider, director Francis Lawrence addressed the status of the proposed follow-up to his 2005 DC Comics adaptation starring Keanu Reeves. The "Constantine" sequel was said to be officially happening with Lawrence returning back in 2022, but updates have been few and far between ever since. And while Lawrence clarified that he doesn't "want anybody to lose their jobs," he said the latest happenings at DC Studios are ultimately beneficial to his "Constantine" follow-up. As he put it:

"We have an idea, and we have a script, and we've been wanting to make it, and the people that were at DC were an impediment to us making it. So, we are now more hopeful as of yesterday's news that maybe now there will be another opportunity. But again, we've been trying to make this for 20-something years, and there's always been obstacles in the road to making it, and it's not me, it's not Keanu, it's not [producer] Akiva [Goldsman]. J.J. [Abrams] is on it as well. We all want to do it.

"It's really going to be people at Paramount, Warner, whoever's running DC now, getting everybody on board to say, like, 'Hey, we can do a sequel of our version of 'Constantine,?" Lawrence added.

Setting aside one's personal feelings about James Gunn and Peter Safran no longer being at DC Studios, this is a movie that all involved have wanted to make for a long time. Keanu Reeves kept pestering Warner Bros. about "Constantine 2" until it said yes, but that happened before Gunn and Safran were installed to launch their DC Universe. That complicated matters. Now, the situation is complicated once again, only this time in a way that could benefit Francis Lawrence and Reeves.

We only just got word that DC Studios is developing a new John Constantine movie, but that was also before the announcement about Gunn and Safran leaving broke. Even so, Lawrence addressed that as well, suggesting that both projects could co-exist:

"Personally, I don't even care if somebody has a plan for some sort of shared universe, and they want to do another version of Constantine. If they just let us do the sequel to our version, they can coexist. So, I have renewed hope as of yesterday that there might be some possibility for forward movement there."

2005's "Constantine" wasn't an out-and-out hit at the time of its release, but it's become something of a fan favorite over time. I previously noted that a "Constantine" legacy sequel would have mixed box office prospects, yet it might just work at the right price. It's simply a matter of whether or not the regime at Skydance, Warner Bros.' new parent company, sees this as a prudent investment. Reeves is currently a bigger star than he's ever been, while Lawrence, who has shepherded the "Hunger Games" movies for years, knows how to make a hit. We'll see how things shake out.

"Constantine 2" doesn't have a release date yet, but stay tuned.

#3461. Atlas Atelier Is Making Makeup for People Who Want to Be Remembered

You know how everyone is debating whether smoking is back? Atlas Atelier is like the subject of the makeup version of that conversation, in both its long, skinny lipsticks that evoke a cheeky cigarette and its past-bedtime, maybe something a little naughty is happening vibe. The Paris-based brand makes just lipstick, blush, and a black liquid eyeliner, all engineered to be best shown off at night, maybe under the light of candles, or as you sip a cocktail or wear a jacket with strong shoulders. It’s makeup that is supposed to look like makeup. Severe is not too strong a word to use.

The brand’s late-30s founder, Michelle Duncan, doesn’t smoke herself and doesn’t do barely there makeup along the lines of Rhode, Rare Beauty, or Glossier. “I am a New Yorker, and I’ve been living in Paris primarily for the last four or five years. When I arrived in Paris, everyone was so well-heeled that you would never see somebody wearing a gym look to go to dinner. This resonated with me about this idea of dressing up to go out no matter what you were doing, even if it’s going to a café. That was a huge inspiration for me,” she says.

Duncan knew the industry she was getting into. She’s a veteran of brands owned by Estée Lauder, including both MAC and Tom Ford Beauty, and she also worked for Cartier. Atlas Atelier—the “atlas” is in homage to Ayn Rand’s Atlas Shrugged—just came out this fall in the US (now available at Violet Grey and Bergdorf Goodman). Vanity Fair spoke to Duncan about Paris expat life, rejecting celebrity brands, and what happens to makeup in unstable times.

The interview that follows has been condensed for length and clarity.

Vanity Fair: You know the challenges of the beauty industry. You’re not an influencer; you didn’t pick a celebrity to be the face of the brand or to partner with. Why not make it easier on yourself?

Michelle Duncan: Friends will ask, “Didn’t you want to do this with a celeb?” I wouldn’t want to. Culture and society is so focused on a quick buck right this second, which I’m totally into. I love making money very fast. This is so much about the world of Atlas, with the packaging and with the storytelling. The brand ethos of Atlas is about the night, about this seductive environment that, to me, will actually cut through the clutter in a long-term way. When a high-profile person launches a brand, the bet that they’re taking is on who they are as a person. For me, the bet is, do you buy into Atlas’s story?

Makeup has gotten very big and plastic and in some ways looks like toys. That was sort of my first remit on it. The whole brief was: We want to create something that looks like an object that you want to be able to keep. My inspirations really are the 1930s, the Art Deco, Paris moment, and how do we make it leap into the ’80s in some ways because that’s obviously also just a second extension of the ’30s?

The 1980s version of Art Deco is so good. All that lacquer and glass blocks and chrome lamps.

It felt like something that was radically different from what’s going on in the world right now, at least in beauty land. We’re exiting this no-makeup era, or hopefully exiting this quiet-luxury era. Those things were very pared back. Maybe focusing more internally about wellness and things like that. I understood that this was missing and that it was going to come back.

The idea of self-expression in a sort of glamorous way. In the 1930s, it was not a great time in the world. And if we remember, the 1980s in New York City was decadent and over the top and seemed very fun, but as a reaction to what was going on. I would argue that we are kind of in that place right now. We don’t really need to go into politics, but it is chaos right now. And so the answer to that is always this other form of self-expression.

The name of the brand is a reference to Atlas Shrugged. Are you a big fan of Ayn Rand?

I’ve always admired and been inspired by Dagny Taggart, one of the most iconic characters in 20th-century literature. She’s written as a fiercely independent entrepreneur in a male-dominated world, who is in control of her own life and embracing its complexity. When creating my business, I was trying to channel that vision of what a woman can be: intellectually formidable, professionally ambitious, and comfortable with her sensuality. I was especially struck by one moment in the novel, when Dagny draws on a statue using her lipstick, reminding us that makeup isn’t just to change our appearance—it can be a tool for women to own their own power. I wanted to create a makeup line that gave women that same feeling of confidence, ambition, and sensuality through tools like lipstick, blush, and eyeliner.

Yes. I have been wearing this winged-eyeliner situation for a very long time. Actually, since I was a teenager. If I don’t have my eyeliner on, I feel naked and I don’t feel like I have everything with me.

So you’re wearing eyeliner at home. What about the people who are reading this who may be thinking, I never go out, or I have kids, or I’m tired, or I work a lot, or all of those things? Do you want people to go out a lot? Do you go out a lot? Is it more just the mindset of going out at nighttime?

The idea of my brand is it should be a pleasure to put on makeup, and I want people to experience pleasure again and just forget about all of the things that are happening, like picking up the kids, or going to the grocery store, or getting the dry cleaning, or whatever it is. Just remembering what it means to have a nice time and be inspired by the night. I, on purpose and by design, did not launch foundations or these technical components of makeup, because that’s just not really what it’s about.

How is expat life? I know so many people who have moved to France, or they would love to move to France. What do you think that’s about?

In my social circle, it tends to consist of either people somehow in the fashion industry, the music industry, or the arts communities. A lot of those industries have just become quite commercial in America, as an example. And I haven’t lived in a lot of other countries, so I don’t really know expat life so well. But the amount of Italians that are here, the Spanish, the Germans, the Americans, and everyone just has this chaotic, frenetic energy of being around each other and doing things together. It’s pretty remarkable.

I know you’re not doing celebrity spokespeople, but who would you want if you didn’t have to think about money or access or if they already had a beauty contract?

Somebody like [the artist] Nadia Lee Cohen. She’s super glamorous. She’s quite creative. She’s a genius in a lot of ways, and she actually uses makeup as art. And then somebody like Dakota Johnson. I think she’s so chic now. Dua Lipa. I love her. She’s got the perfect energy for this. She’s there, she’s having a good time, and she’s powerful.

Do you want to expand into other products ? It feels like you could do a fragrance. Or maybe a very chic makeup remover?

I can’t wait for the day that we are able to launch a fragrance because that is one of those things you remember, along with lip color. You remember what they smell like, and when they leave the room, and so that’s the impression that Atlas is supposed to be giving—you’re remembered when you left the room.

#3460. Sony Wants to Give You Up to $400 for Your PS5

Companies usually want you to buy something from them. They might cut prices to make their products more enticing, or introduce perks and upgrades to make stagnant prices (or even price hikes) more appealing. But rarely do I see companies encourage customers to sell their products.

Such is the case with Sony and its PlayStation console. This week, the company began reaching out to some customers with an odd prompt: Rather than buy a new PS5 or PS5 Pro, you can sell your existing PS5 console for up to $400. There are stipulations there, of course: Your console needs to be in good working order, and, apparently, come with two controllers—even though Sony only includes one in the box. The price could also fluctuate depending on your console model, storage capacity, and included accessories. But, still, the company says it'll help you net up to $400 for your existing PS5.

It's a bizarre deal, especially when you consider who you're trading your console to. Sony isn't necessarily accepting trade-ins itself. Instead, it's partnering with BackMarket. The thing is, you can trade in your PS5 directly through BackMarket and get a better value than Sony is offering through its direct link. When I try to trade in my standard PS5 with one controller, BackMarket offers $435, $35 more than Sony's highest offer. If I add a second controller to that deal, BackMarket bumps up the total to $455.

You might also be wondering why Sony would do this. Not only is it weird for a company to encourage you to sell one of its products, but the PS5 is about to have a big moment. Grand Theft Auto VI is finally about to launch, and it'll likely be one of the biggest video game launches, if not the biggest video game launch, of all time. Why, then, would Sony encourage users to jump ship?

While Sony doesn't say, the answer likely has to do with how expensive it is to pick up a PS5 right now. Even though the console launched back in 2020, units are few and far between, jacking the price up to unreasonable levels. Sony raised international prices due to tariffs last year, but the current shortage is more probably tied to the ongoing memory crisis that's putting a strain on all tech, including game consoles. A new PS5 on Amazon will easily cost you over $800. If you want to find a PS5 Pro, don't be surprised to find it well over $1,000. Sony likely wants players who aren't using their consoles to sell them, so that active players (who will also buy games like GTA VI) will pick them up. It's not just Sony, either: Microsoft has been offering similar deals to inactive Xbox gamers this year.

If Sony reached out to you directly, you can take advantage of the deal without issue—just click the link in the email. But if you never received such an offer, you still have options. For one, that BackMarket deal is live for anyone. That links takes you to the deal for the standard PS5, but you can also head to this link to enter the info for your specific PS5 model. GameStop, of course, will happily take your PS5 off your hands, but it doesn't seem as generous as BackMarket. Right now, it seems you can get up to $275 in store credit, or $192.50 in cash for a standard PS5.

#3459. GTA 6's Game Awards Nominations Are Exactly What Everyone Predicted

Going into Tuesday’s reveal of the 2026 Game Awards nominees, the question wasn’t whether or not Grand Theft Auto 6 would pick up any nominations. It was more about how many nominations it would get. And now that the dust has cleared, GTA 6’s Game Awards nominations rolled out pretty much…exactly as expected.

But it’s nevertheless an unconventional situation. The game isn’t out yet. Reviews haven’t been published. Still, GTA 6 ultimately picked up eight nominations — the most of any game in 2026, immediately cementing it as a frontrunner for the GOTY race. It was nominated in the following categories:

This falls short of records set by Sandfall Interactive’s beloved parry simulator Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, which Polygon’s Oli Welsh predicted was an impossible gambit for GTA 6 anyway.

In 2025, Clair Obscur was nominated for 13 categories and won nine awards. That means GTA 6 could win every category it’s nominated in and still fall short of Clair Obscur’s record. At best, it could tie, depending on how the Player’s Voice category — which is voted on entirely by the public — plays out. As far as sheer number of nominations, purely on grounds of eligibility, it was never going to set the bar. Clair Obscur was up for two categories GTA 6 would never be eligible for (Best Indie Game and Best Debut Indie Game), and its ensemble cast carried it to three Best Performance nominations (Ben Starr, Charlie Cox, and Jennifer English, the latter of whom won).

Whatever happens, GTA 6’s raft of nominations reveals details about a wildly anticipated game that, to date, has only been seen through selected marketing materials and curated media coverage. A Best Score and Music nomination suggests Grand Theft Auto’s pedigree of killer soundtracks remains unshaken. A Best Game Direction nomination reaffirms Rockstar’s pedigree of immaculately conceived game design. Snagging a Best Narrative nomination — in a year full of narratively rich games that nevertheless excluded the sprawling, ambitious, deliciously messy Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave from the field — suggests GTA 6 might be something more nuanced than a mayhem-packed sandbox.

But perhaps the biggest reveal is in Perez’s nomination for Best Performance. The Game Awards did not officially say what role she plays in GTA 6, but these things tend to go to lead characters, which aligns with a long-standing rumor among fans that Perez portrays Lucia, one of the game’s protagonists. That GTA 6 only nabbed one Best Performance nomination additionally suggests one of two things: that she’s the only good performance in GTA 6, or that her performance is miles above and beyond everyone else in the game (which includes recent Emmy winner Stephen Root among its officially revealed cast).

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

All told, GTA 6 ended up nominated in basically every category it conceivably could’ve been nominated in: the top category, the top of one genre category (games are only allowed to compete in one of those), all three technical categories, and all three general artistic categories.

At the top of 2026, much ado was made about the shadow cast by GTA 6 over this year’s GOTY race — if the game was released in time, of course. For a large part of the year, particularly when it was still hard to believe that this thing was actually coming out, when it still felt like it might’ve been delayed, there were hints that this year would fold out in interesting, unexpected ways. On a podium left empty, who clambers to the top? A licensed Star Wars game? A 120-hour tactical soap opera? Another indie darling? None of those ended up nominated for the evening’s top prize. Now that we’re fast approaching the finish line, the race is playing out precisely as many expected a year ago.

#3458. Christian Bale Pushed To Play Batman Before Christopher Nolan's Reboot Was Announced

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

The Tim Burton "Batman" films introduced the wider public to a more gothic Batman, but they only scratch the surface of Batman's (Michael Keaton) own character. Conversely, the Joel Schumacher movies drowned in their attempts to recreate the campy 1960s "Batman" show, but both "Batman Forever" and "Batman and Robin" at least try to understand Bruce Wayne (Val Kilmer then George Clooney).

Christopher Nolan's still-beloved "Batman Begins" finally struck the balance, putting Batman (Christian Bale) in a darker movie and also creating a believable and compelling lead out of Bruce Wayne. In effect, "Batman Begins" perfects what "Batman Forever" tried. Since he starred in the most consistently good "Batman" movies, it's also little surprise Christian Bale is still considered one of the best Batman actors.

In 2005, during the "Batman Begins" press cycle, in an interview with Blackfilm, Bale said he had wanted to play Batman for a while. He'd claimed he even asked his agent to "keep [their] eyes out" for a Batman movie before it was announced Nolan was doing "Batman Begins." Bale continued:

"By the time I actually came to be cast I [had] kind of gotten so obsessed about it that, I kind of viewed it as it being mine already. It would've been more like...if they had told me like 'No, it's not yours,' I would've been like 'No way that's not working out, that's not going to happen.'"

Indeed, Bale wasn't Nolan's only choice for the role. Josh Hartnett turned it down, while Cillian Murphy's screen test got him cast as the Scarecrow instead. But considering Bale's determination, and talent (he'd recently cast off his child actor image with "American Psycho"), it's little surprise he got the part. What quality is more like Batman than refusing to accept defeat?

In the aforementioned Blackfilm interview, Bale claims he wasn't a Batman fan from childhood, but reading some comics won him over. He specifically listed Grant Morrison and Dave McKean's "Arkham Asylum," Frank Miller and David Mazzucchelli's "Batman: Year One," and Jeph Loeb and Tim Sale's "The Long Halloween" and "Dark Victory." He named those same four in a 2005 interview with Wizard Magazine, as well as Alex Ross' "War on Crime."

"I realized that [Batman] was a really great character, a dark severe character unlike anything that I had realized he [could] be before," Bale said to Blackfilm. Now, keep in mind, every actor who appears in a superhero movie says during the press cycle they read the comics and fell in love with the character. And, every time, I'm skeptical that it's more than just PR talking points (unless the actor's name is "Nicolas Cage" or "Iman Vellani").

The comics Bale named are all from the late 1980s through the 1990s, when "dark Batman" was becoming the norm and comic writers/artists were now considering the character a prestige assignment. To this day, those books remain some of the essential Batman stories recommended to new readers, in part because they can make you take Batman seriously.

Part of the sales pitch for "Batman Begins" was, coming off of the disastrous "Batman and Robin," that this Batman would be different. Naming comics the fans love as influences is a great way to get them on your side. Bale claiming he wasn't a Batman fan until reading those comics showed him the darker side of Batman, with the implicit promise "Batman Begins" would do the same for the moviegoing public, is even a compelling fan-friendly meta-narrative.

Where Christian Bale's claims about his comic reading have some substance is that those books do influence "Batman Begins." As an origin story, the movie takes the most from "Year One." Like in that comic, "Batman Begins" features Bruce learning to be Batman through trial and error, as well as forming an alliance with Detective Jim Gordon (Gary Oldman). "Begins" also includes mob boss Carmine Falcone (Tom Wilkinson), who was introduced in "Year One."

"Batman Begins" isn't outright horror like "Arkham Asylum" is, but many scenes do have a genuinely scary and intense atmosphere because of the League of Shadows' fear toxin. In turn, "The Dark Knight" takes after "The Long Halloween," having Batman, Gordon, and District Attorney Harvey Dent (Aaron Eckhart) form a triumvirate to take down the Gotham mob.

Christopher Nolan, for his part, cited 1989 comic "The Man Who Falls" by Dennis O'Neil and Dick Giordano, which tells Bruce Wayne's life from childhood to crime fighting. "Batman Begins" has a similar scope of time. During the 1970s, O'Neil (who wrote novelizations of both "Batman Begins" and "The Dark Knight") had pushed Batman in a darker direction alongside artist Neal Adams. The pair notably created the villain Ra's al Ghul, who appears in "Batman Begins" (played by Liam Neeson) as Bruce's mentor and the twist villain. A scene of Bruce and Ra's sword-fighting mirrors their duel in O'Neil and Adams' "Batman" #244.

The O'Neil/Adams Batman stories were also a stylistic influence on "Batman: The Animated Series." In turn, "Batman Begins" lifted one of its plot points from that show's episode "Dreams in Darkness," where the Scarecrow tries to poison Gotham's water supply. The people who made "Batman Begins" respected the character and that respect shows onscreen.

Amidst all the tributes and wonderful stories about Patrick Stewart that hit the internet after his passing, one other viral video stood out. Stewart's fight with actor and comedian James Corden onstage at the 2011 Glamour Awards was a rare public outburst by the legendary Star Trek actor, and one that he deeply regretted as the years passed.

For those unfamiliar, the video went viral back then when Stewart took the stage and criticized Corden, the host, for looking disinterested between awards. Corden told Stewart to "get on with presenting," which then escalated to Stewart telling the audience he could see Corden's belly sticking out from the back row. Corden jabbed back that he could see Stewart "dying" onstage due to his age, and after one odd joke involving the Jonas Brothers, the moment ended. People have seen that, but fewer might know how Stewart felt afterward.

Stewart later expressed deep regret about the incident while speaking about it to Classic FM (via Glamour). The Star Trek actor admitted he'd been drinking, and it all went off the rails once he took the stage:

My part of the evening came late and it was alcohol (that prompted the remark), I'm afraid. I went too far, I was somewhat out of control. I have nothing but admiration for Mr Corden. I still blush in remembrance of it.

Buzzfeed also reported that Stewart said elsewhere he was upset by a comment Corden made toward another actress earlier in the evening. He began to drink and, unfortunately, made comments that he regretted. Fortunately, he also confirmed that he'd spoken to the Corden since then, and they agreed to bury the hatchet.

The resurfaced viral video was the most I've seen of James Corden since he retired from late-night, and based on how he spoke about the event, I'm sure he wasn't thrilled to see it back in the news either. The comedian later said he had zero problem with Sir Patrick Stewart, and said that despite how it looked at the moment, he was not mad:

I couldn't have less of a problem with him. He just went for it, he was unscripted, and I've no idea where it was going... And I wish I hadn't looked like I was so angry. Because I was just bemused. I'm not entirely sure what he wanted to happen, but I'm sure what happened wasn't what he wanted. But you know, he's Sir Patrick Stewart and he's great. Everyone's allowed a mistake. My hunch is he's a nice guy.

It's important to know the context of how both sides felt after the fact, because unfortunately, I think people unfairly pushed a narrative about the interaction that wasn't true. The implication was that Patrick Stewart hated James Corden, who has been a polarizing figure since stepping into the limelight.

In reality, the moment went down as one of Stewart's biggest embarrassments, and went against many of the other pleasant interactions that the world knew him for. I'm glad that he found the time to reconcile with Corden after what happened all those years ago, but it's sad to see it resurface again after his death.

CinemaBlend continues to pay respects to Patrick Stewart and offers condolences to his friends and family as they mourn his death. I'm sure more stories about the actor will surface ahead of his appearance in Avengers: Doomsday, which is out in theaters on December 18th.

#3456. No, We Aren’t All Eating 'Too Much' Protein

If you’ll permit me a rant—I promise to make it fact-filled and interesting—I am sick of the articles that seem to pop up every few months claiming that we are all eating “too much” protein. They convey an inaccurate picture of how the body uses protein, and they demonize perfectly healthy meals that happen to be high in protein. It’s time to set the record straight.

It is true that most of us eat more than the RDA (recommended daily allowance) of protein, but that's a good thing—the RDA is meant as a minimum. It's true that protein-boosted foods are trendy, and that they're not necessarily great dietary choices in the big picture. It's also true that you can eat a healthy diet with little to no meat, but meat is not synonymous with protein. Let's look at what we actually know about the role of protein in a healthy diet, and how to tell if you're eating too much or too little.

As a refresher, protein is one of the three calorie-containing macronutrients (fats, carbs, protein) that make up most of the food we eat. Proteins are made of amino acids, and these amino acids are required for the growth, repair, and functioning of our bodies.

We can get protein from a variety of sources. Meats are particularly protein-dense; a chicken breast contains about 35 grams of protein. Other animal products, like milk and eggs, are also rich in protein. Plant-based foods tend to have less protein than animal products, but it’s not hard to meet or exceed protein requirements even on a vegan diet. Beans, grains, and soy products like tofu contain significant amounts of protein, for example.

If you’d like a cheat sheet on how much protein you’re supposed to eat based on your activity level, you can find one here. And that’s a good place to start dissecting this “too much protein” myth, because before we can declare an amount of protein to be “too much,” we need to understand how much is “enough.”

The government communicates targets for different nutrients to encourage us all to eat a healthy, balanced diet. These targets are the basis for the “% daily value” labels on the back of packaged foods, and for the nutrient makeup of school lunches. The RDA, or recommended daily allowance, is defined as “the average daily dietary intake level that is sufficient to meet the nutrient requirement of nearly all (97 to 98 percent) healthy individuals in a group.”

In other words, if 100% of us were to eat the RDA of protein, at least 97% of us would be getting enough protein—we'd be meeting the minimum to be healthy. That's right, this number is a minimum to avoid malnutrition, not a maximum, and not a recommendation for optimal health.

By the way, if you're wondering how that number is determined? For protein, it is based on nitrogen balance. Humans break down proteins, as part of our body’s daily function, and we excrete nitrogen as a result. If you eat enough protein (which contains nitrogen), the amount of nitrogen you excrete will be the same as, or more than, the amount you eat. In other words, if you aren’t breaking your own body proteins down (in excess of what you eat), then whatever you’re eating must be, in some sense, enough.

In this way of thinking, the RDA is the minimum to stay healthy. More is fine; less would mean that you may not be getting enough. For some nutrients, there is also an UL, or upper limit, telling you that more than a certain amount is too much. Upper limits are calculated for vitamins and minerals; there is no upper limit defined for protein.

Therefore, there is no official definition for “too much” protein. If somebody eats more than the RDA, they’re not eating too much; they’re just eating more than the minimum. You’re supposed to eat more than the minimum.

The RDA for protein is set at 46 grams per day for a 125-pound woman, and at 56 grams per day for a 154-pound man. (The USDA chose those as their examples.) That’s based on an RDA of 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram bodyweight, which works out to 0.36 grams per pound. So a 200-pound person would need 72 grams of protein per day.

This USDA report found that most adult men average roughly 90 to 100 grams of protein per day, although men aged 70 and up only get about 80 grams of protein per day. Women tend to average around 70 grams per day, with those aged 70 and up averaging 62 grams.

Above the RDA? Yes. Too much? I don’t see any way of arguing that. And before you say that we’re getting almost double the recommendation, let's check the math. Those RDA numbers are for 125- and 154-pound people. On the other hand, the averages for what we eat are based on actual people, not ideals. The average American man is 200 pounds, and the average American woman is 171 pounds. So, to compare the numbers:

The average woman is 171 pounds, so her RDA would be 62 grams per day. (Women, on average, eat 70 grams of protein per day.)

The average man is 200 pounds, so his RDA would be 72 grams per day. (Men, on average, eat 90 to 100 grams of protein per day.)

Again, there’s no need to stick to the minimum; going 8 grams over, or even 28 grams over, is fine. It’s probably better to go over than to just scrape by, and many of us arguably don’t get enough. Let me explain.

Let’s start with older adults. Not only does protein intake tend to decrease with age, older adults are vulnerable to issues that stem from a loss of muscle mass. People tend to lose 3-5% of their muscle mass per decade starting at age 30, but strength training and protein intake can support maintaining our muscle, and thus likely prevent or reduce that decline.

The Dietary Guidelines include a note that “About 50 percent of women and 30 percent of men 71 and older fall short of protein foods recommendations.” Meanwhile, a study found that older adults who don’t meet the recommendations are “more likely to be limited when stooping, crouching, or kneeling, standing or sitting for long periods, walking up 10 steps, preparing meals, and walking for a quarter mile.”

So even if it’s true that the average adult gets more protein than recommended, there are clearly a lot of elderly folks who don’t. These are the same people who have more issues functioning in everyday life. This may be a chicken-and-egg situation—was the functional decline a cause or an effect of the change in their diet?—but this sure does not seem to be a group of people who should be eating less protein.

There’s another large group of people who benefit from more, not less, protein: people who are pregnant or lactating. Instead of 0.36 grams of protein per pound of body weight (62 grams for a 171-pound person), the RDA for people who are pregnant or lactating is 0.5 grams/pound (so, 86 grams of protein per day).

When you’re pregnant, you also have higher caloric needs, so the increased total amount of food makes it easier to get the higher protein amount. Still, it makes more sense to spend your energy on making sure you’re getting enough protein, rather than worrying about getting too much.

You knew we were heading in this direction (I say between reps of barbell squats, wiping protein shake off my lips): People who exercise should get more protein than just the RDA.

While the fear-mongering “too much protein” articles sometimes mention that bodybuilders or elite athletes need their protein, they tend to hand-wave this away as a special concern that doesn’t apply to normal people. But I think it’s worth a closer look—and honestly, this situation applies to a lot more people than just a few athletes.

Officially, there isn’t an RDA for athletes; people who exercise can stave off malnutrition with the same 0.36 grams per pound as everyone else. But that doesn’t mean that the RDA is the best target to aim for.

The International Association of Athletics Federations, which governs track and field competitions, recommends that most athletes who are maintaining or gaining weight eat 0.59 to 0.77 grams of protein per pound of bodyweight per day. That’s 101 to 131 grams for the average 171-pound woman, and 118 to 154 grams for a 200-pound man.

A group of organizations, including the American College of Sports Medicine, largely agrees, recommending a range from 0.54 to 0.9 grams per pound for all athletes whose weight is stable or gaining. That includes people who do endurance training like distance running, as well as strength athletes whose exercise involves mainly lifting weights. Those ranges would go as high as 153 grams for our 171-pound woman, and 180 grams for our 200-pound man.

You don’t need to be an Olympian to consider yourself an “athlete” in this sense. If you’re training for a half marathon, you’re doing plenty of distance running, and should fuel accordingly. And if you’re “just” lifting weights in the gym, but taking it seriously enough that you’re training regularly and working hard, you should consider eating in these ranges as well.

Dieting to lose weight is not only a popular American pastime, it’s also arguably good for at least some people's health. If you’ve been on a diet recently, or if you’re planning to go on one, you aren’t a person who should settle for the RDA either.

Research shows that protein intake (and strength training—they go together!) is important to maintain muscle mass when we’re losing weight. After all, you’re aiming for fat loss, not trying to get your muscles to waste away. Muscle loss is especially a concern with weight-loss drugs like Ozempic, but any dieter should be aware of this issue.

For example, this study found that diets ranging from 0.48 to 0.72 grams of protein per kg of body weight (that’s 82 to 123 grams for our 171-pound woman, 96 to 144 for our 200-pound man) resulted in less weight regain after the diet, and helped people to maintain muscle mass and feel more full while they were dieting.

And if you’re losing weight and exercising? The IAAF recommends that athletes who are “undertaking high-quality weight loss” need at least 0.72 grams per pound of bodyweight, and possibly as much as 1.09 grams per pound. That would be 186 grams for a 171-pound athlete, or 218 grams for a 200-pound athlete. Most people won’t need to go that high, and it’s unclear whether athletes need to go that high. But I’m including these numbers so you see how high the ranges actually go.

Ultimately, weight loss is widely understood to be more effective and have healthier results with higher protein intakes rather than lower ones. When people focus on just eating less, without thinking about what their diet actually consists of, it’s easy to forget about protein. But the evidence suggests that you should increase protein when you’re decreasing overall calories.

The idea that protein causes weight gain is a common talking point in those articles about “too much” protein, and it’s sort of true—but it also doesn’t mean what you think it means.

When you eat more food than your body needs, your body can store it as fat. That’s true no matter what the excess is made of—protein, carbs, fat, or even alcohol. The protein you eat gets used for many different things in your body. You can build it into muscle tissue, use it for growth and repair of different kinds of cells, and so on. You can also use it for energy—basically, burning it for the calories.

So if you were eating a perfectly balanced diet, and then decided to add an extra 100 grams of protein per day, then sure, a lot of that protein would be used for energy, and since we’d have excess energy, it would get stored as fat.

But if you ate more protein, but that protein replaced other foods in your diet, then there would be no excess calories to store. Nobody is saying you should chug a couple of protein shakes on top of your regular diet. They’re saying (I’m saying) that you should plan your meals and snacks to include more protein.

For example, if your regular lunch is a turkey-and-cheese sandwich with a side of chips, you could improve the protein content of your diet by adding more turkey to the sandwich and replacing the chips with an apple. Same total calories, but more protein. As long as your total calories for the day aren’t in excess of your needs, the “extra” protein won’t get stored as fat.

In general, high protein diets don’t have any serious health consequences. There’s a major exception, though: in some medical conditions, you may be told to limit your protein intake to protect your health.

For example, people with chronic kidney disease are often advised to use the RDA (0.36 grams per pound of body weight) as a maximum rather than a minimum. Your kidneys play a role in processing protein for excretion, so a lowered protein intake reduces the amount of work that a damaged kidney has to do. That said, once a person with chronic kidney disease begins dialysis, they may be advised to increase their protein intake for better health now that their body has help to handle the higher levels.

People with certain other disorders, like phenylketonuria and homocystinuria, may also be advised to eat a low-protein diet. Obviously, if you have one of these conditions, you should be getting your dietary advice from your medical team (ask for a referral to a dietitian!) rather than from general articles on the internet.

Besides those known medical issues, the occasional findings about eating “too much” protein tend to fit into the “X is good for you/X is bad for you” ricochet news cycle. They’re not holistic assessments of protein in general on health in general, but rather specific research questions that are still being figured out.

For example, this 2017 study found that a high-protein (and high-fiber) diet seemed to slightly worsen one measure of insulin resistance, but it also improved metabolic health and body composition. The researchers concluded that the subjects’ body chemistry was probably just responding appropriately to the changed nutrient content of their diet. A few years later, a study of high-BMI women with insulin resistance saw improvements to their insulin resistance on a high-protein diet.

Or to take another example, a study in 2024 found a link between high-protein diets and atherosclerosis. But if you look at what the researchers were actually studying, they were looking at how leucine (one amino acid found in protein) affects the mTOR biochemical pathway in certain types of white blood cells. By the way, that mTOR pathway is involved in a lot more body processes than atherosclerosis, and does a lot of good things too.

So are these results interesting, and worth further study? Definitely. Worth changing protein recommendations? Only if this effect turns out (1) to actually lead to worse health outcomes, and (2) to outweigh the known benefits of higher protein. The body of evidence doesn’t yet support lowering protein recommendations, nor adding an upper limit.

So if protein is good for us, and most of us can’t really get “too much,” why are so many people arguing that we’re overdoing it? I think part of the reason is just misunderstanding (the writers don’t tend to have a background in nutrition and especially not in sports nutrition), but more often, I think they’re talking about a different issue entirely.

Often the “too much protein” stuff is just a way of talking about the environmental effects of meat consumption or dairy farming. People making this argument are trying to pry the double cheeseburgers out of our hands and reassure us that we’ll be okay. I don’t think an attack on protein is an appropriate way to make that point, since plant-based proteins exist and are a fine alternative. But I understand where they’re coming from.

Ultimately, if you’re trying to make the argument that we’re eating “too much” protein for our health, you really can’t do that without some evidence that we’re eating so much protein that it’s harming our health on a widespread level. And that evidence just doesn’t exist.
