#3455. Vanity Fair Announces New Hires and Promotions Across Departments

Vanity Fair Global Editorial Director Mark Guiducci today announced 11 new hires and appointments to the magazine’s masthead, deepening the magazine’s coverage across technology and politics, while adding talent to its operations and creative teams.

Vanity Fair’s new hires bring fresh perspectives to the magazine’s reporting on power and influence, alongside new creative voices to help shape its visual storytelling.

Maggie Coughlan is promoted to global managing editor. Since joining the team in 2021, she has held several positions at Vanity Fair, most recently as executive editor. She previously held editorial roles at the New York Post and People.com. She holds a master’s degree in digital publishing from NYU.

Emily Shugerman joins Vanity Fair as a senior staff writer reporting on wealth and politics on the West Coast. Emily comes from The San Francisco Standard, where she covered the shifting political allegiances of Silicon Valley’s richest, the fight over California’s proposed billionaire tax, and the growing power of AI lab workers. Before that, she was a reporter at The Daily Beast, where her investigations spurred leadership changes at national nonprofits and policy shifts at major corporations. Her work has also appeared in The Cut and The Guardian. She lives in San Francisco.

Jack Holmes joins as a senior editor for Vanity Fair, where he’s been editing features and political coverage since January. He will continue that work and expand into society and technology. Previously he was a senior staff writer and political editor for Esquire. He’s also the founder and publisher of The Football Weekend, a publication covering world soccer. Jack graduated from Vanderbilt University with a degree in philosophy and political science.

Nina Joyce is vice president of communications, based in New York, leading Vanity Fair’s communications globally. With 17 years of experience, she previously oversaw media relations for Condé Nast’s UK business and portfolio of brands, managing corporate reputation, brand strategy and major cultural events. Prior to joining Condé Nast, Nina spent a decade at Vice Media Group, holding senior roles across VICE, Refinery29, and i-D, and ultimately leading corporate PR across EMEA.

Roxanne Doucet joins as global visuals director. She has worked across New York and Paris, and collaborated with renowned artists and luxury houses including Dior, Loewe, and Balenciaga, building a practice rooted in fine art, documentary photography, and editorial storytelling. She was previously visual director at Vogue US and has consulted for Vogue France.

Dondre Stuetley joins Vanity Fair as senior visuals editor. Previously he was the photo editor at WSJ Magazine, commissioning stories on art, fashion, entertainment, design, food, and architecture.

Sameet Sharma joins as senior visuals editor. He was most recently the visuals director at V Magazine, and prior to V, he oversaw visual production at G-III, working on brands such as DKNY and Karl Lagerfeld. He also brings experience from Hearst magazines, where he worked on the photo teams at ELLE, Marie Claire, and Esquire.

Christian Zelaya joins as a senior designer. He brings more than five years of experience shaping editorial reporting into creative and clever visual stories for digital and social platforms and attracting readers for global brands like NBC, Forbes, and Scholastic.

Michael Kanyongolo joins Vanity Fair as audience development manager. He was most recently the news producer for Quanta Magazine, where he carried out web development, visual design, and production. He previously worked on web production at the New York Post and has a background in media and psychology.

Nazanin Hakim joins Vanity Fair as a creative producer on the video team. She brings a background in documentary filmmaking, having worked on a range of projects exploring politics, culture, and technology, including the Emmy-nominated series Turning Point: 9/11 and the War on Terror and What’s Next? The Future With Bill Gates.

Chris Black joins Vanity Fair as a contributing editor. He is a writer, photographer, and cohost of How Long Gone. He lives in New York and Los Angeles.

#3454. Ted Lasso Star Jason Sudeikis Starred In A Gritty Crime Thriller With Marvel Actors

Plenty of comedic actors have played dramatic roles that didn't work out too well. The same can't quite be said of "Ted Lasso" star Jason Sudeikis, who proved he could handle a dramatic role in "South of Heaven," a crime thriller that should have been much better than it was. Oddly enough, the film also happens to be a surreptitious comic book team-up event movie, with a cast full of Marvel Cinematic Universe alumni.

We don't often talk about the "Saturday Night Live" to noirish crime thriller pipeline. But a fair few "SNL" stars have made the transition, from Adam Sandler in "Uncut Gems" to Jim Belushi in "Gang Related." Sudeikis, who appeared on the legendary sketch comedy series from 2003 to 2013, found his biggest post-"SNL" success by playing the lead role in Apple TV's "Ted Lasso." The actor's inherent charm has served him well as the endearingly optimistic college football coach tasked with leading a British soccer team to greatness. But with "South of Heaven," the "SNL" alum clearly wanted to branch out and try something new. He was close to succeeding, too.

The film sees Sudeikis play a convicted felon who's released from a prison sentence early to spend a year with his terminally-ill girlfriend. Unfortunately, things don't quite go to plan, and Sudeikis' ex-con finds himself in a fight for his and the life of his beloved. It's a sort of okay crime thriller that starts out great before taking a major turn part-way through. Luckily, it also has a solid cast to help carry the melodrama, a surprising amount of whom have played MCU characters.

"South of Heaven" — not to be confused with the Western flop Vince Vaughn and Billy Bob Thornton would probably like you to forget about, "South of Heaven, West of Hell" — is directed by Israeli filmmaker Aharon Keshales, who also co-wrote the script with Navot Papushado, and Kai Mark. Keshales similarly co-wrote and co-directed his first feature, "Rabies" in 2010, and his second, "Big Bad Wolves," in 2013, earning him and his co-director, Papushado, praise from Quentin Tarantino who called it the "best film of the year." "South of Heaven" represents Keshales' first solo feature and sees him team up with Jason Sudeikis for a gritty thriller that sadly devolves into a fairly rote genre exercise. Hey, at least the director brought together some MCU vets to support his leading man.

Sudeikis plays convicted felon Jimmy Ray, who's serving a 15-year sentence for his role in a robbery, but convinces the parole board to set him free after 12 to spend a year with his dying girlfriend, Annie Ray (Evangeline Lilly). For the first half of the movie, Keshales presents a noir-infused love story with an indie drama spirit that sees Sudeikis and Lilly demonstrate some surprisingly good chemistry. Jimmy is trying to go straight as best he can, turning down offers to meet up with his prison buddy Frank (Jeremy Bobb) and generally trying to do right by Annie. Then, things go off the rails.

When Jimmy reluctantly accepts a "side job" from his crooked parole officer Schmidt (Shea Whigham), he winds up stoking the ire of crime boss Whit Price (Mike Colter), who kidnaps Annie. Jimmy then takes Whit's son, Tommy Price (Thaddeus J. Mixon) captive and the whole thing devolves into violence.

You might have noticed that almost everyone in "South of Heaven" has been involved in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. The most obvious is, of course, Evangeline Lilly, who portrayed Hope van Dyne/Wasp in the "Ant-Man" movies and "Avengers: Endgame." Mike Colter, meanwhile, played the title role in Netflix's "Luke Cage" series from 2016 to 2018, and appeared in the team-up miniseries "The Defenders" in 2017. That same miniseries also featured Krysten Ritter's Jessica Jones, who had her own Netflix show that featured yet another "South of Heaven" actor, Jeremy Bobb.

That's not all the MCU connections, either. Shea Whigham played Roger Dooley in 2015's "Agent Carter" Season 1, while Jaime Zevallos, who plays Julio in "South of Heaven," previously portrayed Father Francis Xavier Delgado in Freeform's "Cloak & Dagger." As such, Jason Sudeikis' crime thriller is secretly one of the most significant unofficial Marvel team-up movies ever made.

Sadly, that didn't translate to one of Sudeikis' best films. "South of Heaven" bears a 48% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes, with Amy Nicholson of the New York Times calling it a "Texas melodrama that's as convincing as a taxidermied jackalope." Craig D. Lindsey of the AV Club saw two very different films in "South of Heaven," one "straight-faced and suspenseful" and another "almost randomly nihilistic." Meanwhile, the Minneapolis Star Tribune's Chris Hewitt found Sudeikis' "subdued performance" to be "hugely likable" and Owen Gleiberman of Variety seemed to agree. "The movie gives Jason Sudeikis a chance to act without the safety net of comedy, and he proves that he's got the right stuff," he wrote, even if he also felt Sudeikis should have showcased his dramatic talent in a different movie — one that "offers the safety net of believability."

There are few things I love more than a reality show, and after years of devouring The Traitors with my Peacock subscription, I was thrilled to hear that the folks behind that Emmy-winning series were creating another. Enter The Mob, another campy competition show that's available in its entirety with a Hulu subscription. The show once again proved that RuPaul's Drag Race alum Willam Belli is a top-tier TV personality, but it turns out that not even the cast knew the rules when cameras went up.

The Mob's jobs feel more urgent than The Traitors' missions, but it took some adjusting to its format. Even the cast had a hard time with this, mostly because they didn't actually know all of the rules of the show they were competing on. During a recent clip from Gayety's Instagram, Willam spoke about her experience shooting the series, saying:

I asked for the rules every episode and I didn't get them until Episode 4, a printed copy. We did not know what was going on and we really wanted to. But information is power, and I understand that you don't want a reality show contestant to have power. So keeping them in dark leads to better stakes for the game and I understand that now.

Well, my mind is blown. It was hard enough to nail down the rules and format of The Mob as a viewer, but the fact that the cast was similarly clueless is truly wild to me. It didn't make the show's first four episodes any less entertaining, even though many of my favorite contestants got whacked way too early. Still, I'd think that the powers that be on production would want the reality TV personalities to at least know everything about the game they were expected to play.

As much as I enjoyed the first season of The Mob, I have to assume that the gameplay might have been even more dynamic if the cast knew the show's rules from the jump. Indeed, the first few eliminations were a little sleepy, such as Dancing with the Stars judge Bruno Tonioli pledging allegiance to Joe Gorga and then immediately getting whacked.

You can see Willam Belli's comments about The Mob and feeling a bit clueless at the start of filming below:

Willam might be the only contestant from RuPaul's Drag Race to get disqualified, but that doesn't mean she went against the rules in every situation. After all, The Mob cast were starting a brand new competition series, and didn't have any previous episodes to use as a reference. The folks who caught on seemed to make it the farthest, but it was curtains for other favorites like Willam, Bruno, and Debi Mazar.

The Mob is streaming in its entirety on Hulu as part of the 2026 TV schedule. We'll just have to see if it gets renewed for a second season, and how the gameplay changes with contestants who know what to expect.

#3452. Five Race-Day Smartwatch Hacks Every Marathon Runner Should Know

I love my Garmin Forerunner 970, but the fact is, most runners don't need all the features it has to offer. In fact, for most road races, you can get by with whatever smartwatch you already own—as long as you know how to use it. If you've got a marathon or half-marathon coming up, these five tricks will only take a few minutes to set up, and they can save you from one of many of the small-but-avoidable disasters that can derail a good race.

Nothing spikes pre-race anxiety like standing in a corral of hundreds of people watching your watch fail to latch onto a signal. Tall buildings, crowded starts, and a sea of other devices make the first minute of GPS unreliable, which can leave your opening mileage pace wildly off.

The fix is simple: start the GPS search early. Step outside, into the open, as soon as you've dropped your bag, and select your run activity at least 10 to 15 minutes before the starting gun. If your watch supports multi-band or dual-frequency GPS, turn it on in the activity settings, since it's noticeably better in dense downtown starts. Then, don't press start until the gun goes off (or you cross the line, if you want chip-accurate pacing).

Bonus tip: If you're in a start corral with a long wait, you can lock the signal and then pause the activity screen. Just remember to hit start when you actually take off.

Multiple data screens are great for training, but overwhelming during a race. Too many numbers invite overthinking, and seeing the "wrong" number at mile two can lead you into a very stressful mile ten.

My recommendation is to build a dedicated race screen with three to four fields at most:

Lap pace or average lap pace (not instant pace, which jumps around constantly with GPS)

Distance or lap distance, so you know where you are relative to the mile markers

Heart rate, especially in the early miles when adrenaline tempts you to go out too fast

Elapsed time, for splits against your goal

Keep it clean and stripped down, and avoid the temptation to add cadence, power, vertical oscillation, and everything else. You can always review those stats during your cool-down.

A text from your boss at mile 14 is nobody's idea of a good time. Before race day, switch your watch to Do Not Disturb or Airplane mode, or turn on a dedicated activity mode that blocks notifications. This also saves battery, which matters if your marathon is going to take you four-plus hours.

After blocking the outside world, you can set race-specific alerts, like a high heart-rate alert to keep you honest in the first half. I also know runners who set a recurring time or distance alert for fueling—say, every 30 to 40 minutes, or every 5 miles—so remembering to down a gel or a sports drink doesn't depend on your fading brain.

Here's one thing I learn the hard way, every time: Your watch will almost always say you've run farther than the race course says you have. Race courses are measured along the shortest possible route, but along the way, you'll weave around people, take wide turns, and generally add extra distance. I've run marathons where my watch reads closer to 26.6 miles (nearly an extra half mile), so my "on pace" watch is actually behind my chip time.

The hack: Ignore the watch's auto-lap and press the lap button manually at each mile marker (or at every kilometer marker, if that's what the course uses). This gives you pace data aligned to the official course, not the satellite's best guess. It also gives you a quick mental check against your plan. If you've set up your watch for it, display average lap pace, then glance at it a few hundred meters after each marker to see how you're tracking. And don't panic if your watch beeps for a mile before you pass the marker—trust the course and your lap presses, and do your best to ignore the mismatched distance adding up.

Rain, sweat, high-fives, and a hasty cup grab at an aid station can all trigger accidental taps on a touchscreen watch. Few things are worse than discovering at mile 18 that you accidentally paused, ended, or switched screens on your activity. So before the race, turn on your watch's screen lock, so a stray touch doesn't do anything.

If your watch has a configurable wake gesture, consider turning it off to save battery, and set the backlight to a short timeout. While we're talking watch-wearing protocol, remember to wear it snugly, one finger-width above your wrist bone, for a better heart-rate reading as you sweat. Finally, if your watch has one, use the post-race auto-save reminder. (Otherwise, do your best to hit stop after you cross the finish line.)

Again, you don't need the most premium running-specific watch ahead of race day. If you have time, test these hacks on a long run, so that you're not wasting any precious mental energy during the big day.

#3451. Magic: The Gathering Boss Reveals the Next Marvel Set’s Surprising Origin Story

Aaron Forsythe said Magic’s original narrative got ‘total buy-in’ from Marvel

Aaron Forsythe said Magic’s original narrative got ‘total buy-in’ from Marvel

Magic: The Gathering has already released two Universes Beyond sets based on Marvel Comics, with Marvel’s Spider-Man in 2025 and Marvel Super Heroes in 2026. The game’s designers are taking a very different approach to their third tie-in set, Darkhold Destiny, which will launch in 2027. Rather than simply making cards based on iconic characters and comic book arcs, Wizards of the Coast designers worked with Marvel to create an entirely new storyline designed with the game’s mechanics in mind. Magic’s vice president of design Aaron Forsythe told Polygon at MagicCon Atlanta that the inspiration for the new approach came from an unlikely source.

“My daughter was actually playing the Guardians of the Galaxy game on Xbox, which has a cool story,” Forsythe says. “It’s not from a comic, it’s not from a movie. They just let the game studio make their own story that fit the medium they were trying to use. It seems like they should let us do that.”

Forsythe says he received “total buy-in” from Marvel as soon as he brought up the idea.

“I think a lot of that was the trust we had built up working on the first two sets and the Secret Lair,” he said. “They saw that we aren't just a licensing team that wants to put the Hulk on a T-shirt. We create our own worlds and stories, and as creators, they could really appreciate the work we did and gave us the green light right away.”

Development on Darkhold Destiny actually began before Marvel’s Spider-Man launched — Forsythe said all Universes Beyond sets take four years to develop, as opposed to the typical three-year timeline for in-universe sets, because they need to get so much feedback from licensing partners. But even without player feedback, Forsythe says he realized something was missing from Spider-Man and Marvel Super Heroes that hadn’t been a problem in other Universes Beyond sets.

“The Marvel sets in particular are not driven by any real narrative,” he says. “We have some saga cards that talk about the death of Gwen Stacy, which we know people know. The Lord of the Rings has a linear story. Everybody knows how that story plays out. In Final Fantasy, there were 16 mostly linear stories woven together in a way that everyone who's touched those games has experienced. Marvel, with 60 years of stuff and us not using the movies — which are the stories people mostly know nowadays — we’re just picking moments in time, characters, and different sagas and whatnot. As a whole, it did not feel like it was telling much of a story.”

Magic’s designers created an original character, Fraxi, Scion of Yggdrasil, who will appear in Darkhold Destiny and a tie-in comic alongside Marvel favorites like Thor and Doctor Strange. The goal is to satisfy Magic players who want a story while still bringing in Marvel fans who will become committed players.

“I'm not going to say there aren't any tourist fans that just want buy their Spider-Man cards and go home,” Forsythe says. “But mostly once you dip your toes in, once you start building a deck, once you see your friend's Commander deck, once you go online and start reading about all the stuff that's out there, once you go to a store or a tournament or a convention, sure Spider-Man brought you in, but this aperture opens up into this vast, incredible world.”

Forsythe says Darkhold Destiny and the two other still unannounced Universes Beyond sets releasing next year will incorporate feedback they’ve been getting from players about the game’s various crossovers. He hopes these improvements will encourage even the most skeptical Magic players to give Universes Beyond a chance as the licensed sets have also helped bring lapsed players back to the hobby.

“There are some parts of the audience that are doubling down on the Magic IP stuff, being holdouts against UB like, ‘We'll show them! We'll all buy Reality Fracture!’” Forsythe says. “I would just say that UB is both getting new fans, and it's reactivated a lot of people too. I've heard 25 times in the last two days of some IP reactivating somebody like, ‘I'd forgotten about Magic, but it was fun and this thing you did got me back in. And now I'm here.'”

#3450. Nvidia’s Jensen Huang May Just Survive His Scandal

Read A Billion to One: From the mad scientists to the megadonors, a dispatch on the money, power, and influence of technology.

Exactly three years ago today, the tech world found itself in an all-too-familiar crisis. On an otherwise ordinary Friday afternoon, the board of OpenAI abruptly fired Sam Altman, following a secretive deliberation about what was believed to be a pattern of deceptive behavior by the CEO. A shock wave of panic rippled through the industry: Employees rallied around Altman, who set up a makeshift war room in his Russian Hill home; investors made furious calls to the board to demand a reversal; and Satya Nadella offered to create the conditions within Microsoft for Altman and his loyalists to rebuild OpenAI from the ground up.

As the members of OpenAI’s board racked their brains for who might make a worthy replacement, the extent of their miscalculation quickly dawned on them. OpenAI could not survive without Altman, and the tech industry might not survive without OpenAI. Within four days of Altman’s firing (an event so fleeting that it came to be known as “the blip”), he was reinstated as CEO, and the board coup that failed to kill him only made him stronger.

Three years later, the foibles of a different man at a different AI company—Jensen Huang, who resigned from his post as CEO of Nvidia last week after the revelation of several compromising affairs—have thrown the industry and the stock market into tumult.

Not one to go down without a fight, Huang has reportedly hunkered down with his inner circle to plot his own comeback. Meanwhile, a petition to reinstate him, pending an independent investigation not unlike the one that exonerated Altman, has garnered nearly 200,000 signatures, including from the likes of Elon Musk, Travis Kalanick, and Garry Tan. Even President Trump has weighed in, noting that he “would certainly not mind” if Huang were reinstated. The news from today’s earnings report that the company had brought in a record-breaking $100 billion+ in sales last quarter under Huang’s leadership will only help their cause.

While an inside source told CNBC yesterday that Nvidia’s board is not considering reinstating Huang, the former executive is continuing to court public opinion independently. “I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a public statement Tuesday. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

It would be difficult to overstate Huang’s influence on the AI industry and US tech policy at large.

This entire mess has felt uncannily validating of the thesis behind Vanity Fair’s New Establishment list this fall, for which I wrote, “Never in the list’s history have the scale and the stakes of individual influence felt so high,” noting the “Ouroboros of investments and insular networks that make you realize how small and self-serving circles of power can be—and how quickly they could come tumbling down.”

We’ve officially entered the age of the too-big-to-fail CEO, in which our economy increasingly hinges on—and endlessly forgives—the moods and misdeeds of a handful of powerful men with few accountability structures. It’s not just the companies they founded that have become entwined with these founders. “The whole economy has basically been financed by Nvidia and in turn by Jensen’s ability to raise money,” says Yoni Rechtman, a partner at Slow Ventures.

Huang deserves a great deal of credit for having built his company from the ground up. But his trespasses—namely, becoming romantically involved with someone the State Department has linked to Chinese intelligence, and who has undeniably helped get America’s high-performance chips into the hands of our adversaries—are more than worthy of the scrutiny they’ve received.

Like a person who’s sick with a life-threatening illness but refuses to make a will, Huang demonstrated a staggeringly hubristic leadership. He had no real succession plan, installed a board and executive staff of yes-men and women, and created a “culture of omertà,” as his biographer, Stephen Witt, put it, that allowed his affairs to become an open secret within the company. Nvidia didn’t even protect itself with basic D&O insurance, which would have shielded it from the kinds of shareholder lawsuits it could now face. The Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq have all continued their precipitous decline since the news of his departure was announced last week.

As a result, how many of us have found ourselves asking, Why should the fate of my 401(k) have anything to do with one man’s sex life?

If you need another example, consider Musk, who has gained almost single-handed control over our space and satellite infrastructure. At SpaceX, he’s also become a master of the newly popular dual-class voting structures that have allowed founders like himself and Mark Zuckerberg to consolidate control of their companies. On more than one occasion, his erratic whims have left our geopolitical fate hanging in the balance.

Perhaps start-ups do need these larger-than-life characters to get off the ground. As Rechtman puts it to me, “Great businesses don’t get built by committee. They get built by small groups of people and singular leaders. And necessarily, in the pursuit of some huge and lofty project, a person becomes elevated to the status of ‘great.’”

But as companies mature—and especially as they go public—they owe it to themselves and to investors to outgrow their founders. Plenty of the companies keeping our economy afloat, like Apple, Amazon, Microsoft, and Netflix, have indeed survived the parting of their founders.

Unfortunately, public markets are now falling victim to the same hype frenzy as VCs. AI-linked stocks now account for nearly half of the S&P 500, and 47 of those stocks made up three quarters of the index’s gains in the first half of this year. Nvidia, in one way or another, is connected to just about all of those companies through an intricate web of loans, partnerships, and investments.

So how do we deal with tech’s “great man” problem? This extreme concentration of power has helped foster a startling lack of resilience in our geopolitical and economic systems. But ask any antitrust expert, and they’ll remind you that it can also erode product quality, endanger consumer protections, and raise prices.

The answer cannot simply be for these men to improve their moral character, and it cannot be for us to become more forgiving. After all, any one of them could drop dead of a heart attack and leave us in the same predicament.

Walter Isaacson, the Silicon Valley biographer who is now interviewing many of the field’s “great men” on his new podcast, The Builders, believes the only possible answer “is to have more entrepreneurs who can build competing products, who can shoot off rockets and get them into orbit and create satellites and create chips and build fabrication plants.”

Rumors are already circulating that if he does not return to Nvidia, Huang may start his own competitive chip manufacturer, which helps explain why VCs are lining up to demonstrate their goodwill.

In the meantime, as we prepare for more mega IPOs, we would be wise to examine the structure of these deals to see what checks on power exist within these companies, from strong succession plans to empowered boards. Unfortunately, Anthropic is preparing super-voting shares for founders, which will give them decisive control over the company following its $1.4 trillion IPO. But hey, at least there are seven of them.

#3449. This '80s R-Rated Superhero Movie Is Unlike Anything Marvel Or DC Has Made

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

We've been living in a world of mass entertainment dominated by superheroes and comic book characters for more than 25 years now, dating back to Marvel's earlier blockbuster hits like "X-Men" and "Spider-Man." Even small screen stuff like "The Walking Dead" has comic book roots. But decades before any of that, an indie film pioneer made a superhero movie unlike any other.

Lloyd Kaufman is independent film, in many ways, as the founder of Troma Entertainment. His media empire was built on the backs of low-budget schlock like "Surf Nazis Must Die" and "Pterodactyl Woman from Beverly Hills," among many others. But Kaufman's defining hit came in 1984 in the form of "The Toxic Avenger," an ultra violent, campy, R-rated superhero affair. It remains a distinct piece of punk rock cinema more than 40 years removed, unmatched in its insanity by anything Marvel or DC has done on screen.

The movie takes place in the fictional town of Tromaville, known as the toxic waste capital of America. A bullied young janitor in a popular gym falls into a vat of toxic waste and turns into a super strong but disfigured man. He begins cleaning up the streets from evildoers in an often funny yet violent fashion.

"The Toxic Avenger" has a long history on screen and is now a cult legend, but that legend began in '84, at a time when superheroes were far from bankable fare in the mainstream. Co-directed by Michael Herz and Kaufman himself, the resulting movie can't be accused of being high art, but it's one heck of a wild swing, and a testament to what the indie filmmaking spirit can accomplish.

At the time, Hollywood had only had the occasional superhero movie hit it big. "Superman: The Movie" in 1978 being the biggest one, while Batman didn't become a box office hero until 1989. Even that movie just led to the "Batman" franchise taking off rather than a broader trend of superheroes becoming big business. The '90s saw many try but few succeed, with stuff like "Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles" more the exception rather than the rule.

All of this to say, when Lloyd Kaufman decided to make a dark superhero comedy — an R-rated and super violent one no less — it wasn't exactly a recipe for success. At least not on paper. But decades before "Deadpool" broke the Marvel mold by going R-rated and injecting comedy into the genre, "The Toxic Avenger" dared to venture into that territory.

What's more, Kaufman and Co. did it on a shoestring budget of well under $1 million. "Deadpool" gets a lot of credit for being low-budget, but it still cost north of $50 million. What Kaufman pulled off with latex, old school special effects, and can-do indie spirit is nothing shy of impressive. Even those who are put off by the nature of this sort of exploitation film should be impressed by what was accomplished here with so little.

"The Toxic Avenger" has a demented sense of humor, and it doesn't give us a typical hero either. Toxie isn't a square-jawed, muscle-bound vigilante. He's a mutant who decides to clean up the streets with straight-up violence. The film has more in common with revenge driven horror/thrillers than it does any mainstream superhero movie. All the same, it became a cult hit and started a wildly unlikely franchise.

"No theater would play it," Lloyd Kaufman said of "The Toxic Avenger" to Parallax View in 2010. "We couldn't get one theater to play it anywhere and then we took it to Cannes and not one deal. Nothing! And then a few months later we got one movie theater in Greenwich Village, New York, and there was a line around the theater."

That single theater paved the way for more to follow. This was also at the dawn of the VHS home video craze, which is where the movie really thrived — so much so that Kaufman eventually produced a series of sequels. That includes 1989's "The Toxic Avenger Part II" and "The Toxic Avenger Part III: The Last Temptation of Toxie," also released in '89. Much later, "Citizen Toxie: The Toxic Avenger IV" would arrive in 2000. A gore-soaked remake of "The Toxic Avenger" starring Peter Dinklage was also released in 2025.

Kaufman's crown jewel is an elbow grease style, gory, raunchy, rubber-suit take on superheroes that doesn't resemble anything we've seen in the 2000s, really. Sure, "Clayface" brought body horror to the DC Universe, but it's completely without a sense of humor. It's also slick and relatively expensive (for a horror movie).

It was cutting edge then and it's impressively distinctive even now. More than that, "The Toxic Avenger" helped make the empire that is Troma. It's easy to write it all off as schlock, but Troma has been a haven for indie film for decades, with filmmakers like James Gunn ("Guardians of the Galaxy") cutting their teeth there. Without this movie, who knows if the empire as we know it even exists?

You can grab "The Toxic Avenger" on 4K, Blu-ray, or DVD from Amazon.

Much of its appeal comes from a slim 3.1-inch profile that lets it reach under beds, sofas, and other low furniture where taller robot vacuums often can’t fit. #3445. Apple, Chase, United Outages: What’s Going On?

Read A Billion to One: From the mad scientists to the megadonors, a dispatch on the money, power, and influence of technology.

Every time I see a new headline about yet another system outage this week, the beat of “We Didn’t Start the Fire” starts playing in my head: “Microsoft, NSA, grounded planes from FAA / United Airlines, Chase Bank, can’t send funds on Apple Pay…”

It feels like I could write a parody verse a day at the rate our infrastructure is faltering. A few weeks ago I wrote about the spate of cybersecurity incidents that led the industry to label last month “Black October.” Now my phone is blowing up, with everyone from colleagues to high school friends asking, what the hell is going on out there?

Are we under attack by a rogue nation? Are outdated software systems suddenly all throwing in the towel? Is this all just cyber-business as usual, with an unusually on-edge public?

I’m inclined to believe it’s some combination of all of the above. The FBI issued an urgent warning today that bad actors have been using ARTEX, the open-source AI penetration testing platform, to attempt widespread attacks. A source at a financial services company tells me, “It’s been a miserable month…. Just constant probing and hacking attempts.” Companies—and especially government agencies—with outdated software systems are scrambling to patch these vulnerabilities, and are often unable to do so securely without taking their systems entirely offline.

“What used to take a skilled operator days or weeks of chaining is now happening in hours,” says Snehal Antani, cofounder and CEO of the cybersecurity firm Horizon3. In other words: With AI, bad actors can pretty easily jiggle every doorknob around the globe to see who’s left their doors unlocked.

Meanwhile, the total lack of clarity from the Trump administration hasn’t exactly been reassuring. Even one administration-aligned VC partner I spoke with this morning called the joint presser between Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin a “clown show.”

For now, I’d urge you to heed the same advice I gave last time I wrote about this: Make sure those passwords are airtight and that multifactor authentication is activated. And maybe, just maybe, stock up on some light supplies you’d like to have around if 21st-century services stop working the way they’re supposed to.

“Going forward, expect this to become normal rather than exceptional,” Antani tells me. “We should expect persistent disruption of digital services—travel, banking, commerce, etc.—in the coming months as these organizations scramble to quickly improve their cyber resilience.”

$7 billion: That’s how much Sound Ventures, the firm founded by actor turned VC Ashton Kutcher and former music manager Guy Oseary, stands to profit from its 0.5% stake in Anthropic after the IPO this week.

#3444. How To Watch The Social Reckoning At Home

"The Social Reckoning" is finally hitting the home market. It will become available to buy or rent on digital starting November 24, 2026, prior to its physical media release on January 12, 2027.

In case you're unfamiliar with "The Social Reckoning" writ large, here's the gist. Almost two decades after he won an Academy Award for writing the screenplay for "The Social Network," a 2010 dramatization of the founding of Facebook directed by David Fincher, Aaron Sorkin decided to make a sequel that focuses on what Facebook has become in the 2020s. Jesse Eisenberg, who earned an Oscar nod for playing Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg in "The Social Network," declined to return to the role and was replaced by "Succession" veteran, Emmy and Tony winner, and Sorkin's "The Trial of the Chicago 7" collaborator Jeremy Strong. With Mikey Madison, Jeremy Allen White, Bill Burr, Wunmi Mosaku, Betty Gilpin, and Billy Magnussen starring alongside Strong, the project seemed almost too big to fail before it premiered in theaters on October 9, 2026.

Fail it did, though. Though it reportedly only lost a couple million for Sony (per Deadline), the film absolutely underperformed at the box office, and its rating on Rotten Tomatoes is a middling-to-bleak 54%. So what happened here? Well, from my perspective, "The Social Reckoning" is just a bad movie ... and /Film's chief film critic Chris Evangelista agrees with me. What went wrong as Sorkin tried to make a legacy sequel to one of the best films of the 21st century? Quite a lot actually!

I'll circle back to the "Social Network" of it all shortly, but the bottom line here is that "The Social Reckoning" just ... stinks to high heaven. From the embarrassing prologue featuring Portia Doubleday as a caricature named Kayleigh (I'm not kidding) to the fact that Aaron Sorkin keeps forcing Oscar winner Mikey Madison into outfits that would make her title character from "Anora" blush (in the name of corporate espionage), I found "The Social Network" to be a uniformly dreadful watch from start to finish. Not only is the script clunky as all hell — unfortunately, an ongoing problem with many of Sorkin's recent screenplays — but the story is attempting to make some sort of larger point that doesn't just fall flat but thuds directly to the floor. We already know social media makes everyone angry and insane, and we also know that social media has contributed to right-wing radicalization. Sorkin making a movie that beats us over the head with these two ideas and also ends in a full recreation of the January 6, 2021 insurrection is just as bad as it sounds in theory.

It's also incredible to me that Sorkin managed to cast a lot of great actors and coach them into giving some of the worst performances of their careers. Madison is an enigmatic and compelling performer, and Sorkin transforms her into the robotic Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen, a deeply unlikable person who doesn't seem to understand human behavior. Jeremy Allen White's journalist Jeff Horwitz is nothing but an exposition machine, and Jeremy Strong's Mark Zuckerberg has no interiority and sounds like Kermit the Frog. The only person who's good in this movie is Bill Burr. Think about that for a second.

"The Social Network" might be one of my very favorite movies of all time, but I can tell you, from a completely unbiased perspective, that "The Social Reckoning" is a wholly undeserving sequel to that 2010 masterpiece. It's clear now, with plenty of hindsight and movies like this, that "The Social Network" was good because of director David Fincher and despite Sorkin. To be fair to Sorkin, he basically admitted that to The Hollywood Reporter after "The Social Reckoning" got soundly panned.

"I would have rather David Fincher directed it — I would rather David Fincher direct everything — but David has an exclusive deal at Netflix, and this was owned by Sony," Sorkin told the outlet on their "Awards Chatter" podcast. Not only did Sorkin also admit that he's "very worried that the parts of directing that [he's] not good at are those parts that you can't learn," he also said, "I was surprised by how little of the science of filmmaking I'd managed to absorb [from other directors] ... I have no visual sensibility, it turns out."

I have to agree with him. Despite the same cinematographer — Jeff Cronenweth — working on both "Network" and "Reckoning," the sequel is visually bland, unimaginatively shot, and even recycles a couple reaction and establishing shots throughout its run time. Basically, "The Social Reckoning" is a poorly made film that I cannot in good conscience recommend; in fact, I'd recommend you just watch "The Social Network" instead. But if you're still interested, you can check out "The Social Reckoning" at home once it's available.

Yellowjackets is arguably one of the best Paramount+ shows, although it required fans to get a Paramount+ subscription including Showtime. I'm personally a hardcore fan who is hyped about the fourth and final season's premiere this month. Folks are hoping to have Yellowjackets' biggest mysteries solved before it ends its run, and hopefully joins the ranks of TV shows that actually ended well. We know that the series guards it secrets from the public, but it turns out that even the cast is left in the dark about spoilers.

Yellowjackets' cast is an incredible multi-generational ensemble who tell the story across two timelines. The pressure is on for the Emmy-nominated series to stick the landing, and provide answers about various long-standing mysteries. In a recent interview with ScreenRant, Teen Shauna actress Sophie Nélisse was asked if she knew her character's fate ahead of time, to which she said:

No, we actually don't get the scripts more than like a week in advance, which is kind of fun because on set we're all sort of plotting and trying to reflect on what we have. We were coming up with our own theories of what the finale was going to look like, but we had no idea how they were going to get rescued, how their time in the wilderness would end. I obviously knew that Shauna was going to get married because we saw that.

Well, my mind is blown. While Yellowjackets fans are being kept away from spoilers, I had no idea how tight the security was for even the cast. They only got each new script a week in advance, so Nélisse and her costars weren't able to use the full arc of their character to inform each performance. Instead they had to take things episode by episode and play each moment with honesty without looking ahead.

Fans have lingering questions about the No Eyed Man as well as the mystery involving Crystal's dead body. While we're still in the dark for now, so was the cast. The Heated Rivalry actress went on to say:

We just kind of went day by day with it. We were just always so excited when we got a new script because, as the audience feels when they finish an episode, it always kind of leaves us on a cliffhanger. That's how, whenever we read a script, we'd all message in the group chat, being like, ‘Oh, this one is so good! I love this bit, and I love that bit.’

Celebrities: sometimes they really are just like us. Despite being the actors bringing Yellowjackets to life, they were left with episode cliffhangers in the midst of shooting Season 4. I have to wonder if Sophie Nélisse and her co-stars even know all the twists that are coming with the show's final season on the air.

Yellowjackets Season 4 will premiere on November 20th as part of the 2026 TV schedule. The pressure is on for the drama series to stick the landing, but it looks like we'll get plenty of surprises in the final set of episodes.

#3441. ChatGPT's New GIF Generator Is Fun, but Won't Replace Us Humans (Yet)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

When it comes to generating AI images, both Gemini and ChatGPT do a passable job. In most cases, the results will look AI-generated, but they likely won’t have glaring spelling issues or missing limbs. Now, OpenAI is trying something new, introducing GIF support for ChatGPT. It's the company's first "moving images" feature since OpenAI shut down Sora, and while you can generate hyper-realistic videos in Gemini, this new ChatGPT feature is trying to fill in the gap, in a small way.

OpenAI is pitching the new feature as an animation tool, not exactly as a way to create looping videos—though that’s how I ended up using it. You give ChatGPT a prompt, as detailed as you can make it, and the chatbot produces a GIF in just a few seconds. You can start with your own drawings or images, too. ChatGPT uses sketches as the base for animations, though it can turn any still image into animated GIFs. Like other AI editing tools, you can edit it if ChatGPT didn't quite get it right: You can ask ChatGPT to make the GIF longer or shorter, remove certain objects, change the style, slow down transitions, among other edits.

AI art can be quite sterile, but I was surprised by how adding motion and animation to the mix makes generating images a lot more fun. Unlike traditional GIFs, which usually pull from existing video clips, you can turn anything you want into a GIF, which is especially cool if you're using your own art. In my testing, I found this to be the most rewarding part. It’s not always possible to one-shot a GIF with a single prompt. But after a few rounds of edits, I ended up creating some GIFs that I actually wanted to share in my WhatsApp groups.

That being said, I think human-made GIFs are still the gold standard here. For example, I asked ChatGPT to generate a video of someone brewing a pour-over, with a gooseneck kettle, showing the coffee blooming process. It did okay, but it’s nothing like actually making a pour-over. The kettle doesn’t move in circles, the water doesn’t rise evenly, there are no bubbles, and the steam is all over the place.

Compare that to the GIF below, which comes from a royalty-free video. Even though it’s a compressed, low-quality, and noisy GIF, it still shows the movement of the pour, the water rising, and even the bubbles. The details captured by a real video just aren’t there in ChatGPT GIFs. If that’s what you’re expecting, you will be disappointed. But I don't think that's the point of this feature anyway.

I found that ChatGPT excels when you’re making something fun, and you don’t look into the details too much. It pulled off a loop of a cat playing with a ball, and it was great at making a festive GIF for Diwali. It even made a GIF based on a photo. I asked it to create a fun promotional GIF for my JBL Bluetooth speakers, and it did the job quite well. At first, the transitions were too jarring, and the movement just made no sense. After some editing, though, I got it to a decent place.

Still, the main issue with ChatGPT GIFs is that complex movement and transitions aren’t nailed down. A hand shifts position weirdly between frames, and colors and objects appear out of nowhere. But if you can get over these issues, you can make some fun, lighthearted GIFs and memes to share with your friends on Instagram or WhatsApp.
